Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 1:

﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan) upon His servant, that he may be a warner to the worlds.﴾

This is a wondrous opening, rare in the speech of the eloquent Arabs, for most of their openings are either bare nouns, or nouns joined to a non-detached particle, such as the saying of Tarafa:

"For Khawla there are traces at Burqat Thahmad"

or with imperfect verbs and the like, such as the saying of Imru' al-Qays: "Halt, let us weep" (the verse in full), or with particles of emphasis, interrogation or alerting, such as (inna) "indeed," (qad) "certainly," the hamza of interrogation, and (hal) "is it not?" Of the same kind as this opening is the saying of al-Harith ibn Hilliza:

"Asma' has informed us of their separation"

and the saying of al-Nabigha:

"I concealed you by night at al-Jumumayn, wakeful, and two concerns, one hidden and one apparent."

With this rarity, the opening of this surah possesses the excellence of an exordium (bara'at al-matla'), for rarity is part of distinction (al-'izza), and distinction is among the beauties of expressions, whose opposite is vulgarity (al-ibtidhal).

"Tabaraka" means: its good is magnified and abundant, and by its good is meant its perfections and its transcendence (of every defect). It has been discussed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-A'raf: 54] in Surat al-A'raf.

And "al-baraka" is goodness. It has been discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you﴾ [Hud: 48] in Surat Hud, and at His saying: ﴿a greeting from Allah, blessed and good﴾ [al-Nur: 61] in Surat al-Nur.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion﴾ is that it is an informative statement about the greatness of Allah and the abundance of His perfections, so its purpose is instruction and awakening. It is also permissible that it be an indirect expression of producing praise of Allah, exalted is He, by which Allah has produced praise of Himself, like His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1], following the manner of Arabic speech in expressing wonder at the attributes of the speaker in a context of pride and greatness, or in showing marvels that have occurred, like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"And on the day I slaughtered my mount for the maidens, how marvellous is its saddle that I carry!"

He marvels only at his boldness in making the saddle of the mount, which he himself carries after slaughtering it. Of the same kind is the saying of al-Find al-Zimmani:

"O what a blow from an old man, great, decrepit, worn!"

He means a blow that he struck against his opponent.

The One who sent down the Criterion is Allah, exalted is He. Since the relative clause consists of attributes specific to Allah, exalted is He, the verb is as though attributed to the pronoun of the speaker, so it is as if it were said: "Blessed be (He)."

The relative pronoun indicates the cause of what precedes it, so it is an indirect expression of the magnification of the status of the Criterion and its blessing upon people, from His saying: ﴿that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾. That is a great favour which necessitates praise of Allah. It is also an indirect expression of the magnification of the status of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.

The definition by the relative pronoun here is because the relative clause consists of attributes of Allah in reality and in the view of the believers, and although the disbelievers deny them, they know that the Messenger proclaimed them, so Allah is known by them through these attributes, a knowledge by way of description, not by way of essence, which they deny.

"Al-Furqan" is the Qur'an, and it is originally a verbal noun of faraqa, as in His saying: ﴿And We did not send down upon Our servant on the Day of al-Furqan﴾ [al-Anfal: 41] and His saying: ﴿He will give you a criterion (furqanan)﴾ [al-Anfal: 29]. It was made a proper name by predominance for the Qur'an, because it distinguishes between truth and falsehood by what it clarifies of the proofs of truth and the refutation of falsehood. It has been discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ("And We sent down the Criterion") in Surat Al 'Imran.

The choice of the name al-Furqan to be mentioned here is to indicate that what will be mentioned of the proofs of God's oneness and of the sending down of the Qur'an are sound proofs which distinguish between truth and falsehood.

The description of the Prophet as ﴿His servant﴾ brings him near and prepares for the refutation of their demand of him in His saying: ﴿And they said: "What is this Messenger that he eats food?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], and what follows.

By "al-'alamin" is meant all the nations of mankind, because "al-'alam" is applied to the genus, the species and the category, according to what the context permits, and warning is only for rational beings who are addressed with obligation. The discussion of the word "al-'alamin" has already passed in Surat al-Fatiha.

"Al-Nadhir" is one who informs of an evil that will befall, and it is fa'il in the sense of mef'il in the form of the active participle, like "al-Hakim." The restriction in describing the Messenger here to the warner, without the bringer of good tidings, as in His saying: ﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [Saba': 28], is because the context here is the threatening of the polytheists, since they denied the Qur'an and the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. So it required mentioning warning rather than good tidings, and in that there is sufficiency, because good tidings come to the mind of the hearer when warning is mentioned. And it will come: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [al-Furqan: 56] in this surah.

In this verse he combined the exaltation of the status of the Qur'an, that it was sent down from Allah, with the exaltation of the status of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, the elevation of his rank with Allah, and the universality of his mission.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 2:

﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, who has not taken a son, and who has no partner in the dominion, and who created everything and determined it precisely.﴾

Page 318
These four attributes are applied to the Name of God, Exalted, in the manner of the relative construction (ta'rif al-mawsuliyyah), because some of the attributes (sila) are known to the addressees as belonging to God, namely the first and the fourth attributes. Since these two were known, the two other attributes mentioned along with them are treated as known as well, because they are applied to the one who is known through the first and fourth attributes. The polytheists did not doubt that God is the owner of the heavens and the earth, nor that God is the creator of everything, as in His saying: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the mighty Throne? They will say: "God."﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 86], and the verses that follow in Surah al-Mu'minun. However, they attributed to God a son and a partner in the dominion.

Among the eloquent features of the arrangement is that the two disputed attributes, along with them, were placed in the middle between the two attributes about which there is no doubt, so that the two accepted attributes serve as the premise at the beginning and the conclusion at the end. For the One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth is not fitting to take a son or to take a partner, because His great dominion requires His absolute self-sufficiency (ghina), and so taking a son or a partner would require it to be purposeless (abath), since it would have no end. And if the actions of rational people are protected from being purposeless, how much more so the actions of the Most Wise of the wise, exalted and sanctified is He.

So His saying: ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿He who sent down the Criterion﴾ [al-Furqan: 1].

The repetition of the relative pronoun is due to the difference in the purpose of the two attributes: the first attribute serves the purpose of the favour of sending down the Qur'an as guidance, and the second attribute serves the purpose of describing God, Exalted, with unity (wahdaniyyah).

In "the dominion" there is an allusion that sharing in dominion contradicts the complete reality of dominion, which is not fitting for Him other than it.

And al-khalq (creation) means origination (al-ijad), i.e., He brought into existence every existent, from the greatest of things to the smallest. And His saying ﴿and created everything and determined it precisely﴾ is a consequence of ﴿created everything﴾, because it is evidence of perfection in creation, a perfection which indicates that the Creator is characterized by the attributes of perfection.

Page 319
The meaning of (qaddarahu) is that He made it according to a measure and a specific limit, not merely by coincidence; i.e., He created it determined, that is, firm, precise, and suitable for what it was created for, without any disparity or defect in it. This implies that He created it by will and knowledge, in a manner that He willed and specified, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have created everything in measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49]. It has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17] in Surah al-Ra'd. The emphasis of the verb by the absolute object with His saying (taqdiran) indicates that it is a complete determination within the category of determinations.

What has come from the beginning of the surah up to here is an excellent opening (bara'at istihlal) that introduces its purposes, and it functions as the preamble (khutbah) of a book or a letter.

[p. 320]

This is a digression taken up to seize the opportunity to describe the misguidance of the polytheists and the baseness of their thinking. It is coordinated with the clause ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Furqan: 2] and what follows it, which is an argument for His sole divinity. It is followed by His words, ﴿and He created everything﴾ [al-Furqan: 2], which covers the fact that what they took as gods are created beings. Thus what preceded prepares for a wonder at the polytheists' taking gods besides that God, who is described with the attributes of perfection and majesty.

The statement is therefore not intended to convey information. It is meant to express wonder at their condition: how they met the blessing of the sending down of the Furqan with denial and rebellion, and how they associated with the One who has these attributes other gods whose attributes are the opposite of those of the One they associated with Him. Otherwise, the fact that the polytheists take gods is already known to them and to the believers, so the statement is not aimed at informing them of the ruling it contains.

Between His words ﴿and He has not taken a son﴾ [al-Furqan: 2] and His words ﴿and they have taken, besides Him, gods﴾ there is a *tibaq* (antithesis), which is a rhetorical embellishment.

The pronoun in *ittakhadhū* (they took) refers to the polytheists, though they have not been mentioned previously in the discourse. They are known in such a context, especially from His words ﴿and He has no partner in the dominion﴾ [al-Furqan: 2].

The clause ﴿they do not create anything﴾ corresponds to the clause ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Furqan: 2]. The clause ﴿while they are created﴾ corresponds to the clause ﴿and He has not taken a son﴾ [al-Furqan: 2], because the son of the Creator must be begotten of Him, and so he cannot be created.

The clause ﴿and they have no power to harm or benefit themselves﴾ corresponds to the clause ﴿and He has no partner in the dominion﴾ [al-Furqan: 2], because partnership in dominion entails partnership in disposal (of affairs).

The pronoun in *li-anfusihim* (for themselves) may refer to *ālihah* (gods), meaning that the idols and the like cannot bring harm upon themselves or benefit themselves. It may also refer to what the pronoun in *ittakhadhū* refers to, meaning that the idols cannot benefit those who worshipped them or harm them.

Know that *ḍurran wa-lā naf'an* (harm nor benefit) here functions as an idiom, used to intend comprehensiveness regarding circumstances. It is as if it were said: they have no power to dispose of any circumstance whatsoever. This is like saying *sharqan wa-gharban* (east and west), or *laylan wa-nahāran* (night and day). By this, what might seem problematic at first glance is resolved: the negation of their power to harm themselves is not an issue, since no one's will is directed toward harming his own self. For the same reason, there is no need to seek a reason for placing harm before benefit, because the context calls for equality in placing either of the two first. The speaker is free in this, and the variation in the order between the verses is merely a matter of stylistic variety (*tafannun*).

The prepositional phrase *li-anfusihim* is related to *yamlikūna* (they have power).

*Ḍurr* (with a fatha on the ḍād) is a verbal noun of *darrahu*, meaning he afflicted him with something disagreeable. A parallel to it has already occurred in His words, ﴿Say: I have no power to harm or benefit myself except as God wills﴾ [Yunus: 49], in Surat Yunus.

The clause ﴿and they have no power over death, nor life, nor resurrection﴾ corresponds to the clause ﴿and He created everything and determined it with precise measure﴾ [al-Furqan: 2], because the greatest manifestations of the determining of creation are the manifestations of life and death, and these are among the things observed. As for His words ﴿nor resurrection﴾, it completes the rebuke of the polytheists who deny resurrection, because the negation that the gods have power over resurrection entails the affirmation of the reality of resurrection in fact, since in the speech of the Arabs it is most common that the negation of a thing entails the establishment of its essence. As for such a statement as the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*'alā lāḥibin lā yuhtadā bi-manārihi*
*On a faded track whose signposts give no guidance,*

he means: there are no signposts in it. And as for the words of Ibn Aḥmar:

*lā tufzi'u al-arnaba ahwāluhā ∗∗∗ wa-lā tarā al-ḍabba bihā yanjaḥiru*
*Its terrors do not frighten the hare, nor do you see the dhabb lizard creep into it,*

he means: there is no hare in it, nor any dhabb lizard. This belongs to the category of *tamlīḥ* (allusive wit).

In this verse, among their statements, is mentioned the contrast to the sentences with which God is described, out of concern to refute their disbelief concerning God's attributes, because that is the root and foundation of disbelief.

Know that the meaning of ﴿and they are created﴾ is "and they are made," that is, they are fashioned by makers, because all their idols are hewn stones, so craftsmanship has shaped them. Thus the word *khalq* (creation) is applied to shaping and carving by human action, although *khalq* has become common for bringing into existence after non-existence. This usage is either in consideration of the original root meaning of *khalq*, which is the measuring of the amount of a hide before cutting it, as Zuhayr said:

*wa-la'anta tafrī mā khalaqta wa-ba'ḍu al-nāsi yakhluqu thumma lā yafrī*
*Indeed you cut what you have measured, while some people measure and do not cut.*

So *khalq* is applied to carving, either as a metonymy (*majāz mursal*), or as a *mushākala* (figure of association) with His words ﴿they do not create anything﴾.

The verb *yamlikūna* (they have power) in His words "*lā yamlikūna*" is used in the sense of ability and capacity, as has already been mentioned in His words, ﴿Say: who has power against God in anything, if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 17], in Surat al-'Uqud, and His words in it: ﴿Say: Do you worship, besides God, that which has no power to harm or benefit you?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 76], meaning: that which has no ability to harm you or benefit you. So His words here, "*li-anfusihim*" (for themselves), are related to "*yamlikūna*," and the *lām* in it is the *lām* of causation, meaning they have no power for the sake of themselves, that is, for their benefit.

Furthermore, the intended meaning of "*anfusihim*" (themselves) may be that the plural there is in consideration of distribution over the individuals implied by the pronoun in "*yamlikūna*," meaning that each one of them has no power to bring harm or benefit to himself. The intended meaning of "*ḍurr*" would then be averting it, with an elided *muḍāf* (a governed noun) understood from the context, because a person's concern does not center on harm to his own self such that he would be rebuked for being unable to harm himself.

The indefiniteness of "*mawtan wa-ḥayātan*" (death and life) in the context of negation is for generality, meaning neither the death nor the life of anyone among people.

*Nushūr* (resurrection) means bringing back to life after death. Its root meaning is the spreading out of a folded thing.

The commentary shifts from mentioning their disbelief in their deeds to mentioning their disbelief in their false statements.

The pronoun here serves to show that the content of the relative clause is the cause of this saying of theirs. That is, what emboldened them to this calumny was only their polytheism and their obstinacy in it, not any doubt that prompted them to this claim, since there is no such doubt. This differs from what was mentioned just before, their disbelief in God, for they received that from their fathers. So the attribute applied to them here suits their statement, because it is the root of their disbelief.

This sentence corresponds to the sentence ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan: 1]. It is therefore the purpose of the opening of the discourse, as the opening of the surah indicates. The sentence that corresponds to the first sentence was delayed, although the apparent requirement of correspondence was that it be mentioned before the sentence ﴿and they have taken, besides Him, gods﴾ [al-Furqan: 3], out of concern for refuting the disbelief related to the attributes of God, as was mentioned just before.

The restriction contained in their statement, derived from the negative ﴿in﴾ and the exception ﴿illa﴾, is a restriction by reversal (qasr qalb). By it they intended to reject the claim that the Qur'an was sent down from God.

Among those who made this statement were al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abd Allah ibn Umayya, and Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid. The attribution of this statement to all the disbelievers is because it occurred among them and all of them were passing it on. This is a familiar manner of attributing an act to a tribe, as one says: "The Banu Asad killed Hujr."

The demonstrative referring to the Qur'an is a quotation of their words when they hear the verses of the Qur'an.

The pronoun of the subject in ﴿fa-tarahu﴾ refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), known from his words ﴿upon His servant﴾.

Al-ifk means falsehood. It was discussed at the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who brought the slander﴾ [al-Nur: 11] in Surat al-Nur. Al-iftira' means fabricating reports, that is, inventing them, and it is lying deliberately. It was discussed at His words: ﴿But those who disbelieve invent lies against God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103] in Surat al-'Uqud.

﴿And others assisted him in it﴾: that is, other people assisted him in what he says of the Qur'an by teaching him some of what he says. By "the other people" they meant the Jews. This interpretation was narrated from Mujahid and from Ibn 'Abbas: they pointed to four Persian slaves who belonged to the Arabs, namely: Addas, a freedman of Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza; Yasar, Abu Fukayha al-Rumi, a freedman of al-'Ala' ibn al-Hadrami; and in the Sira of Ibn Hisham it is said that he was a freedman of Safwan ibn Umayya ibn Muharrith; and Jabr, a freedman of Amir. These were among the clients of Quraysh in Mecca, who adhered to Christianity and knew something of the Torah and the Gospel, and then embraced Islam. This has passed in Surat al-Nahl. The polytheists therefore claimed that the Messenger (ﷺ) used to visit these men secretly and draw from them reports of what is in the Torah and the Gospel.

The restriction derived from His words ﴿This is nothing but a falsehood he has invented, and others have helped him with it﴾ governs both sentences together. That is, this Qur'an cannot be free of the combination of the two matters: that he fabricated part of it from himself, and that a people assisted him with part of it.

On the basis of the narration of their statement, it follows that they committed by their statement an injustice (zulm) and a falsehood (zur), because when they said that, it became evident that their statement was falsehood and injustice, since it is invention and transgression.

The word ﴿jā'ū﴾ (they have committed) is used with the meaning of "they did." It is a metaphor (majaz) for attentiveness to the deed and intending it, because whoever is concerned with achieving something goes toward it. By this usage its transitivity to an object is valid, as in this verse.

Al-zulm is transgression against the right without justification, by speech or by action. The Exalted said: ﴿He said, "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe be added to his ewes"﴾ [Sad: 24].

It was discussed at His words: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114] in Surat al-Baqarah. The injustice they committed is their attribution to the Messenger (ﷺ) of invention, since it is a transgression against his right, which is truthfulness.

Al-zur is falsehood. The best that has been said about al-zur is that it is a falsehood made attractive and disguised so that it resembles truth.

That their statement is a lie is evident, because it contradicts reality. The Qur'an contains nothing of fabrication, and those whom they claimed to be assisting him are not able, any one of them, to produce speech in Arabic that reaches the utmost eloquence and rises to the level of inimitability. And if some of them had knowledge of some reports of the messengers, that knowledge is only meagre and unverified, like the knowledge of the common people and the masses.

[Page 325]

The pronoun refers to "those who disbelieved." The relative clause (*silah*, the clause that completes a preceding relative pronoun) is taken into account in this pronoun, as a hint that this statement is one of the effects of their disbelief.

*Asatir* (أساطير) is the plural of *ustura* (أسطورة), with the hamza vowelled with a *damma*, like *uhdutha* and *ahadith*, and *ughluta* and *aghalit*. It means a narrated story (*al-qissa al-mastura*). Its meaning was explained in detail under the verse "until, when they come to you disputing with you, those who disbelieve say: 'This is nothing but the fables of the ancients'" [al-An'am: 25] in Surah al-An'am. The one who made this statement was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith al-'Abdari, who said: "The Qur'an is stories from the stories of the past." This al-Nadr had learned in al-Hirah the stories of the kings of Persia and the tales of Rustam and Isfandiyar. He would say to Quraysh: "By God, O assembly of Quraysh, I am better at storytelling than Muhammad (ﷺ), so come, let me tell you," and he would say about the Qur'an: "It is the fables of the ancients." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Whatever is mentioned in the Qur'an as 'the fables of the ancients' is intended to refer to the statement of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith." This has been mentioned in Surah al-An'am and at the beginning of Surah Yusuf.

The clause *iktatabaha* (اكْتَتَبَها) is a descriptive (*na't*) or circumstantial (*hal*) clause modifying *asatir al-awwalin*.

*Iktitab* (الِاكْتِتابُ) is a form VIII verbal noun derived from *kitaba* (writing). The *iftiʿal* pattern indicates effort or exertion in bringing about the action, so the phrase *iktatabaha* means that he took pains to have it written. The meaning of this effort is that the Prophet (ﷺ), since he was unlettered (*ummi*), the attribution of writing to him is a metaphorical attribution (*isnad majazi*). The meaning therefore becomes: he asked someone to write it for him, that is, to transcribe it. Thus the attribution of *iktitab* to him is metaphorical, because he was its cause. The indication (*qarina*) is what is established for everyone, that he was unlettered and did not write, and from the words "so it is dictated to him," for if he had written it for himself, he would have read it himself. The meaning is that he had it copied. All of this is a quotation of al-Nadr's statement, either in his words or in its meaning. al-Nadr's purpose in this description was to market his slander, because he knew that this falsehood is obvious and might not be accepted by people, given their knowledge that the Prophet was unlettered. So how could he derive his Qur'an from the books of the ancients? Therefore, to make it acceptable, he claimed that it had been written down for him, so he took it as his own, and he hands it over to someone who is skilled at reading, and he dictates to him what the Qur'an recounts.

*Imla'* (الإمْلاءُ) means *imlal*, which is the delivery of speech to someone who writes its words, or narrates them, or memorizes them. The connection of *imla'* to *iktitab* is made in view of the fact that dictating them to him was so that he could read them or memorize them.

*Bukra* (البُكْرَةُ) is the beginning of the day, and *asil* (الأصِيلُ) is the end of the evening. This was mentioned in the verse "in the mornings and the evenings" [al-A'raf: 205] at the end of Surah al-A'raf. That is, it is dictated to him at both ends of the day. This is used figuratively (*kinaya*) to express the great frequency of practice in receiving the fables.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 6:**

﴿Say: He has sent it down who knows the secret within the heavens and the earth. Indeed, He is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

God taught His Messenger the answer to refute the slander of those who said: "This Qur'an is nothing but a fabrication, and it is the myths of the ancients," [claiming] that God sent it down upon His Messenger.

(Page 326)

He expressed the one who sent down the Qur'an by means of the relative form (al-mawsul), because of what the relative clause requires: a call upon the Messenger to bear witness to God regarding what is in his secret, since God knows every secret in every place. Thus the relative clause is used for its necessary implication, which is that the speaker, i.e., the Messenger, knows this. In this there is a metonymy (kinaya) for his being mindful of God in what he conveys from Him. In this also is an awakening for them, so that they would reflect upon what they claimed to be a fabrication or the myths of the ancients, in order that its inclusion of clear truths, which none encompasses except God, the One who knows the secret, might become evident to them. Then they would be certain that the Qur'an can only be from His sending down, and they would know the innocence of the Messenger ﷺ from seeking help from those whom they claimed were assisting him.

The definite article in (al-sirr) is the definite article of genus, encompassing every secret, and among them is the concealed speech of those who revile the Qur'an out of arrogance and slander, i.e., He knows that they say about the Qur'an what they do not believe, through injustice and falsehood on their part. By this, the placement of the clause (﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾) is understood as an encouragement for them to desist from this arrogance and to follow the religion of truth, so that God may forgive them and have mercy upon them. This is an implicit warning that if they do not desist and repent, then wrath and retribution are due upon them.

**[Page 327]**

This is a transition from relating their criticisms of the Qur'an and refuting them to relating their criticisms of the Messenger ﷺ.

The pronoun refers to "those who disbelieved," so the implied meaning of the description is taken into account, as was explained earlier.

They stated their criticism of the Prophet's ﷺ prophethood in the form of a question about a condition specific to him. They used the interrogative particle and the *lam* of specificity (*lam al-ikhtisas*), along with the circumstantial clause whose content is the subject of the question.

The question is an *ta'ajjubi* interrogative (a question expressing wonder), used to imply its consequence, which is the invalidity of his being a messenger. This rests on the premise that wondering at a claim implies that it is impossible or false. The construction *ma li-hadha* and similar forms indicate a question about something that is established for him. So the interrogative word is the subject (*mubtada'*) and *li-hadha* is its predicate. Thus the subject of the question in this verse is the established condition of eating food and walking in the markets for the one who claims to be a messenger from God.

The clause *yakulu al-ta'am* ("he eats food") is a circumstantial clause (*jumlat hal*). Their phrase *li-hadha al-Rasul* ("this Messenger") ascribes to him the attribute of messengership in a manner of going along with his own claim, though they do not believe in it. They built upon it so that the wonder could be formed, and what is meant by it is denial and invalidation.

The demonstrative refers to something present in the mind, and the demonstrative is clarified by what follows it: the noun defined by the *lam* of prior reference (*lam al-ahd*), namely *al-Rasul*.

They used eating food and walking in the markets as euphemisms for being similar to people in their circumstances, as a pretext for invalidating his being a messenger. They claimed that a messenger from God must have circumstances unlike those of people. They specifically mentioned eating food and walking in the markets because these are observable, recurring conditions. God responded to this claim with His words: ﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾ [al-Furqan: 20]. Then they moved on to proposing things that would confirm his message, saying: ﴿Why has no angel been sent down to him so that he might be a warner with him?﴾ They singled out from the Messenger's circumstances the condition of warning, because it is what stirred up their resentment against him.

*Lawla* is a particle of urging (*harf tahdid*) used for challenge (*ta'jiz*), meaning: if an angel were sent down to him, we would follow him.

*Fa-yakuna* is in the accusative as an answer to the urging.

*Aw* ("or") indicates choice among the proofs of the message, in their own imagination.

**[Page 328]**

The meaning of ﴿A treasure be thrown down to him﴾ [al-Furqan: 8] is: a treasure be sent down to him from heaven, since wealth was a temptation to their hearts. *Al-ilqa'* means throwing, and here it is used metaphorically for giving from God's presence, because they imagine God, exalted is He, to be in heaven.

The word *kanz* (treasure) was discussed earlier in His words, exalted is He: ﴿that they might say, "Why has no treasure been sent down to him?"﴾ [Hud: 12], in Surat Hud. They made the granting of a garden to him a sign of prophethood, because the existence of a garden in Makkah is something extraordinary.

The majority of reciters read ﴿he eats from it﴾ [al-Furqan: 8] with the *ya'* of the third person masculine, and the implicit pronoun refers to *hadha al-Rasul* ("this Messenger").

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read ﴿we eat from it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 113] with the *nun* of the plural. The meaning is that they would be certain its fruit is real and not magic.

The historians (*ashab al-siyar*) mentioned that this statement was made by the leaders of the polytheists, in a gathering they held with the Messenger of God ﷺ, which brought together 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, Shayba ibn Rabi'a, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, Abu al-Bakhtari, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, Zam'a ibn al-Aswad, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, Umayya ibn Khalaf, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, al-'As ibn Wa'il, Nubayh ibn al-Hajjaj, Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. They also mentioned that these things they said were circulated among the attendees of the gathering, since the historians did not specify who said them.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "They spread this among the people, and this verse was revealed concerning it." Something of this has already been mentioned in Surat al-Isra'.

The *lam* of *ma li-hadha* was written separately from the demonstrative noun that follows it in the Imam codex (*al-Mushaf al-Imam*), and the copies followed it, because the orthography of the codex is a precedent in it. The same was done in ﴿What is with this Book that it leaves neither small nor great [deed] unrecorded?﴾ [al-Kahf: 49] in Surat al-Kahf; in ﴿What is the matter with those who disbelieve, rushing towards you with necks outstretched?﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 36] in Surat Sa'ala sa'il; and in ﴿What is the matter with these people?﴾ [al-Nisa': 78] in Surat al-Nisa'. Perhaps the reason for this separation is that it is an ancient orthographic practice in which letters were written separately from one another, especially particles of meaning. They treated what consisted of a single letter the same as what consisted of two letters. Some remnant of this was preserved at the hand of one of the scribes of the codex. The original form of all Arabic letters is separation, and so it is in the ancient scripts of the Arabs and others. Joining the letters of a single word was an embellishment of the script and a facilitation of the meaning's immediate understanding. As for what consisted of two words, joining it was a matter of convention. Most of what they joined were words consisting of a single letter, such as the particles of oath, or words that were like a single letter, such as *al-* (the definite article).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 25, verses 8–9:**

( ﴿And the wrongdoers say, "You follow none but a man bewitched."﴾ ﴿See how they strike similitudes for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.﴾ .

**الظّالِمُونَ** (al-zalimun, "the wrongdoers"): they are the polytheists (al-mushrikun). He changed their earlier designation to the designation of wrongdoing, **وهم هم** ("and they are they"), as an alert that this saying is an aggression against the Messenger (ﷺ) by slandering him with what he is free of, while they know that he is not like that. Therefore their wronging of him is the gravest wrong. (ﷺ)

Al-Mawardi mentioned that the speaker of "﴿You follow none but a man bewitched﴾" was Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara. That is, he was the originator of this calumny. The saying was attributed to all the wrongdoers because they seized upon it and kept repeating it.

**al-mashur** (al-masḥur, "the bewitched"): the one afflicted by sorcery, which, in their view, causes disorder of the intellect. That is, "You follow none but a man whose reason has been disturbed, so he says what sensible people would not say."

By mentioning **رَجُلًا** (rajulan, "a man") here, they prepared the ground for the impossibility of his being a messenger, since he is a man among men. This address was directed at the Muslims who followed the Prophet (ﷺ).

The meaning of **﴿See how they strike similitudes for you, so they have gone astray﴾**: they struck false similitudes for you by likening you to a bewitched man.

The word **انْظُرْ** (unzur, "see") is used figuratively for the sense of knowing, comparing an intelligible matter to a visible one because of its great clarity. **كَيْفَ** (kayfa, "how") is a noun denoting manner and condition, here stripped of the sense of interrogation.

Following on from this expression of wonder, there is a report about them that they went astray in fabricating attacks on the Messenger's mission. They followed paths that do not lead them to a convincing proof for their aim. So the verb **ضَلُّوا** (dallu, "they have gone astray") is used in both of its figurative senses: the sense of failing to achieve soundness in argument, and the sense of failing to reach the true religion. Here it is an expression of wonder at their folly and a turning away from answering them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 10:

﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow, and He will give you palaces.﴾

The surah opens by glorifying Allah and praising Him for having sent down the Furqan (the Criterion) upon His Messenger. It then follows this with the reception that the polytheists gave to this favour: denial and rejection, arising from their adherence to what they had taken as gods, whose attributes include what is incompatible with divinity. Then they slandered the Qur'an and the one who brought it, with what amounts to ingratitude for the blessing and for the one who brought it.

When the aim became turning away from their falsehood and turning towards addressing the Messenger, to strengthen him and the believers, the words with which the surah began were repeated, in the manner of connecting speech, with His saying: (﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that﴾).

This sentence is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) occupying the place of an answer to their saying: (﴿Or he be given a garden﴾ [al-Furqan: 8]) and so on. That is, if He wills, He will give you better than what they proposed, i.e. more excellent than it, namely, if He wills, He will hasten it for you in this world. The reference is to what was mentioned in their saying. It is therefore possible that what is meant by the gardens and palaces are gardens in this world and palaces therein, i.e. better than what they proposed as evidence of your truthfulness in their claim: a number of gardens with palaces among them. On this interpretation the majority of the exegetes have explained it. On this interpretation, the conditional (in) takes the place of (law), i.e. He did not will it, and had He willed it He would have done it; but wisdom required not expanding provision for the Messenger in this world, and the polytheists do not perceive lofty aims.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that what is meant by the gardens and palaces are not those of this world; that is, they are the gardens of eternity and the palaces of Paradise, and so it is a promise from Allah to His Messenger.

The coupling of this promise with the condition of His will accords with what the divine majesty requires; otherwise the context of the promise requires certainty of its fulfilment, for Allah certainly wills that. It could be said: Blessed is He who has given you better than that. Thus the position of (if He wills) is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD).

The original meaning is: Blessed is He who has given you better than that, gardens and so on to the end. This is supported by the recitation of Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim: (wa yaj'alu laka qusuran) with the verb (yaj'alu) in the nominative, as a resumptive statement without the conditional particle operating; whereas the recitation of most readers is with the jussive, in coordination with the conditional verb. The conditional verb is certain to occur by the context. This interpretation is more forceful in rebuking the polytheists and cutting off their disputation. Its indication is His saying after it: (﴿Nay, they denied the Hour, and We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blaze﴾ [al-Furqan: 11]), which is the opposite and counterpart of what He has prepared for His Messenger and the believers.

The qusur (palaces) are great, spacious structures upon the face of the earth. It has been mentioned earlier in His saying: (﴿You take from its plains palaces﴾ [al-A'raf: 74]) in Surat al-A'raf, and in His saying: (﴿and a lofty palace﴾ [al-Hajj: 45]) in Surat al-Hajj.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 11:

﴿Nay, but they denied the Hour. And We have prepared a blazing fire for those who deny the Hour.﴾

(Bal) is used for iḍrāb (a turning away, a change of subject). It may be an iḍrāb of transition (intiqāl) from mention of their misguidance regarding the attributes of the Messenger ﷺ to mention of their misguidance in denying resurrection, according to the interpretation of the majority of the scholars of the statement of Him (Exalted), ﴿If He wills, He will assign to you better than that﴾ [al-Furqan: 10], as has already been discussed.

It may also be an iḍrāb of nullification (ibṭāl) of what is contained in His statement, ﴿If He wills, He will assign to you better than that﴾ [al-Furqan: 10], according to the interpretation of Ibn 'Atiyya that it is a promise of giving him that in the Hereafter. That is: "Nay, they are not content that the Messenger's portion with his Lord is not in the fleeting, base enjoyments of this world, but rather in the everlasting, endless good things of the Hereafter." That is, this is a refutation of them and a persuasion to them, had they believed in the Hour; but they denied it, so they persist in their misguidance and arguments do not persuade them.

Al-Sa'a (the Hour) is a name that came to be applied to the world of eternity, named after its starting point, which is the Hour of Resurrection (sa'at al-ba'th). He restricted their denial to the Hour only because they denied resurrection, and so their denial of what lies beyond it is even more certain.

The clause ﴿And We have prepared a blazing fire for those who deny the Hour﴾ is an interjected (mu'taridah) threat against them. Its generality includes the polytheists under discussion, so it is a tadhyil (a concluding addition). Among its purposes is the contrast between what Allah has prepared for the believers in the final outcome and what He has prepared for the polytheists.

Al-sa'ir (the blaze) is intense burning. It is of the form fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, that is, maswur (kindled), meaning that fuel has been added to it. It is treated as masculine because it pertains to the states of flame. It has been mentioned in His statement (Exalted), ﴿Whenever it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾ [al-Isra: 97], in Surah al-Isra. It may also be used as a proper name for Jahannam by dominance, and this is by elision of a modifier, that is, "one possessing a blaze" (dhat sa'ir).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verses 12–14:

﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they will hear its raging and roaring.﴾ ﴿And when they are thrown into it, bound together in a narrow place, they will call out there for destruction.﴾ ﴿Do not call out today for one destruction; call out for many destructions.﴾

This transitions from the despair of their conviction to the description of the blazing Fire prepared for them. The pronoun in (ra'athum, "it saw them"), referring to the Fire, is feminine because the Fire is interpreted as Jahannam (Hell), which is its specific name by predominance, as was mentioned earlier.

Attributing seeing to the Fire is a metaphor (isti'arah). The meaning is: when they are driven toward it and find themselves at a place from which the one who reaches it can be seen, they hear from it raging (taghayyuz) and roaring (zafir) from a distant place. It is also possible that the meaning of "it saw them" is that its angels saw them; they release its outlets, so its tongues of flame burst forth with sounds like the sounds of one who is enraged and his roaring. In that case, attributing seeing to Jahannam is an intellectual metaphor (majaz 'aqli).

Taghayyuz (raging) means the intensity of rage (ghayz). Ghayz is intense anger. It was discussed earlier at the words (﴿They bite their fingertips at you out of rage (al-ghayz)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119]) in Surat Al 'Imran. The form tafa''ul here, which in origin signifies effort in performing an action, is used figuratively to denote its intensity, since one who makes an effort at an action performs it with the greatest possible force.

The intended meaning here is the sound of one who is enraged, as indicated by its connection to the verb (sami'u, "they heard"), so this is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh).

Zafir is the prolonging of breath from intense rage and constriction of the chest, i.e., a sound like zafir, so this is also an eloquent simile. It is also possible that God has created in Jahannam a perception of visible things, such that its states intensify when visible things are imprinted upon it, so it churns, surges, and prepares to devour its inhabitants, and from it arise sounds of raging and roaring. In that case, attributing seeing, raging, and roaring to it is literal, and the affairs of the other world are not measured by the conditions familiar in this world.

In accordance with these two possibilities is understood what has come in the Qur'an and the hadith, such as the words of the Exalted: (﴿On the Day We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ [Qaf: 30]), and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Fire complained to its Lord and said, 'My Lord, some of me has consumed others of me.' So He permitted it two breaths: a breath in summer and a breath in winter." Narrated in the Muwatta'. Muslim's narration adds: "What you feel of the intensity of cold is from its zamharir (extreme cold), and what you feel of the intensity of heat is from its samum (scorching wind)."

Their being driven to the Fire from a distant place is mentioned as an increase in their torment, because the distance of the place requires greater hardship in reaching it and prolongs the terror from what they hear.

He describes their arrival at Jahannam from a distant place and their being placed in it with His words: (﴿And when they are thrown into it, bound together in a narrow place, they will call out there for destruction.﴾). Its composition takes the form of describing the clamor of the people of the Fire from His words (﴿they will call out there for destruction﴾), and in the course of that it incorporates a description of the interior of Jahannam and the description of the placement of the polytheists in it, through His words (﴿a narrow place﴾) and His words (muqarranin, "bound together"), as a variation in the style of speech.

Al-ilqa' (throwing) means casting down, and here it is a metonymy (kinayah) for humiliation.

Makanan (a place) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, i.e., "in a narrow place."

The majority read (đayyiqan) with a shadda on the yaa'. Ibn Kathir read (đayqan) with the yaa' sukun. Both serve to intensify the description, like mayyit and mayt; the form with the shadda indicates that the quality is firmly established in the thing described, while the form with sukun is a description by way of the verbal noun.

Muqarranin is a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in (ulqu, "they are thrown"), i.e., with some of them bound to others, like the condition of captives and prisoners, in which a number of them are bound in a single chain, as He said: (﴿and others bound together in shackles﴾ [Sad: 38]). Muqarran means maqrun, and the form of tafil was used for it to indicate the intensity of the binding.

Ad-du'a' is calling out with the loudest voice, and ath-thubur is destruction. That is, they cry out, "Woe to us!" (ya thubura-na), or "Woe to me!" (wa thubura-h) in the form of lamentation. On both possibilities, the calling is a metonymy for wishing, i.e., they wish for destruction to come, so they call upon it as one calls for someone whose presence is sought, or they lament it as one laments someone whose loss is felt, meaning they wish for destruction in order to be relieved from terrible punishment.

The clause (﴿Do not call out today for one destruction; call out for many destructions﴾) and to its end is a saying with an omitted speaker, i.e., it is said to them. Describing destruction as "many" is either because of the multiplicity of its calling through repetition, which is a metonymy for the non-attainment of destruction, since calling ends when the one called upon is present, or it is despair that requires repeating the wish or the lament.

Their being driven to the Fire from a distant place is mentioned as an increase in their torment, because the distance of the place requires greater hardship in reaching it and prolongs the terror from what they hear.

He describes their arrival at Jahannam from a distant place and their being placed in it with His words: (﴿And when they are thrown into it, bound together in a narrow place, they will call out there for destruction.﴾). Its composition takes the form of describing the clamor of the people of the Fire from His words (﴿they will call out there for destruction﴾), and in the course of that it incorporates a description of the interior of Jahannam and the description of the placement of the polytheists in it, through His words (﴿a narrow place﴾) and His words (muqarranin, "bound together"), as a variation in the style of speech.

Al-ilqa' (throwing) means casting down, and here it is a metonymy (kinayah) for humiliation.

Makanan (a place) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, i.e., "in a narrow place."

The majority read (đayyiqan) with a shadda on the yaa'. Ibn Kathir read (đayqan) with the yaa' sukun. Both serve to intensify the description, like mayyit and mayt; the form with the shadda indicates that the quality is firmly established in the thing described, while the form with sukun is a description by way of the verbal noun.

Muqarranin is a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in (ulqu, "they are thrown"), i.e., with some of them bound to others, like the condition of captives and prisoners, in which a number of them are bound in a single chain, as He said: (﴿and others bound together in shackles﴾ [Sad: 38]). Muqarran means maqrun, and the form of tafil was used for it to indicate the intensity of the binding.

Ad-du'a' is calling out with the loudest voice, and ath-thubur is destruction. That is, they cry out, "Woe to us!" (ya thubura-na), or "Woe to me!" (wa thubura-h) in the form of lamentation. On both possibilities, the calling is a metonymy for wishing, i.e., they wish for destruction to come, so they call upon it as one calls for someone whose presence is sought, or they lament it as one laments someone whose loss is felt, meaning they wish for destruction in order to be relieved from terrible punishment.

The clause (﴿Do not call out today for one destruction; call out for many destructions﴾) and to its end is a saying with an omitted speaker, i.e., it is said to them. Describing destruction as "many" is either because of the multiplicity of its calling through repetition, which is a metonymy for the non-attainment of destruction, since calling ends when the one called upon is present, or it is despair that requires repeating the wish or the lament.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verses 15–16:

﴿Say: Is that better, or the Garden of eternity which the God-fearing have been promised? It shall be a reward and a final destination for them.﴾ ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, abiding forever. It is a promise incumbent upon your Lord, one to be sought.﴾

Page 335

The command "Say" (qul) requires an addressee to whom it is said. It may be intended as: "Say to them," that is, to the polytheists who hear the preceding threat and warning: "Is that better, or the Garden?" In that case the sentences are connected in context, and the interrogation is then for mockery (tahakkum), since there is no doubt that the described Garden is better. It may also be intended as: "Say to the believers," in which case the sentence is an interjection between the verses of warning, for the purpose of displaying the great difference between the state of the polytheists and the state of the believers. The interrogation is then used for gentle allusion and courtesy (talattuf). This is like His saying: ﴿Is that better as a hospitable gift, or the tree of Zaqqum?﴾ [al-Saffat: 62] in Surat al-Saffat.

The reference (al-ishara) is to the narrow place in Hell.

"Khayr" (better) is an elative noun (ism tafdil), and its original form is "akhyar" on the pattern of the elative, but the hamza was dropped due to frequent usage. The elative, according to the first interpretation of the context of the verse, is used for mockery of the polytheists, and according to the second interpretation it is used for gentle allusion in addressing the believers and for displaying divine favor upon them.

The description of those promised as "God-fearing" (muttaqun) is in accordance with the apparent meaning according to the first interpretation, and according to the second interpretation it is contrary to the apparent meaning, since the apparent meaning would require a pronoun of address. The reason for the shift to explicit mention is what the word "muttaqun" conveys of generality, encompassing the addressees and those who come after them.

The clause ﴿It shall be a reward and a final destination for them﴾ is an appendage (tadhyil) to the clause ﴿the Garden of eternity which the God-fearing have been promised﴾, because of what it contains of honouring the Garden's status through the indefinite form of "reward and destination," together with an indication that they were promised it as a promise of recompense, similar to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿An excellent reward and a good resting place﴾ [al-Kahf: 31], and His saying: "An evil drink, and an evil resting place" in Surat al-Kahf.

The clause ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to ﴿the Garden of eternity﴾, or a second description (sifa). The clause ﴿It is a promise incumbent upon your Lord﴾ is a second circumstantial clause, and the connecting pronoun is omitted, since the implied sense is: a promise for them.

The concealed pronoun in ﴿It is a promise incumbent upon your Lord﴾ refers either to the promise understood from His saying ﴿which the God-fearing have been promised﴾, that is: the promise was a promise to be sought. He described the promise by "a promise" (wa'dan), though it is the same thing, so that "to be sought" (mas'ulan) may be built upon it.

It may also be that the pronoun refers to ﴿whatever they wish﴾, and describing it as "a promise" is from the description of a verbal noun where the intended meaning is the object, like "creation" in the sense of "the created thing."

"ʿAla rabbika" (incumbent upon your Lord) is connected to "wa'dan" by implying in "wa'dan" the meaning of "haqqan" (a binding truth), to convey that it is a promise that is not broken, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A promise upon Us; indeed We are ever doing it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104].

"Al-mas'ul" is the one whom its rightful claimant asks for and demands. That is, it is a truth for the God-fearing that they await its fulfilment, as if it were a reward for them for a deed. This is directed toward the emphasis on affirming the promise and generosity, just as a grateful person thanks you for a kindness and you say: "I did nothing but what was obligatory," since no other meaning comes to mind here, for there is no sense of obligation upon God, exalted is He, except that it is a bounty and a self-binding commitment. The people of the faith do not differ on this, but they differed on the permissibility of breaking the promise.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verses 17–18:

﴿And on the Day when He will gather them, and what they worshipped besides Allah, and He will say: "Did you mislead these, My servants, or did they themselves stray from the way?"﴾ ﴿They will say: "Glory be to You! It was not for us to take any protectors besides You; but You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the Reminder, and they became a people lost (bur)."﴾

The phrase ﴿ويَوْمَ نَحْشُرُهم﴾ is conjoined (ʿuṭifa) either to the sentence ﴿قُلْ أذَلِكَ خَيْرٌ﴾ [al-Furqan: 15], if the intended address is: "Say to the polytheists," or it is conjoined to the sentence ﴿وأعْتَدْنا لِمَن كَذَّبَ بِالسّاعَةِ سَعِيرًا﴾ [al-Furqan: 11], on the possibility that the intended address is: "Say to the believers."

On both views, the accusative of ﴿يَوْمَ نَحْشُرُهم﴾ is as an object (maf'ul bihi) of a verb that is omitted but known from the context of similar passages. Its estimated form is: "Remember that Day," because when He threatened them with the Blaze and what they will encounter of its terror, He then explained to them the state before that, which is their condition at the gathering together with their idols. This is one of the manifestations of terror for them at the place of gathering, when they witness the disappointment of their hopes in their gods, as they see their insignificance before the hands of Allah, and their disavowal of their worshippers, and their testimony against them for their ingratitude for the blessing of Allah and their turning away from the Qur'an, and when they hear the denial of those among the rational beings who were worshipped, namely the angels, ʿIsa (peace be upon him), and the jinn, and they attribute to them that they commanded them with misguidance.

The generality of the relative pronoun in His words ﴿وما يَعْبُدُونَ﴾ includes all kinds of objects of worship that they worshipped, and for this reason the relative ﴿ما﴾ was preferred, because it applies to rational and non-rational beings alike. Yet the predominance here is for non-rational beings. The address in ﴿أأنْتُمْ أضْلَلْتُمْ﴾ is to the rational beings, by the indication of the direction of the address.

Thus the sentence ﴿قالُوا سُبْحانَكَ﴾ is an answer to Allah's question to them: ﴿أأنْتُمْ أضْلَلْتُمْ عِبادِي هَؤُلاءِ أمْ هم ضَلُّوا السَّبِيلَ﴾; it is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) and ﴿يَوْمَ نَحْشُرُهم﴾ is not connected to it.

Ibn Kathir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿يَحْشُرُهم - ويَقُولُ﴾ both with the ya', while Ibn 'Amir read ﴿نَحْشُرُهم - ونَقُولُ﴾ both with the nun. The majority read ﴿نَحْشُرُهم﴾ with the nun and ﴿يَقُولُ﴾ with the ya', so there is a shift (iltifat) from the first person to the third person.

The interrogation is rhetorical (taqriri), for interrogation and bearing witness. The meaning: Did you mislead them, or did they stray of their own accord without misguidance from you? So there is an omission in the speech, indicated by what is mentioned.

He reported with the verb ﴿أضْلَلْتُمْ﴾ about the separate pronoun of the addressees, and with the verb ﴿ضَلُّوا﴾ about the separate pronoun of the absent ones, in order to convey that the placing of the subject before the two verbal predicates strengthens the ruling established by it, by making them aware that they have no escape from acknowledging one of the two matters, and that one of them is certain to have occurred. So the intended emphasis is on the counterpart of the interrogative hamza, which is ﴿أمْ هم ضَلُّوا السَّبِيلَ﴾.

The ones who answer are the rational beings among those worshipped: the angels and ʿIsa (peace be upon him).

Their words ﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ are a word of glorification, used as a euphemism for amazement at a monstrous statement, like the saying of al-A'sha:

"I said, when his boasting came to me: Glory be to the one from ʿAlqama, the boastful!"

It was mentioned in Surah al-Nur: ﴿سُبْحانَكَ هَذا بُهْتانٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ [al-Nur: 16]. Know that the apparent reference of the pronoun in ﴿نَحْشُرُهم﴾ is that it refers to the polytheists whom the verse rebukes with the threat, and they are those who said ﴿مالِ هَذا الرَّسُولِ يَأْكُلُ الطَّعامَ﴾ [al-Furqan: 7] up to His words ﴿مَسْحُورًا﴾. However, what is required by their description as ﴿الظّالِمُونَ﴾ and the report about them that they denied the Hour, and what is required by the apparent meaning of the relative in His words ﴿لِمَن كَذَّبَ بِالسّاعَةِ﴾ [al-Furqan: 11] of the inclusion of everyone in whom the content of the relative clause is realized, all of this requires that the pronoun in ﴿نَحْشُرُهم﴾ refers back to ﴿مَن كَذَّبَ بِالسّاعَةِ﴾, so it includes the polytheists present at the time of the revelation of the verse, those of them who passed away after the call of Muhammad reached them, and those who will come after them among the polytheists.

The description of "servants" here is a registration against the polytheists of their servitude, and an allusion to their ingratitude for its due.

The indication to them is for distinguishing them from the rest of the servants.

This is a principle in giving testimony concerning the very person testified against before the judge.

Attributing speech to what they worship besides Allah implies that Allah makes the idols speak, so that their worshippers hear it; as for other than idols among the rational beings who were worshipped, the speech concerning them is evident.

The repetition of the verb ﴿ضَلُّوا﴾ in His words ﴿أمْ هم ضَلُّوا السَّبِيلَ﴾ is so that a verbal predicate may apply to their pronoun, which conveys strengthening in attributing the straying to them. The meaning: Or did they stray of their own accord without misguidance from you? The proper construction of the verb is with ﴿عَنْ﴾, but it is used directly because it implies the meaning of "they erred," or by dropping the preposition.

﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ is a glorification of Allah the Exalted in the position of acknowledging that they declare Allah transcendent above their claiming for themselves a share with Him in divinity.

The meaning of ﴿ما كانَ يَنْبَغِي لَنا﴾ is: it is not suitable for us to seek that we take worshippers; because (inbaghā) is the reflexive of (baghāhu), when he sought it. So the meaning: it is not possible for us to take them as protectors, that is, as servants. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وهَبْ لِي مُلْكًا لا يَنْبَغِي لِأحَدٍ مِن بَعْدِي﴾ [Sad: 35]. It was mentioned before in His words: ﴿وما يَنْبَغِي لِلرَّحْمَنِ أنْ يَتَّخِذَ ولَدًا﴾ [Maryam: 92] in Surah Maryam. It is here a metonymy for the strong negation of their seeking this taking, that is, we disavow that; because the negation of (kana) and making the object of negation a predicate of (kana) is stronger in negation, and for this reason it is called denial (juhud). The predicate is used in one of its implied consequences, that is, we know that it is not fitting for us, so how would we attempt it?

The ﴿مِن﴾ in His words ﴿مِن دُونِكَ﴾ is for origin, because the original use of (dūn) is as a noun of place, and an omitted genitive is assumed to which (dūn) is attached, as in: "I sat beneath," that is, beneath its place. So the position of ﴿مِن﴾ here is the position of a circumstantial clause relative to ﴿أوْلِياءَ﴾. Its original status was an attribute of ﴿أوْلِياءَ﴾, but when the attribute was placed before the qualified noun it became a circumstantial. The meaning: we do not take as protectors for ourselves, described as being from a side beneath your side, that is, they do not acknowledge You as the One in divinity, for they associate others with You in divinity.

From Ibn Jinni: that the ﴿مِن﴾ here is superfluous. He permitted the superfluity of ﴿مِن﴾ in the object.

The ﴿مِن﴾ in His words ﴿مِن أوْلِياءَ﴾ is superfluous, to emphasize the generality of the negation, that is, its comprehensiveness, because it is an indefinite noun in the context of negation.

Al-Awliya' is the plural of al-Wali in the sense of the follower in allegiance, for al-Wali is synonymous with al-Mawla, so it applies to both parties of allegiance, that is, to the master and the servant, or the helper and the one helped. The meaning here is the follower-wali, as in His words: ﴿فَتَكُونَ لِلشَّيْطانِ ولِيًّا﴾ [Maryam: 45] in Surah Maryam, that is, we do not ask people to be worshippers of us.

The majority read ﴿نَتَّخِذَ﴾ in the active voice. Abu Ja'far read ﴿نُتَّخَذَ﴾ with a damma on the nun and a fatha on the kha', in the passive voice, that is, that people take us as their protectors besides You. So the position of ﴿مِن دُونِكَ﴾ is the position of a circumstantial relative to the pronoun of ﴿نُتَّخَذَ﴾. The meaning according to this: they disavow that they call people to worship them, and this is a rebuke of those who worshipped them and attributed to them their allegiance. The meaning: we do not take for ourselves whoever allies with us besides You, that is, whoever worships us besides You.

The exception (istidrak) conveyed by ﴿لَكِنْ﴾ arises from the disavowal of being the ones who misled them, by following it with an explanation of the cause of their straying; lest it be thought that clearing themselves of misleading them lifts the responsibility of straying from those who strayed. The intended point of the exception is what follows ﴿حَتّى﴾, which is ﴿نَسُوا الذِّكْرَ﴾. As for what precedes it, there has been inserted between the particle of exception and what it governs a statement registering upon them the enormity of their straying, in that they met the mercy of Allah and His blessing upon them and upon their fathers with ingratitude. So the report that Allah gave the straying and their fathers enjoyment is used in praise of Allah for the vastness of His mercy, and in reproach of the polytheists for returning blessing with ingratitude, in anger against them.

Making their forgetting of the Reminder the end-point of the enjoyment is to hint that that enjoyment led to ingratitude because of the corruption of their souls; it is like generosity in barren soil. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وتَجْعَلُونَ رِزْقَكم أنَّكم تُكَذِّبُونَ﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 82].

The mention here of the enjoyment of their fathers, although the forgetting of the Reminder occurred only among the polytheists to whom the Muhammadan call reached and who forgot the Reminder, that is, the Qur'an, is for the sake of magnifying the blessing of enjoyment upon them, as a lasting and inherited blessing; with an allusion that ingratitude for the blessing was passed on to them from their fathers, who established for them the worship of idols. Thus there is in it an allusion to the heinousness of polytheism even before the coming of the Messenger ﷺ.

From this it appears that the pronoun in ﴿نَسُوا﴾ and the pronoun in ﴿كانُوا﴾ refer back to the wrongdoers who denied Islam, not to their fathers, because the fathers did not hear the Reminder.

Forgetting is used, by way of metaphor, for deliberate turning away, because it is a turning away resembling forgetting in being without reflection or insight. It was mentioned before in His words ﴿وتَنْسَوْنَ ما تُشْرِكُونَ﴾ [al-An'am: 41] in Surah al-An'am.

The Reminder (al-dhikr) is the Qur'an, because by it the truth is remembered. It was mentioned before in His words ﴿وقالُوا يا أيُّها الَّذِي نُزِّلَ عَلَيْهِ الذِّكْرُ إنَّكَ لَمَجْنُونٌ﴾ [al-Hijr: 6] in Surah al-Hijr.

Al-bur is the plural of ba'ir, like al-'udh, the plural of 'a'idh. The ba'ir is one who has been struck by ruin (al-bawar), that is, destruction. It was mentioned before in His words ﴿وأحَلُّوا قَوْمَهم دارَ البَوارِ﴾ [Ibrahim: 28], that is, death. The word bawr has been borrowed for severity of bad condition, based on the custom that regards destruction as the last point a living being reaches of bad condition, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿يُهْلِكُونَ أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾ [al-Tawba: 42], that is, the badness of their condition in reality while they are heedless of it. It was said: al-bawar means corruption in the dialect of the Azd, and that it and what is derived from it, which came in the Qur'an, is not in the dialect of Mudar.

The bringing in of the verb (kana) and the construction of ﴿بُورًا﴾ upon ﴿قَوْمًا﴾, rather than saying "until they forgot the Reminder and perished," serve to indicate the firm establishment of ruin upon them, through what (kana) implies of the firmness of the sense of the predicate, and what ﴿قَوْمًا﴾ implies of ruin being one of the constituents of their peoplehood, as was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 164] in Surah al-Baqara.

Yet the predominance here is for non-rational beings. The address in ﴿أأنْتُمْ أضْلَلْتُمْ﴾ is to the rational beings, by the indication of the direction of the address.

Thus the sentence ﴿قالُوا سُبْحانَكَ﴾ is an answer to Allah's question to them: ﴿أأنْتُمْ أضْلَلْتُمْ عِبادِي هَؤُلاءِ أمْ هم ضَلُّوا السَّبِيلَ﴾; it is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) and ﴿يَوْمَ نَحْشُرُهم﴾ is not connected to it.

Ibn Kathir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿يَحْشُرُهم - ويَقُولُ﴾ both with the ya', while Ibn 'Amir read ﴿نَحْشُرُهم - ونَقُولُ﴾ both with the nun. The majority read ﴿نَحْشُرُهم﴾ with the nun and ﴿يَقُولُ﴾ with the ya', so there is a shift (iltifat) from the first person to the third person.

The interrogation is rhetorical (taqriri), for interrogation and bearing witness. The meaning: Did you mislead them, or did they stray of their own accord without misguidance from you? So there is an omission in the speech, indicated by what is mentioned.

He reported with the verb ﴿أضْلَلْتُمْ﴾ about the separate pronoun of the addressees, and with the verb ﴿ضَلُّوا﴾ about the separate pronoun of the absent ones, in order to convey that the placing of the subject before the two verbal predicates strengthens the ruling established by it, by making them aware that they have no escape from acknowledging one of the two matters, and that one of them is certain to have occurred. So the intended emphasis is on the counterpart of the interrogative hamza, which is ﴿أمْ هم ضَلُّوا السَّبِيلَ﴾.

The ones who answer are the rational beings among those worshipped: the angels and ʿIsa (peace be upon him).

Their words ﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ are a word of glorification, used as a euphemism for amazement at a monstrous statement, like the saying of al-A'sha:

"I said, when his boasting came to me: Glory be to the one from ʿAlqama, the boastful!"

It was mentioned in Surah al-Nur: ﴿سُبْحانَكَ هَذا بُهْتانٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ [al-Nur: 16]. Know that the apparent reference of the pronoun in ﴿نَحْشُرُهم﴾ is that it refers to the polytheists whom the verse rebukes with the threat, and they are those who said ﴿مالِ هَذا الرَّسُولِ يَأْكُلُ الطَّعامَ﴾ [al-Furqan: 7] up to His words ﴿مَسْحُورًا﴾. However, what is required by their description as ﴿الظّالِمُونَ﴾ and the report about them that they denied the Hour, and what is required by the apparent meaning of the relative in His words ﴿لِمَن كَذَّبَ بِالسّاعَةِ﴾ [al-Furqan: 11] of the inclusion of everyone in whom the content of the relative clause is realized, all of this requires that the pronoun in ﴿نَحْشُرُهم﴾ refers back to ﴿مَن كَذَّبَ بِالسّاعَةِ﴾, so it includes the polytheists present at the time of the revelation of the verse, those of them who passed away after the call of Muhammad reached them, and those who will come after them among the polytheists.

The description of "servants" here is a registration against the polytheists of their servitude, and an allusion to their ingratitude for its due.

The indication to them is for distinguishing them from the rest of the servants.

This is a principle in giving testimony concerning the very person testified against before the judge.

Attributing speech to what they worship besides Allah implies that Allah makes the idols speak, so that their worshippers hear it; as for other than idols among the rational beings who were worshipped, the speech concerning them is evident.

The repetition of the verb ﴿ضَلُّوا﴾ in His words ﴿أمْ هم ضَلُّوا السَّبِيلَ﴾ is so that a verbal predicate may apply to their pronoun, which conveys strengthening in attributing the straying to them. The meaning: Or did they stray of their own accord without misguidance from you? The proper construction of the verb is with ﴿عَنْ﴾, but it is used directly because it implies the meaning of "they erred," or by dropping the preposition.

﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ is a glorification of Allah the Exalted in the position of acknowledging that they declare Allah transcendent above their claiming for themselves a share with Him in divinity.

The meaning of ﴿ما كانَ يَنْبَغِي لَنا﴾ is: it is not suitable for us to seek that we take worshippers; because (inbaghā) is the reflexive of (baghāhu), when he sought it. So the meaning: it is not possible for us to take them as protectors, that is, as servants. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وهَبْ لِي مُلْكًا لا يَنْبَغِي لِأحَدٍ مِن بَعْدِي﴾ [Sad: 35]. It was mentioned before in His words: ﴿وما يَنْبَغِي لِلرَّحْمَنِ أنْ يَتَّخِذَ ولَدًا﴾ [Maryam: 92] in Surah Maryam. It is here a metonymy for the strong negation of their seeking this taking, that is, we disavow that; because the negation of (kana) and making the object of negation a predicate of (kana) is stronger in negation, and for this reason it is called denial (juhud). The predicate is used in one of its implied consequences, that is, we know that it is not fitting for us, so how would we attempt it?

The ﴿مِن﴾ in His words ﴿مِن دُونِكَ﴾ is for origin, because the original use of (dūn) is as a noun of place, and an omitted genitive is assumed to which (dūn) is attached, as in: "I sat beneath," that is, beneath its place. So the position of ﴿مِن﴾ here is the position of a circumstantial clause relative to ﴿أوْلِياءَ﴾. Its original status was an attribute of ﴿أوْلِياءَ﴾, but when the attribute was placed before the qualified noun it became a circumstantial. The meaning: we do not take as protectors for ourselves, described as being from a side beneath your side, that is, they do not acknowledge You as the One in divinity, for they associate others with You in divinity.

From Ibn Jinni: that the ﴿مِن﴾ here is superfluous. He permitted the superfluity of ﴿مِن﴾ in the object.

The ﴿مِن﴾ in His words ﴿مِن أوْلِياءَ﴾ is superfluous, to emphasize the generality of the negation, that is, its comprehensiveness, because it is an indefinite noun in the context of negation.

Al-Awliya' is the plural of al-Wali in the sense of the follower in allegiance, for al-Wali is synonymous with al-Mawla, so it applies to both parties of allegiance, that is, to the master and the servant, or the helper and the one helped. The meaning here is the follower-wali, as in His words: ﴿فَتَكُونَ لِلشَّيْطانِ ولِيًّا﴾ [Maryam: 45] in Surah Maryam, that is, we do not ask people to be worshippers of us.

The majority read ﴿نَتَّخِذَ﴾ in the active voice. Abu Ja'far read ﴿نُتَّخَذَ﴾ with a damma on the nun and a fatha on the kha', in the passive voice, that is, that people take us as their protectors besides You. So the position of ﴿مِن دُونِكَ﴾ is the position of a circumstantial relative to the pronoun of ﴿نُتَّخَذَ﴾. The meaning according to this: they disavow that they call people to worship them, and this is a rebuke of those who worshipped them and attributed to them their allegiance. The meaning: we do not take for ourselves whoever allies with us besides You, that is, whoever worships us besides You.

The exception (istidrak) conveyed by ﴿لَكِنْ﴾ arises from the disavowal of being the ones who misled them, by following it with an explanation of the cause of their straying; lest it be thought that clearing themselves of misleading them lifts the responsibility of straying from those who strayed. The intended point of the exception is what follows ﴿حَتّى﴾, which is ﴿نَسُوا الذِّكْرَ﴾. As for what precedes it, there has been inserted between the particle of exception and what it governs a statement registering upon them the enormity of their straying, in that they met the mercy of Allah and His blessing upon them and upon their fathers with ingratitude. So the report that Allah gave the straying and their fathers enjoyment is used in praise of Allah for the vastness of His mercy, and in reproach of the polytheists for returning blessing with ingratitude, in anger against them.

Making their forgetting of the Reminder the end-point of the enjoyment is to hint that that enjoyment led to ingratitude because of the corruption of their souls; it is like generosity in barren soil. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وتَجْعَلُونَ رِزْقَكم أنَّكم تُكَذِّبُونَ﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 82].

The mention here of the enjoyment of their fathers, although the forgetting of the Reminder occurred only among the polytheists to whom the Muhammadan call reached and who forgot the Reminder, that is, the Qur'an, is for the sake of magnifying the blessing of enjoyment upon them, as a lasting and inherited blessing; with an allusion that ingratitude for the blessing was passed on to them from their fathers, who established for them the worship of idols. Thus there is in it an allusion to the heinousness of polytheism even before the coming of the Messenger ﷺ.

From this it appears that the pronoun in ﴿نَسُوا﴾ and the pronoun in ﴿كانُوا﴾ refer back to the wrongdoers who denied Islam, not to their fathers, because the fathers did not hear the Reminder.

Forgetting is used, by way of metaphor, for deliberate turning away, because it is a turning away resembling forgetting in being without reflection or insight. It was mentioned before in His words ﴿وتَنْسَوْنَ ما تُشْرِكُونَ﴾ [al-An'am: 41] in Surah al-An'am.

The Reminder (al-dhikr) is the Qur'an, because by it the truth is remembered. It was mentioned before in His words ﴿وقالُوا يا أيُّها الَّذِي نُزِّلَ عَلَيْهِ الذِّكْرُ إنَّكَ لَمَجْنُونٌ﴾ [al-Hijr: 6] in Surah al-Hijr.

Al-bur is the plural of ba'ir, like al-'udh, the plural of 'a'idh. The ba'ir is one who has been struck by ruin (al-bawar), that is, destruction. It was mentioned before in His words ﴿وأحَلُّوا قَوْمَهم دارَ البَوارِ﴾ [Ibrahim: 28], that is, death. The word bawr has been borrowed for severity of bad condition, based on the custom that regards destruction as the last point a living being reaches of bad condition, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿يُهْلِكُونَ أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾ [al-Tawba: 42], that is, the badness of their condition in reality while they are heedless of it. It was said: al-bawar means corruption in the dialect of the Azd, and that it and what is derived from it, which came in the Qur'an, is not in the dialect of Mudar.

The bringing in of the verb (kana) and the construction of ﴿بُورًا﴾ upon ﴿قَوْمًا﴾, rather than saying "until they forgot the Reminder and perished," serve to indicate the firm establishment of ruin upon them, through what (kana) implies of the firmness of the sense of the predicate, and what ﴿قَوْمًا﴾ implies of ruin being one of the constituents of their peoplehood, as was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 164] in Surah al-Baqara.
