The *fa'* here is *fasihah* (the "expressive" *fa'*, which indicates that what follows is an explicit statement of an argument after the preparatory conditions that call for it have been set out). This is an excellent explicit statement, and the shift (*iltifat*, a change of grammatical person) in His saying "*kadhdhabukum*" (they have denied you) adds to its excellence.

The speech contains an ellipsis of a verb of saying that the context indicates. The implied sense is: "If you say, 'These are our gods,' then they have denied you." A clear instance of the implied verb of saying appears in the verse of 'Abbas ibn al-Ahnaf:

*Qalu Khurasanu aqsa ma yuradu bina * thumma al-qufulu fa-qad ji'na Khurasana*

They said: "Khurasan is the farthest that we are aimed at, then the return," so we have come to Khurasan.

That is: "If you say that, then we have come to Khurasan." Omitting the verb of saying in this verse evokes the scene itself, as if it were witnessed and not related. It is as though the listener, at the end of the verse, has heard this exchange directly, without narration. So the testimony of the idols against them strikes his hearing first, and then the address of denial directed at those being testified against strikes it. This is a striking variation in narration that relies on imagining the narrated event as actually taking place. Among its examples is the saying of God Most High: ﴿On the Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces, [it will be said]: "Taste the touch of Saqar."﴾ (al-Qamar: 48).

Thus the clause "﴿fa-qad kadhdhabukum﴾" and what follows is a new, independent sentence (*mustanafah ibtida'iyyah*), which is a turning towards addressing those present. It is a type of *iltifat*, like His saying: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ (Yusuf: 29), after His saying: ﴿Yusuf, turn away from this﴾ (Yusuf: 29).

The *ba'* in "*bima taqulun*" (in what you say) may be in the sense of *fi* for a figurative sense of location, meaning: they denied you with a denial that is real in what you say. It may also be causal, meaning: they denied you because of what you say.

The *ma* is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*). What they said is what is understood from the question and answer, namely that they said they had called them to worship them.

The consequence of announcing their denial of them is the despairing of them benefiting from them in that position, since He made clear to them that they cannot avert harm, that is, averting harm from them, nor give help, that is, inflicting harm on whoever overpowers them. The reason for this consequence is what their saying "*subhanaka*" (Glory be to You) indicates, which requires that they are in a position of servitude and submission.

The majority of readers read "*yastati'un*" with the *ya'* of the third person. Hafs read it with the *ta'* of the second person, taking it as an address to the polytheists who worshipped idols besides God.

* * *

﴿And whoever of you does wrong, We will make him taste a great punishment.﴾

This is a *tadhyil* (a concluding generalization that follows the main statement), whose generality encompasses all people, and the address in "*minkum*" (of you) is to all who are responsible. This indicates that the polytheists being spoken of will be punished with a great punishment. The great punishment is the punishment of Hell.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 20:

﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets.﴾

Page 343

This is a response to their saying: (﴿What is this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]), after He had already answered their saying: (﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him, or he have a garden from which he may eat?﴾ [al-Furqan: 8]) with His saying: (﴿Blessed is He who, if He willed, would give you better than that﴾ [al-Furqan: 10]). However, since their saying (﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him﴾ [al-Furqan: 8]) concerned a condition that was not granted to the messengers in this world, the response to their saying about it was that Allah has given him something better than that in the Hereafter.

As for their saying (﴿What is this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]), they used it as a means to invalidate his messengership by the establishment of human attributes for him. So the response to them was that all the messengers were characterized by human attributes, and the polytheists did not deny the existence of messengers before Muhammad ﷺ. Indeed, they said: (﴿Let him bring us a sign, as the earlier ones were sent [with signs]﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5]). And if they existed, then necessarily they ate food, since they were of mankind, and they walked in the markets of cities and of the desert, because the call takes place in the gatherings of people. Musa said: (﴿Your appointment is the day of adornment, and that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾ [Ta-Ha: 59]). The Prophet ﷺ used to call the Quraysh in their assemblies and their clubs, and he used to call the rest of the Arabs at 'Ukaz and during the days of the season.

The clause (﴿they ate food﴾) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because the item excepted from (illa) is a general state. The estimated sense is: "We did not send before you any messengers in any state except in the state of (﴿that they ate food﴾)." The emphasis by (inna) and the lam serves to affirm the occurrence of the circumstance, treating the polytheists, in their forgetfulness of the conditions of the messengers, as one who denies that the earlier messengers ate food and walked in the markets. The circumstantial clause is not joined by the conjunction "wa" (and), because the presence of the exception particle is sufficient for connection, especially as the connection has been reinforced by the particle of emphasis; so another letter is not added, lest four letters follow in succession: illa, inna, the lam, and then the wa would be added. This is unlike His saying: (﴿And We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree﴾ [al-Hijr: 4]), and His saying: (﴿And We did not destroy any town except that it had warners﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 208]).

Allah left the messengers in the customary condition of mankind with regard to the means of material life, since there is no wisdom in changing their state in that respect; rather, Allah changes their inner life, because changing it prepares their souls to receive the divine effusions.

Allah, exalted is He, maintains the laws of the order of the creatures and the worlds, because He did not create them in vain; so He does not change them except to the extent that His will relates to supporting the messengers with miracles and the like.

* * *

(﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others. Will you be patient? And your Lord is ever Seeing.﴾)

This is a concluding appendage (tadhyil). The pronoun of address in His saying (some of you) encompasses all people by the indication of the context, and both "some" are indefinite, clarified by the situation. The state of the trial differs in both parts: some of it is a trial in belief, some a trial in security, and some a trial in bodies.

Describing it as (a trial) is metaphorical, because it is the cause of the trial. The one of the two parts included the Prophet ﷺ and the believers with him, and the other part the polytheists. So the state of the Messenger was a trial for the polytheists, since they claimed that his state was incompatible with messengership, so they did not believe in him. And the state of the believers in their weakness was a trial for the polytheists, since they disdained faith that would equate them with them. Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-'As ibn Wa'il and their like used to say: "If we embraced Islam when 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Suhayb and Bilal have embraced it before us, they would be placed above us," showing arrogance through precedence. This is like the saying of the chieftains of the people of Noah: "We will not believe until you drive away those who have followed you." He said: (﴿I am not one to drive away those who believe. Indeed, they will meet their Lord, but I see you as a people who are ignorant﴾ [Hud: 29]) (﴿And O my people, who would support me against Allah if I drove them away? Then will you not remember?﴾ [Hud: 30]).

And Allah the Exalted said to the Prophet ﷺ: (﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. You are not accountable for them at all, nor are they accountable for you at all, so that you would drive them away and be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-An'am: 52]) (﴿And thus We have tried some of them by means of others, that they should say, "Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor from among us?" Is not Allah most knowing of those who are grateful?﴾ [al-An'am: 53]).

The statement is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ concerning the aversion of some of his people from Islam. For this reason He followed it with His saying (﴿Will you be patient?﴾), which is an interrogative used in the sense of urging and command, like His saying (﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]).

The position of (﴿And your Lord is ever Seeing﴾) is that of an encouragement to the patience that is commanded; that is, He is Knowing of those who are patient, and it is an announcement that Allah does not waste the reward of the Messenger for what he encounters from his people, and that He will support him against them.

In the attribution to the Lord, described in relation to the pronoun of the Prophet, there is an allusion to this promise, for the Lord does not abandon His friends, like His saying: (﴿And We know that your breast is distressed by what they say﴾ [al-Hijr: 97]) (﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise and be among the prostrators﴾ [al-Hijr: 98]) (﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [al-Hijr: 99]), meaning: the established victory.

**Page 5**

﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say: "Why were the angels not sent down upon us, or why do we not see our Lord?" Indeed, they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression.﴾

This is a report of another of their statements in denying the Messenger, peace be upon him. In this statement he refers to them as "those who do not expect to meet Us," whereas in the earlier statements he referred to them as "those who disbelieved" and "the wrongdoers." This is because there is a contradiction between this description and their statement. They denied the meeting of the Hereafter, which includes seeing Allah and the angels, yet they asked to see Allah in this world and for the angels to descend upon them in this world. They also wished to receive the religion from the angels or directly from Allah. Thus, the reporting of their words and the mention of their description contains a wonder at the contradiction of their faculties.

Know that the people of polytheism testified against themselves by denying resurrection, and they imagined that their doubt about it was the strongest argument they had for denying the messengers. For this reason also, Allah made their statement a means of identifying them through a relative clause (al-mawsul), as He said: (﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who do not expect to meet Us say: "Bring us a Qur'an other than this, or change it."﴾ [Yunus: 15]) in Surat Yunus.

"Law" (لَوْلا) is a particle of exhortation (tahdid, urging or reproach) used here for challenge (ta'jiz) and impossibility, meaning: "Why were the angels not sent down upon us, so that we might believe in what you have brought?" They mean that if he is truthful, let him ask his Lord for another means of conveying the religion to them.

The meaning of "do not expect" (لا يَرْجُونَ) is that they do not think with near assurance; that is, they consider the meeting with Allah to be impossible. Their purpose in this statement is that they regard themselves as too high to receive the religion from a man like themselves. Therefore, He followed it with His words: (﴿They have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression.﴾) in the sense of wondering at their vanity and their false conceit.

**Page 6**

The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that serves as a response to their statement. The emphasis by the oath particle (lam of oath) serves to express the meaning of wonder, because the oath is used to express amazement, as in the saying of one of the Banu Kilab or the Banu Numayr, which Tha'lab recited in his Majalis and al-Qali in his Amali:

"Oh flash of lightning over the peaks of al-Hima, truly you are a noble flash of lightning to me."

Here, his words "a flash of lightning" (مِن بَرْقٍ) have the force of a specification (tamyiz, a specifying accusative or complement), and the specification occurs there only because of the meaning of wonder it contains.

"Istikbar" (arrogance) is an intensification of "takabbur" (pride); the sin and the ta' are for intensification, like "istajaba" (to respond).

The "fi" (in) is for figurative containment: their selves are likened to vessels in the sense that the thing contained is firmly within them. That is, it is an arrogance that is firmly rooted in them, as in His saying: (﴿And in yourselves. Will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21]).

It is also possible that "fi" is for causation (ta'lil), as in the hadith: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat that she confined," and the rest of the hadith. That is, they were arrogant because of the greatness of their selves in their own estimation. The containment is not literal, because of the little benefit in it; for it is well known that arrogance occurs only in the self, since it is one of the mental acts.

"Utuw" (transgression) is going beyond the limit in wrongdoing, and it was mentioned earlier in His saying: (﴿and they defied the command of their Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 77]) in Surat al-A'raf. This is wrongdoing because they exceeded the measure of capacity that Allah had granted them.

In this there is an indication that prophethood is not acquired through effort, but is rather a preparation from Allah, the Exalted. He said: (﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 22:

﴿On the Day they see the angels, there will be no good news that Day for the criminals, and they will say, "A forbidding forbidden."﴾

This is a second resumptive clause (isti'naf), an answer to their statement. After expressing astonishment at it, it follows with a threat in which there is the occurrence of something they had asked to occur now: namely, they will see the angels, but it will be a sight that distresses them, when they see the guardians of punishment driving them toward the Fire. In this resumption there is therefore an allusive mockery of them, because its beginning raises their hopes of a response, while its end dashes them with a threat. The speech follows the manner of the third person (ghayba), because it is a report of their arrogance, while the intended purpose is for it to reach them when they hear it.

"Yawma yarawnahum" (on the Day they see) is in the accusative of time, governed by "la bushra" (no good news). The fronting of the time phrase is for emphasis on it, to stir up hope and to create suspense about the specific time of it, so that when what brings the disappointment of their hope arrives, it has the impact of grief on their souls when they hear it.

The repetition of "yawma'idhin" (that Day) is for emphasis.

The mention of the description "the criminals" is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, to record upon them that they are criminals, after they were described as disbelievers, wrongdoers, and despairing of meeting God. The negation of good news is used to imply its opposite, which is grief.

"Ḥijr" (with a kasra on the ḥa and a sukūn on the jim; it is also said with a fatḥa or ḍamma on the ḥa, which is rare) is a word they say upon seeing what one fears being struck by, and it serves the function of seeking refuge. Al-Khalil and Abu 'Ubayda said: when a man saw a man from whom he feared he would be killed during the sacred months, he would say to him, "Ḥijran maḥjūran," meaning, "Forbidden is my being killed." It is an amulet (ʿawdha).

"Ḥijr" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of "ḥajarahu," meaning he prevented him. God, exalted is He, says: "wa ḥarthun ḥijr" (and a crop that is forbidden). In this usage it is obligatorily in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul muṭlaq) governed by a suppressed verb, like "ma'adha Allah" (God forbid). As for its being in the nominative in the verse of the rajaz poet:

"Qāla fīhā ḥaydatun wa dhu'r / ʿawdhun bi-rabbī minkum wa ḥijr"

this is a licence (taṣarruf) in it, and perhaps according to Sibawayh it is a necessity (ḍarūra), because he did not mention the nominative in the use of these words for this purpose, and this is what the poet reported. As for the nominative of "ḥijr" outside the situation of its use for seeking refuge, there is no objection to it, because it is the original form. It has also come in the Qur'an in the accusative not as an absolute object, in His saying, exalted is He: "wa ja'ala baynahumā barzakhan wa ḥijran maḥjūran" (Al-Furqan: 53), where it is conjoined to the object of "ja'ala," and we will draw attention to this shortly.

"Maḥjūran" is an adjective of "ḥijran," derived from its root, to indicate the firmness (tamakkun) of the meaning from which it is derived, as they say: "laylun alyal" (a pitch-black night), "dhayl dhā'il" (a flowing skirt), and "sh'ir shā'ir" (very poetic poetry).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 23:

﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds, and We will make them scattered dust.﴾

They used to regard good deeds in the Jahiliyyah as a means of attaining the good of this world, because such deeds please God Most High, so He rewards them with blessings in this world, since they did not believe in resurrection. Khadijah said to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he was bewildered about what had begun to come to him of revelation and he said to her: "Indeed, I have feared for myself." She said: "By God, God will never disgrace you. Indeed, you join the ties of kinship, bear the burdens of the weak, provide for the guest, and help in the misfortunes of truth." Thus, it is apparent that when the polytheists heard the verses of warning, they would say to themselves: "If resurrection is true, we will surely find deeds of righteousness that we performed, which will be a cause of our salvation." So God knew what was in their souls and informed that their deeds will be like nothing on that Day.

The verb al-qudum (ﷺ approaching) is used in the sense of intending and willing. Verbs of walking and coming are used, in usage, to express the meanings of intent, resolve and beginning, such as: qama yaf'alu (he set about doing), dhahaba yaqulu (he went to say), aqbala (he turned to), and similar. The origin of this lies in depicting the state of one who intends an act with concern for the state of one who walks toward it, so its placement in speech is more elegant than saying: "wa 'amadnahu" (and We intended it), or "aradna ila ma 'amilu" (We willed toward what they did).

The min in His saying "min 'amal" (of deeds) is explanatory (bayaniyyah) to clarify the vagueness of "ma" (what), and the indefiniteness of "'amal" (deed) is for generality of kind; what is meant by it is the deed of good, i.e., "to what they did of the kind of good deeds."

Al-habaa' (scattered particles): are minute bodily entities that are not seen except in rays of sunlight entering through a window or the like, appearing as though floating in the air, and they are finer than dust. That is, "We made it like scattered dust," and this is a simile for their deeds in terms of not benefiting from them, while they exist, like the dust-particle in that it cannot be held even though it exists. This is an eloquent simile, and here it is elegant. A parallel to it is His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿And the mountains will be pulverized, pulverized, and will become scattered dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5]).

Al-manthur: that which is not arranged in order. It is a descriptive, clarifying attribute, because dust is only ever scattered; this attribute is mentioned to indicate the insignificance and dispersal found in the dust.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 24:

﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day will have a better abode and a finer resting-place.﴾

This is an independent resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), brought to contrast the state of the polytheists in the Hereafter with its opposite, the state of the "companions of the Garden," who are the believers. Since he has described the state of the polytheists in the Hereafter, it is understood that they have no share in the Garden. Thus the Garden is specified, on that Day, for others than the polytheists, namely the believers. For the people of Makkah at the time this verse was revealed were two groups: polytheists and believers. The meaning of the speech is: the believers on that Day are the companions of the Garden, and they are the ones with a better abode and a finer resting-place.

Here "better" (al-khayr) is in the comparative form, and it is used sarcastically toward the polytheists; the same applies to "finer" (ahsan).

Al-mustaqarr (المُسْتَقَرّ): the place of settling.

Al-maqil (المَقِيل): the place to which one retreats for the midday rest (qaylulah), and resting at that time is a habit of the affluent (al-mutrafin).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verses 25–26:

﴿On the day the sky is split open with clouds, and the angels are sent down in a sending down.﴾ ﴿Sovereignty on that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful, and it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers.﴾

This is coordinated with the clause (﴿On the day they see the angels﴾ [al-Furqan: 22]). Its purpose is to make them despair of benefiting from their deeds and their deities, and to reinforce the warning against them. Incorporated into this is a description of some aspects of that day, namely that it is the day when the angels are sent down in full view of the people.

The word "day" (yawm) is repeated by way of explicit mention in place of a pronoun, even though it is one and the same day, because of the distance between the return (to God) and the place of the pronoun.

Al-tashaqquq (splitting) is the opening up between parts that are joined together, and from it comes (﴿When the sky splits asunder﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 1]). Perhaps it is a rupture that occurs in the spheres of those worlds. Those who said that the heavens do not accept rupture and then rejoining built this on their imagining them as domes of solid metals. The philosophers have not reached their reality until now.

The splitting of the sky is a wondrous state that appears on the Day of Resurrection, and its meaning is the removal of the barriers and limits that used to prevent the angels from leaving their heavens, except for those who are given permission to do so. So the lam in "al-malaʾikah" (the angels) is for comprehensiveness (al-istighraq, encompassing all), i.e., among the whole company of angels. It is equivalent to saying: "the day when the gates of the sky are opened." He said: (﴿And the sky is opened up, so that it becomes gates﴾ [al-Naba': 19]). Moreover, tashaqquq is used with the meaning of the light becoming clear, as al-Nabigha said:

*Then the column of dawn broke open from it, a troop running like the fleeing wild oxen, fearing the hunter of the flesh.*

[Page 10]

The essential meaning is that there is there a bursting forth and an outpouring, accompanied by the descent of the angels, because that splitting is a permission for the angels to be present at the place of the gathering and the reckoning.

The expression "sent down" (tanzil) implies that the heavens from which the angels emerge are higher than the place where the angels are present.

Al-Jumhur read (tashsha qqaqu) with a shaddah on the shin. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with the shin unshaddah.

Al-ghamam: thin clouds. It is what covers the place of reckoning. God, exalted is He, said: (﴿Do they await only that God should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels, and the matter be decided?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210]), which was discussed in surah al-Baqarah.

Regarding the preposition ba in His saying "bi'l-ghamam" (with the clouds), it has been said that it means "from" (ʿan), i.e., the sky splits open from clouds that surround the angels. It has also been said that it indicates causation (sababiyyah), i.e., there will be a cloud that God creates, in which there is a power by which the sky is split so that the angels may descend, like the power of lightning that splits the clouds. And it has been said that the ba is for accompaniment (mulabasah), i.e., the sky splits accompanied by a cloud that appears at that time. There is nothing in the verse that requires that the splitting be simultaneous with the descent of the angels, or that the clouds be simultaneous with the angels, so let understanding go in every possible direction in arranging that.

The phrase (nuzzila al-malaʾikah) is emphasised with the cognate accusative (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq, absolute object), to convey that it is a descent in its own right, not merely by a mere luminous connection, like the angelic inspirations that shine in the souls of the people of perfection.

Al-Jumhur read (wa-nuzzila al-malaʾikah) with a single nun, a shaddah on the zay, a fatha on the lam, and raising "al-malaʾikah" as the passive form with a deputy subject. Ibn Kathir read (wa-nunzilu) with two nuns, the first with a damma and the second sukun, with a damma on the lam and "al-malaʾikata" in the accusative.

His saying "al-mulku yawma'idhin" (sovereignty on that day) is the opening of the coordinated clause, so it is linked to (﴿And on the day the sky is split open with clouds﴾). It was placed first for the reason mentioned in placing His saying (﴿On the day they see the angels﴾ [al-Furqan: 22]), and the same applies to the repetition of "yawma'idhin" (on that day).

[Page 11]
Al-haqq: the pure, as in your saying: "this is gold, truly (haqqan)." It is the sovereignty that is evident that nothing resembles it, because the state of sovereignty in this world varies. Complete sovereignty belongs only to God, but minds may not pay attention to the deficiency and weakness in kings, and the glitter of their conduct and gifts dazzles them, so they forget the realities. But on that day the realities are laid bare, and there is no one there who claims any kind of control. In a hadith: "Then God says: I am the King; where are the kings of the earth?"

The day is described as "difficult" in consideration of the difficult matters it contains for the polytheists.

The placing of "ʿala al-kafirin" (for the disbelievers) before the predicate is for restriction (qasr). It is a restriction relative to a specific context (qasr idafi), i.e., it is restricted to them, not to the believers.

[Page 12]

﴿On the Day when the wrongdoer will bite on his hands, saying, "Oh, I wish I had taken a path along with the Messenger!"﴾ ﴿"Woe to me! Oh, I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend!"﴾ ﴿"He led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me. And Satan is ever a deserter of man."﴾

This is that Day. The discourse about it is repeated, considering another state of the polytheists in it, or considering the state of some of the polytheists who are the intended meaning of the verse.

The definite article in (al-zalim, "the wrongdoer") may be for comprehensiveness (al-istighraq, the inclusive definite, meaning every individual of the category). The meaning of "wrongdoing" is polytheism (al-shirk), so it includes all polytheists who committed shirk after the Muhammadan call became manifest, by the indication of His saying: (﴿saying, "Oh, I wish I had taken a path along with the Messenger!"﴾). His saying (﴿"Oh, I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend!"﴾) serves as an informing of what companionship among them with one another cannot be free of, and of one of them inciting the others to oppose Islam.

It may also be for a specific known reference (al-'ahd al-makhsus). The meaning of "wrongdoing" is the particular transgression known from a specific story, namely the story of 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt and what Ubayy ibn Khalaf incited him to do. Al-Wahidi and others said, citing al-Sha'bi and others: "'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt was a close friend of Umayya ibn Khalaf. 'Uqba would not return from a journey without preparing food and inviting the nobles of his people to it. He used to frequently sit with the Prophet (ﷺ). Once he returned from one of his journeys, prepared food, and invited the Messenger of God. When they brought the food near, the Messenger of God said: 'I will not eat of your food until you testify that there is no god but God and that I am the Messenger of God.' 'Uqba said: 'I testify that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God.' So the Messenger of God ate of his food. Ubayy ibn Khalaf had been absent, and when he returned he was informed of the matter. He said: 'You have turned away (sabta), O 'Uqba!' He said: 'By God, I have not turned away, but a man came to my house and refused to eat of my food until I testified for him. I was ashamed that he should leave my house without eating, so I testified for him and he ate.' Ubayy said: 'I will never be pleased with you unless you go to him and spit in his face.' So 'Uqba disbelieved and set about carrying out what Ubayy ibn Khalaf had commanded him." Then the intended meaning of (fulan, "so-and-so") is a kinaya (metonymy) for Ubayy ibn Khalaf. His specificity implies the inclusion of similar polytheists who obeyed their close friends in shirk and did not follow the path of the Messenger. No polytheist is free of a polytheist close friend like himself who prevents him from following Islam when he intends to do so, and keeps him firm in the religion of shirk. Thus on the Day of Recompense he regrets obeying him, and mentions him by name.

Al-'add (biting) is clenching something with the teeth in order to cause it pain or to hold it. Its basic construction is transitive without a preposition, but it has frequently been transitive with (ʿalā, "on") to indicate getting a firm grip on what is bitten when they intend a strong bite, as in this verse.

Biting on the hand is a kinaya for regret, because they became accustomed in some of their speech to accompanying it with bodily gestures, such as al-tashadhdhur, which is lifting the hand away from speech of anger. Labid said:

*Mighty ones who lift their hands in disdain when entering, as if they were jinn of the desert, whose feet are firmly planted.*

Likewise is placing the hand over the mouth in astonishment. God the Exalted said: (﴿so they put their hands to their mouths﴾ [Ibrahim: 9]). Among regret is striking the tooth with a finger, biting the index finger, and biting the hand. It is said: "He burned his teeth" and "he burned al-'Urram" (on the pattern of rukka') meaning the molars or the tips of the fingers. In anger there is biting the fingertips. God the Exalted said: (﴿they bite their fingertips out of rage against you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119]) in Surat Al 'Imran. These were kinayat (metonymies), based on what accompanies them in common usage of psychological meanings, and their origin lies in the agitation of the nervous force resulting from anger or grief.

Al-Rasul (the Messenger) is the known one, namely Muhammad (ﷺ).

Taking a path (ittikhadh al-sabil) means taking it. The basic meaning of "taking" (al-akhdh) is grasping with the hand, so it is applied here to the intention of traveling along it. God the Exalted said: (﴿and he took his path into the sea﴾ [Al-Kahf: 63]).

And (ma'a al-Rasul, "along with the Messenger") means: following the Messenger, as a traveler follows a guide who leads him by the best and most direct routes to the intended destination. He turned away from expressing the act of following, or similar, by saying "Oh, I wish I had followed the Messenger," to this elaborate construction, because in this construction there is an image of the state of emulation through the state of accompanying a guide, an image containing a comparison of the Messenger's call to a path, and implying a comparison of the salvation resulting from traversing that path to a traveler reaching the intended place. Thus these meanings are achieved, with elaboration turning into brevity. As for the word "following" (al-mutabaʿa), its use for emulation has become common, so it does not evoke this image. He knew that this path is the path of success for the one he wished for, because wishing (al-tamanni) is seeking a hidden, rare, hard-to-attain matter.

(Ya layta-ni, "Oh, I wish") is a call addressed to the utterance that indicates wishing, by treating the word as an intelligent being that is summoned, because need calls for it in the state of regret, as if he were saying: "This is your place, so come forth," similar to His saying: (﴿Oh, our regret over what we neglected concerning it!﴾ [Al-An'am: 31]) in Surat Al-An'am. This calling increases the wisher's sense of the thing being unlikely to happen.

Likewise his saying (ya wayla-ta, "Oh, woe to me!") is an expression of grief by way of calling out to woe. Al-wayl is bad condition, and the alif is a replacement for the first-person ya', and this is a well-known substitution in calling an item attached to the first-person ya'.

The discussion of woe has already been presented in His saying: (﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands﴾ [Al-Baqara: 79]) in Surat Al-Baqara, and of (ya wayla-na, "Oh, woe to us!") in His saying: (﴿Oh, woe to us! What is this Book?﴾ [Al-Kahf: 49]) in Surat Al-Kahf.

He followed the grief with wishing that he had not taken so-and-so as a close friend.

The clause (﴿"Oh, I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend!"﴾) is a substitution (badal) for the clause (﴿"Oh, I wish I had taken a path along with the Messenger!"﴾), a badal ishtimal (inclusive apposition, where the second element includes the meaning of the first), because following the path of the Messenger includes abandoning the friendship of those who turn away from his path. So wishing for the first of the two to occur includes wishing for the second to occur.

The clause (ya wayla-ta, "Oh, woe to me") is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridha) between the clause (﴿"Oh, I wish I had taken a path along with the Messenger!"﴾) and the clause (﴿"Oh, I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend!"﴾).

(Fulan, "so-and-so") is a noun used as a kinaya for one whose proper name is not mentioned, just as (fulana, "so-and-such, feminine") is used as a kinaya for one whose proper feminine name is not intended to be mentioned, whether this occurs in narration or elsewhere. This was stated by Ibn al-Sikkit and Ibn Malik, in contrast to Ibn al-Sarraj and Ibn al-Hajib, who stipulated that it occur in a quoted speech. So (fulan) is treated like a proper noun with the added nun, and (fulana) like a proper noun with the feminine ta' marker. A poet combined both in his verse:

*Oh, may God curse the slanderers and their saying: "So-and-such has become a close friend of so-and-so!"* He meant himself and his beloved.

Al-Marrar al-'Absi said:

*When so-and-so dies leaving a noble quality, they fill the lack of his loss with another so-and-so.*

He meant: when one who has a name among them dies, they replace him with another in nobility. Likewise is the saying of Ma'n ibn AwS:

*Until I asked for a loan from every wealthy one, and so-and-so returned my need, and so-and-so.*

Abu Zayd said in his Nawadir: al-Mufaddal recited to me a verse by a man of Dabba who died more than a hundred years ago, i.e., in the middle of the first century of the Hijra:

*Indeed, for Sa'd among us there is a register that disgraces so-and-so and his son so-and-so.*

The motive for using the kinaya "so-and-so" is either intending to conceal his name for fear of him, or for fear of his family, or due to ignorance of him, or because mentioning him is of no benefit, or for the purpose of referring to a type of person who has a proper name. These last two are the ones that apply in this verse if it is understood as referring specifically to 'Uqba and Ubayy, or if it is understood as referring to every polytheist who has a close friend who prevented him from following Islam.

He wished that he had not taken him as a close friend rather than wishing that he had obeyed him in what he embellished for him, because the aim is to express revulsion toward his close friend from its very root, since misguidance is among the features of such friendship.

In it is an indication that the nature of close friendship is trust in the friend, and taking his counsel as sincere advice. A person should not place his friendship except where he is certain of safety from evil suggestions. God the Exalted said: (﴿O you who believe, do not take intimate associates from outside your own folk; they will not spare you from corruption﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118]). So whoever wishes to choose a close friend should follow his conduct in his private affairs, for he will drive whoever he befriends toward what he himself pursues. Khalid ibn Zuhayr, who was the nephew of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali, said:

*The first to be pleased with a practice is the one who follows it.*

In my view, this is the sense of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "If I were to take a close friend other than my Lord, I would have taken Abu Bakr as a close friend." For the station of prophethood demands morals above the common noble qualities among people, so it befits him only to follow what belongs to God of perfections to the extent of his capacity. For this reason 'A'isha said: "His character was the Qur'an." From this we know that Abu Bakr is the best of the Ummah in noble character after the Prophet (ﷺ), because the Prophet made him the one chosen for his friendship, had he taken a close friend other than God.

The clause (﴿"He led me astray from the Reminder"﴾) is a causal clause (ta'lili) explaining his wish that he had not taken so-and-so as a close friend: this friend of his has caused him the greatest loss, since he led him astray from the truth after he had almost become firmly established in it.

His saying (﴿"He led me astray from the Reminder"﴾) means: he embellished for me turning away from the truth. Al-dalal (misguidance) is losing the way and erring in it, to the point that one takes a path other than the intended one and ends up in a place other than the one he meant, perhaps falling into enemy territory or a place of wild beasts. Misguidance is used metaphorically for deviating from truth and right guidance toward falsehood and foolishness, just as its opposite, guidance (al-huda), which is reaching the path, is used metaphorically for recognizing truth and correctness, until the two literal meanings and the two figurative meanings became equal through frequent usage. These last two are the ones that apply in this verse if it is understood as referring specifically to 'Uqba and Ubayy, or if it is understood as referring to every polytheist who has a close friend who prevented him from following Islam.

He wished that he had not taken him as a close friend rather than wishing that he had obeyed him in what he embellished for him, because the aim is to express revulsion toward his close friend from its very root, since misguidance is among the features of such friendship.

In it is an indication that the nature of close friendship is trust in the friend, and taking his counsel as sincere advice. A person should not place his friendship except where he is certain of safety from evil suggestions. God the Exalted said: (﴿O you who believe, do not take intimate associates from outside your own folk; they will not spare you from corruption﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118]). So whoever wishes to choose a close friend should follow his conduct in his private affairs, for he will drive whoever he befriends toward what he himself pursues. Khalid ibn Zuhayr, who was the nephew of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali, said:

*The first to be pleased with a practice is the one who follows it.*

In my view, this is the sense of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "If I were to take a close friend other than my Lord, I would have taken Abu Bakr as a close friend." For the station of prophethood demands morals above the common noble qualities among people, so it befits him only to follow what belongs to God of perfections to the extent of his capacity. For this reason 'A'isha said: "His character was the Qur'an." From this we know that Abu Bakr is the best of the Ummah in noble character after the Prophet (ﷺ), because the Prophet made him the one chosen for his friendship, had he taken a close friend other than God.

The clause (﴿"He led me astray from the Reminder"﴾) is a causal clause (ta'lili) explaining his wish that he had not taken so-and-so as a close friend: this friend of his has caused him the greatest loss, since he led him astray from the truth after he had almost become firmly established in it.

His saying (﴿"He led me astray from the Reminder"﴾) means: he embellished for me turning away from the truth. Al-dalal (misguidance) is losing the way and erring in it, to the point that one takes a path other than the intended one and ends up in a place other than the one he meant, perhaps falling into enemy territory or a place of wild beasts. Misguidance is used metaphorically for deviating from truth and right guidance toward falsehood and foolishness, just as its opposite, guidance (al-huda), which is reaching the path, is used metaphorically for recognizing truth and correctness, until the two literal meanings and the two figurative meanings became equal through frequent usage. For this reason they called the guide who leads the caravan along the intended route a hadi (guide).

Misguidance (al-idlal) is used here metaphorically for diverting from truth, because of the correspondence with the metaphor of the path for the guidance of the Messenger. It is not used here in the sense that has become dominant for falsehood, as indicated by its transitivity with the particle (ʿan, "from") in his saying (ʿan al-dhikr, "from the Reminder"). For if misguidance were the embellishment of error, he would not need to be made transitive with it. Rather, what is intended here is the continuation of the previous image. So in his saying (aḍallani, "he led me astray") there is an implicit metaphor (makniyya) that requires comparing the Reminder to the path leading to salvation, and affirming misguidance from it is an imaginative figure (takhyil), like attributing claws to death. These are some of the subtleties of the eloquence of the structure of the verse.

The Reminder (al-dhikr) is the Qur'an, i.e., it forbade me from reflecting upon it and listening to it after I had come close to understanding it.

The coming (al-majiʾ) in his saying (idh jaʾani, "after it had come to me") is used to mean causing him to hear the Qur'an, as if the Qur'an came and alighted with him. From this comes the expression "the news of such-and-such came to me." Al-Nabigha said:

*It came to me, may you not be cursed, that you blamed me.*

If the wrongdoer in His saying (﴿"on the Day when the wrongdoer will bite on his hands"﴾) is understood as a specific individual, namely 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, then the meaning of the Reminder's coming to him is that he used to sit with the Prophet (ﷺ) and feel at ease with him, until Ubayy ibn Khalaf turned him away from that and led him to enmity and harming him. If the wrongdoer is understood in general, then the coming of the Reminder is the spread of the Qur'an among them and the possibility of their hearing it. Misguidance of their close friends from it means each one diverting his friend from that, and their cooperating with one another in that.

It has been said: the Reminder is the statement of testimony (kalimat al-shahada), based on restricting the wrongdoer to 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt as mentioned above, and the previously mentioned interpretations apply in this regard. For since the statement of testimony was the cause of salvation, it was represented by the path of the guiding Messenger, and turning away from it was represented by misguidance from the path.

(Idh) is an adverb of past time, meaning "at a time when the Reminder had come to me." Using the adverbial phrase here, rather than saying "after the Reminder came to me" or "after it had come to me," indicates the firm establishment of the Reminder, since it has settled in a time and become certain. Among its parallels is the verse: ﴿And Allah would not have misguided a people after He had guided them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 115], meaning that His guidance had firmly taken hold among them.

The clause ﴿And Satan is ever, for man, a deserter﴾ is a concluding remark (tadhyil) from the words of Allah, not from the words of the wrongdoer. It serves as an admonition to people that all this misguidance is the work of Satan, for it is he who beautifies to the friend of the wrongdoer the misguiding of his friend, because Satan is a khadhul (one who forsakes) of man, meaning he is inherently disposed to great forsaking.

Al-khadhl (forsaking) is leaving off the support of one who seeks help while being able to support him. It was already discussed under the verse ﴿And if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him?﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 160], in Surat Ali 'Imran.

So when he aids in the defeat, that is the greatest forsaking, and this is the intended meaning of the intensive form in describing Satan as one who forsakes man, because Satan schemes against man and thrusts him into harm, and so he is a khadhul.

Page 17

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 30:

﴿And the Messenger says, "My Lord, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned."﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the statements of the polytheists. Its connection to His saying ﴿Indeed, he almost led me away from the reminder after it had come to me﴾ [al-Furqan: 29] is that the reminder (al-dhikr) is the Qur'an. So the Messenger's complaint to his Lord about his people is related, concerning their rejection of the Qur'an through the enticement of their leaders and chiefs who led them astray from the Qur'an, that is, from reflecting upon it after it had come to them and they had been able to consider it. This statement took place in the world, and the Messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ). It is a report used in the sense of a complaint.

The purpose of relating the Messenger's statement is to warn the Quraysh that the Messenger has turned to his Lord regarding this matter, so he seeks His help, and He is about to grant him victory. Its emphasis with (inna) is for the sake of giving it importance, so that the complaint may be stronger. Referring to the Quraysh as (my people) is to increase the sense of grievance at their conduct toward him, because it is the nature of a man's people to agree with him.

The verb of taking (ittikhadh), when it is qualified by a state, indicates the intense care the one who takes it has for that state, to the point that he committed the act for its sake and made it his intention. Thus this is more emphatic in describing their abandonment of the Qur'an than saying: "My people abandoned the Qur'an."

The demonstrative in (this Qur'an) serves to magnify it, and [indicates] that the like of it should not be taken as abandoned; rather it is worthy of being turned to and benefited from.

Al-mahjur: that which is left and forsaken. The meaning here is abandoning concern for it and listening to it.

This is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ: that what he encountered from some of his people is a customary pattern (sunnah) among the nations with their prophets. It also serves as a warning to the polytheists, so that they might examine their own circumstances in light of this historical rule and come to know that their situation is like that of those who denied the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud.

Page 18

As for the expression (wa-kadhalika), it was discussed earlier in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. The word 'aduww (enemy) is a term that applies to the singular and the plural, and what is meant here is the plural.

He described the enemies of the prophets as being "of the criminals" (min al-mujrimin), meaning from among the body of criminals, since criminality (ijram) is more general than enmity toward the prophets, though enmity toward them is the gravest form of it. What is intended here is to establish that the enemies of the prophets are enrolled within the company of criminals, because that is more emphatic in description than saying "enemies who are criminals," as was discussed earlier at the words of the Exalted: ﴿He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67] in Surat al-Baqarah.

He followed the consolation with the promise of guidance for many of those who at that time turn away from him, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Perhaps Allah will bring forth from their loins one who will worship Him." And with the promise that He will help him against those who persist in their enmity toward him, because the statement ﴿and sufficient is your Lord as guide and helper﴾ carries an implication of entrusting the matter to Him, for He is sufficient for guidance and for victory.

The letter ba' in His saying "bi-Rabbika" (by your Lord) is for emphasis, affirming the connection of the agent to the verb. Its original form is: "Your Lord suffices in this situation."

He returns to their excuses and their baseless objections. They criticized the Qur'an on the grounds that it was revealed in installments, and they said: "If it were from Allah, it would have been sent down as a single book all at once." The pronoun in (قالوا) appears to refer to the polytheists. This is ignorance on their part regarding the revelation of the books of the Messengers. None of those books was revealed all at once. Rather, they were revealed as dispersed revelation. The Tawrah (Torah), which was revealed to Musa (peace be upon him) on the tablets, consisted of ten words, about the length of Surat al-Layl in the Qur'an. The Injil (Gospel) was nothing but statements that 'Isa (peace be upon him) uttered before the assembly. Likewise, the Zabur (Psalms) was revealed in many fragments. So the polytheists either attributed this to the earlier books or were ignorant, and they said: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down upon Muhammad all at once, so that we would know that he is the Messenger of Allah?" It has been said that the one who made this claim was the Jews or the Christians. If that is correct, then it is slander from them, because they know that the Tawrah, the Injil and the Zabur were not revealed except in installments.

[p. 19]

Therefore, the lengthy discussion by the exegetes about the difference between the condition of our Messenger, who was unlettered, and the condition of the Messengers to whom books were revealed is an occupation with what is of no benefit. Those books were never revealed as complete volumes at all.

Here (نُزِّلَ) is synonymous with (أُنْزِلَ), and it does not carry the notice of intensification that the form of tafʿil (the intensive form) indicates, as was mentioned in the first introduction of this tafsir (exegesis), because of the indication in their words: "all at once."

His statement (﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾) came as a response to their objection. It is therefore a resumed statement containing a rejection of what they intended by their words: (﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾). In it, he turned away from addressing them to addressing the Messenger (peace be upon him), informing him of the wisdom behind its being revealed in installments. Implicit in this is a favor upon the Messenger, in that it strengthens his heart and makes things easier for him.

His statement (كَذَلِكَ, "thus") is an answer to their words (﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾). It refers to the revelation implied by (﴿the Qur'an was sent down to him﴾), which is the state of the Qur'an being revealed in installments. That is, "We revealed it in that manner," meaning the installment-wise manner, the manner whose wisdom they were ignorant of. The demonstrative (اسم الإشارة, the demonstrative word) is in the accusative position, as it is a substitute for an absolute object (مفعول مطلق, an adverbial object of the verb's own noun) that came in place of the verb. The implied meaning is: "We revealed it with a revelation like that installment-wise revelation." The position of the clause (كَذَلِكَ) is therefore that of a resumption in the discourse. The lām in (لِنُثَبِّتَ, "that We may strengthen") is connected to the implied verb that is indicated by (كَذَلِكَ). Al-tathbit (strengthening) means making a thing firm. Al-thabat (firmness) means a thing's settling in its place without being shaken. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿like a good tree whose root is firm﴾ [Ibrahim: 24]). Firmness is also used metaphorically for certainty and for tranquility about good coming to its possessor. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿it would have been better for them and stronger in firmness﴾ [al-Nisa': 66]). These are widespread metaphors based on comparing the occurrence of doubts in the soul to the agitation of a thing in its place, a comparison of an intelligible matter to a perceptible one. The fu'ad (heart) here means the intellect. Strengthening it through that revelation means making it firm in its wording and its meanings so that it is not agitated.

The wisdom behind revealing the Qur'an in installments is expressed in one comprehensive phrase: (﴿that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾), because strengthening the heart requires everything that is good for the soul. Among what al-Zamakhshari said about this is: "The wisdom in its being revealed in dispersed form is that by dispersing it We strengthen your heart so that you may understand and memorize it, because the one who receives knowledge is only able to keep it in his heart when it is delivered to him one thing after another and part after part,"

[p. 20]

"following one part after another." And he also said: "that it used to be revealed according to the occasions, the events, and the answers to questioners." End of quotation. That is, they would be more attentive to what was revealed, because they were in need of its knowledge, so the practice of what it contains would increase. This is among the things that strengthen the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ) and expand his breast.

And what he said after that: "Its being revealed in installments, and its challenge to them to produce something like those installments each time something was revealed, is more effective for the miraculous nature (i'jaz) and more illuminating for the proof than if it had been revealed all at once." End of quotation.

Among what was also said is what the grandfather, the minister (al-Jadd al-Wazir), may Allah have mercy on him, stated: "If the Qur'an had not been revealed in installments according to events, then the correspondence of many of its verses to what the situation requires and their suitability to the context would not have appeared, and that is part of the completeness of its miraculous nature." I say: its being revealed in installments is more helpful to its memorizers in understanding it and reflecting upon it.

His statement (﴿and We arranged it in arrangement﴾) is coordinated with his statement (كَذَلِكَ, "thus"): We revealed it in installments and We arranged it. Al-tartil (measured arrangement) is attributed to speech when it is well composed and clear in meaning. The linguists unanimously agree that this tartil is derived from their saying: thaghr murattal wa ratil, meaning a mouth whose teeth are well spaced and resemble the brightness of the chamomile flower. They did not cite any evidence for it from the speech of the Arabs.

The tartil may be a state of the Qur'an's revelation, meaning: We revealed it in dispersed form, arranged in its wording and meanings, not piled up together. It is dispersed in time, so that when the revelation of a surah was completed, its verses came in an ordered and harmonious arrangement, as if they had been revealed all at once. And it is dispersed in composition in that it is detailed and clear. In this there is an indication that this is among the signs that it is from Allah, because the way of human speech, when its composition is dispersed over widely separated times, is that it becomes disjointed and its sentences lack resemblance.

It is also possible that what is meant by (رَتَّلْناهُ, "We arranged it") is: We commanded its recitation in a measured way (tartil), meaning reciting it in a measured manner, with deliberation, without hurrying through its recitation, so that all of its letters and vowels are clearly articulated at a leisurely pace. This is what is mentioned in Surat al-Muzzammil in His saying, the Exalted: (﴿and recite the Qur'an in measured recitation﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 4]).

And (تَرْتِيلًا, "measured arrangement") is a verbal noun in the accusative as an absolute object. Its indefinite form is intended to convey the meaning of magnification, so the verbal noun comes to specify the kind of tartil.

[Page 21]

﴿And they will not bring you any example but We will bring you the truth and better explanation.﴾

When he (Allah) had thoroughly enumerated most of their excuses and pretexts, and had silenced them with rebuttals that stopped their mouths, He followed this with a comprehensive summation that covers what has preceded and whatever doubts and deceptions they might yet bring, on the basis that all of it is refuted by the clear proof that exposes their nonsense.

*Al-mithl* means the similar. The verb *al-ityan* ("bring") is used figuratively for their statements and their disputation with them. The indefinite *mathal* ("example") in a negative context implies generality: any example whatsoever. What is meant is an example of the same kind as those previously mentioned, beginning with His words: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "This is nothing but a fabrication he has invented, and other people have helped him with it."﴾ [al-Furqan: 4], ﴿And they say, "Tales of the ancients, which he has had written down."﴾ [al-Furqan: 5], ﴿And they say, "What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], ﴿And the wrongdoers say, "You follow only a man affected by sorcery."﴾ [al-Furqan: 8], ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Why have the angels not been sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 21], and ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]. The context supports this, since the sentence follows the enumeration of their doubts. This meaning is also indicated by His earlier words in relation to "example": ﴿See how they have coined examples for you﴾ [al-Furqan: 9], which comes right after His words: ﴿And the wrongdoers say, "You follow only a man affected by sorcery."﴾ [al-Furqan: 8]. The transitive form of the verb *ya'tunaka* ("they bring you") to the pronoun of the Prophet ﷺ indicates that their bringing of examples is intended to overwhelm him.

*Al-ityan* is used figuratively here to mean manifesting. The meaning is: they will not bring you any likeness by which they liken some state of yours, seeking to show that your condition does not resemble that of a messenger from Allah, but We will refute their comparison and show them that the state of receiving a message from Allah does not necessarily entail what they claim. This applies whether what they bring is an explicit comparison with the conditions of non-prophets, such as their saying: ﴿Tales of the ancients, which he has had written down﴾ [al-Furqan: 5], and their saying: ﴿What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], and their saying: ﴿You follow only a man affected by sorcery﴾ [al-Furqan: 8]; or whether it is a denial of the similarity of his condition to the conditions of the messengers as they claim. For the denial of resemblance to a thing implies the affirmation of its opposite, as in their saying: ﴿Why have the angels not been sent down to us, or do we not see our Lord?﴾ [al-Furqan: 21]. Likewise their saying: ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ [al-Furqan: 32], if they said it with the meaning that it differs from the manner in which the Torah and the Gospel were sent down. This, then, is a denial of the assimilation of the condition of the Messenger ﷺ to the conditions of the earlier messengers, as they claim. Included in this category is what they claim that prophethood requires in terms of rank with Allah, that he should ask Him and be granted it, as in their saying: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him to be a warner with him, or a treasure not been thrown to him, or a garden not been given to him from which he may eat?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7].

[Page 22]

The imperfect form in His words "they will not bring you" includes whatever they may yet bring of this kind, such as their saying: ﴿Or cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed﴾ [al-Isra': 92].

The exception in His words ﴿but We will bring you the truth﴾ is an exception from general states implied by the generality of the examples, because the generality of persons entails the generality of states.

The clause ﴿We will bring you﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), as mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿Greatly [arrogant]. And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food﴾ [al-Furqan: 19].

His words ﴿We will bring you the truth﴾ are the counterpart of His words ﴿they will not bring you any example﴾, and the bringing here is figurative. The contrast between ﴿We will bring you the truth﴾ and ﴿they will not bring you any example﴾ indicates that what they bring is false. For example, their saying: ﴿What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7] is refuted by His saying: ﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾ [al-Furqan: 20].

The expression concerning what Allah supports with proof as "We have brought you" (*ji'naka*) rather than "We have come to you" (*atayna*), just as what they bring is expressed by "they bring you" (*ya'tunaka*), is either merely for stylistic variation (*tafannun*), or because the verb *al-ityan*, when used figuratively, is frequently applied to what is harmful and disliked, such as threats and satire. Shaqiq ibn Sharik al-Asadi said:

*A threat came to me from Abu Anas, so my body was drawn out of the anger of al-Dahhak.*

And the saying of al-Nabigha:

*"There has come to me, may you not be blessed with curses, that you have blamed me..."*

And his saying:

*"Surely there will come to you poems, and there will push against you an army whose forefront is the saddles' riders."*

He means poems of satire. And the saying of the angels to Lot: ﴿And We have brought you the truth﴾ [al-Hijr: 64], meaning the punishment of his people, and for this reason they said to him in the literal sense of coming: ﴿Rather, we have brought you that about which they were doubting﴾ [al-Hijr: 63]. This was discussed in Surat al-Hijr. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The command of your Lord has come by night or by day﴾ [Yunus: 24], ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl: 1], ﴿So Allah came to them from where they did not expect﴾ [al-Hashr: 2]. This differs from the verb *al-maji'* (coming) when used figuratively, for it is most often used for the arrival of good, of promise, of victory, and of a great matter. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿There has certainly come to you proof from your Lord﴾ [al-Nisa': 174], ﴿And your Lord has come, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ [al-Fajr: 22], ﴿When the victory of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nasr: 1]. And in the hadith of the Night Journey (*al-Isra'*): "...Welcome to him, and what a welcome he has received!" And: ﴿And say, "The truth has come, and falsehood has departed"﴾ [al-Isra': 81]. The object of the verb may have two aspects depending on the viewpoint, so both verbs may be used, as in: ﴿Until when Our command came and the oven gushed forth﴾ [Hud: 40], for the command here is viewed as a beneficial support for Noah.

*Al-tafsir* (exposition, explanation): clarification and disclosure of meaning. Its meaning has been discussed in detail in the first introduction of this book. What is intended here is the disclosure of the proof and the evidence.

The meaning of its being "better" is that it is more deserving in argumentation. The superlative here is for emphasis, since there is no beauty in their argument; or what is meant by beauty is the glitter of their sophistry and doubts, whereas the disclosure of the truth has a better effect on the hearts of the listeners than their deceptions. In this sense the superlative is in its literal sense. This is a subtle point of the usage and of the subtleties of the revelation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 34:

﴿Those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell—those are worse in position and further astray from the way.﴾

This is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), serving to console the Messenger (ﷺ) and to threaten and censure the polytheists.

The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) stands in the place of a pronoun, as if it had been said: "They are gathered upon their faces." Thus the pronoun refers back to "those who disbelieved" in His words: (﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not revealed to him all at once?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]). The explicit noun is used in place of the pronoun in order to convey the benefit that the owners of the pronoun are the ones to whom the content of the relative clause applies, and in order to base upon the relative clause the position of a demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah). The apparent arrangement of the discourse would have been: "And they do not bring you any example except that We bring you the truth and better explanation; they are worse in position and further astray from the way, and We will gather them upon their faces to Hell," just as He said in Surat al-Isra' (﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces﴾ [al-Isra': 97]) following His words: (﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them except that they said, "Has Allah sent a human as a messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra': 94]). It is known from the context, by way of allusion, that those who are gathered upon their faces are those who bring forth examples in denial of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Since their purpose in the examples they bring forth is to belittle the status of the Prophet (ﷺ), they are reminded that they are the people of the worst place and the most misguided path, not the Prophet (ﷺ). So the relative pronoun is the subject (mubtada') and the demonstrative noun is the predicate about it.

The meaning of (﴿they are gathered upon their faces﴾) has already been explained in Surat al-Isra' at His words: (﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces﴾ [al-Isra': 97]). The hadith concerning the question of how they walk upon their faces has also been mentioned previously.

"Sharr" (worse) is a superlative noun (ism tafdil), its original form being "ashharr." The two superlative forms in His words, "sharr" and "adall" (more astray), are used for intensification in the attribution of evil and misguidance, like His words: (﴿He said, "You are worse in position"﴾ [Yusuf: 77]) in answer to the statement of Joseph's brothers: (﴿If he steals, there has already stolen a brother of his before﴾ [Yusuf: 77]).

The definiteness of the two parts of the sentence conveys restriction (qasr), and it is a restriction for intensification, by placing them in the position of those in whom evil and misguidance are confined. It is narrated from Muqatil that the disbelievers said to the Muslims, "They are the worst of creation," so this verse was revealed; the restriction is then qasr qalb (restriction by reversal), meaning: they are worse in position and further astray, not the Muslims. The two superlative forms are, on both interpretations, stripped of comparison.

"Makan" means place of residence, and "sabil" means way. Their place is Hell, and their way is the path leading to it, which is the one upon which they are gathered on their faces.

The use of the demonstrative noun after what preceded serves to draw attention to the fact that those indicated are deserving of the worst place and the most misguided way, because of what preceded of their conditions, among which is their saying: (﴿Why was the Qur'an not revealed to him all at once?﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]).

"Sabilan" is a tamyiz (specification) transferred from the subject; its original form is: "wa dalla sabiluhum" (and their way went astray). Attributing misguidance to the way in the transferred construction is an intellectual metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because the way is the cause of their misguidance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 35–36:

﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book and made his brother Harun a helper with him.﴾ ﴿So We said, "Go to the people who denied Our signs," and We destroyed them with complete destruction.﴾

When the warning and the consolation were mentioned through the account of the state of those who denied the Messenger (ﷺ),

he followed that with their illustration through the nations that denied their messengers, so that from it there would be an admonition for these people and an increase in consolation for the Messenger, along with an allusion to his promise of victory over them.

The mention began with Musa and his people because they are closer in time to those mentioned after him, and because remnants of his law and his community remained well known among the Arabs. If it is authentically reported that those who said, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" [al-Furqan: 32] were the Jews, then the rationale for beginning with what was given to Musa is more evident.

The particle of certainty (harf al-tahqiq) and the oath-lam are for emphasizing the report in view of what it contains of the warning concerning their destruction. By "the Book" is meant the revelation that is written down and preserved, and this was from the very first of what was revealed to him. The intended meaning is not the tablets, because his being given the tablets came after the time of His saying, "Go to the people" [al-Furqan: 36]. So His saying "then We said: Go" is a consequence of the giving of the Book, and the giving is therefore prior to it.

In describing the revelation as a Book there is an allusion to the ignorance of the polytheists who said, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" [al-Furqan: 32], for the books that the messengers were given were nothing but revelation that descended in portions, which the messengers then gathered and their followers wrote down.

The allusion here also points to supporting Musa with Harun, and it is an indirect rebuttal of the polytheists when they said, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him so that he might be a warner with him?" [al-Furqan: 7]. When wisdom required Musa's support, he was not supported with an angel, but was supported with a messenger like himself.

The wazir (minister/helper) is the one who assists and backs, who gives aid and support. It is derived from al-azr, which means strength. The root of azr is tightening the back with a waist-wrap when one sets about a laborious task, and this was discussed earlier in Surah Ta-Ha. Harun was a second messenger, while Musa was the principal. "The people" are the Copts of Egypt, the people of Pharaoh.

The phrase "who denied Our signs" is a description of the people and is not part of what was said to Musa and Harun, because the denial had not yet occurred from them at that time. Rather, it is a description serving to inform the readers of the Qur'an that Musa and Harun conveyed the message and that God manifested the signs through them, yet the people of Pharaoh denied them and thereby deserved destruction. This is an allusion to the polytheists in their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ), and a preparation for the consequence stated by "so We destroyed them with complete destruction," which is the very purpose of the admonition and consolation.

صفحة ٢٦
The relative pronoun in "who denied Our signs" serves to indicate the reason for the report about their destruction.

This arrangement has achieved a remarkable concision by which the story is abbreviated, mentioning only its two edges: its beginning and its end, because these are the purpose of the story, namely the deserving of the nations' destruction through their denial of their messengers.

Destruction (tadmir) is annihilation, and ruin (halak) is dumur.

The following of the verb with the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq) is due to what the indefiniteness of the verbal noun contains of magnifying the destruction, which was immersion in the sea.
