Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 37:

﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them and made them a sign for mankind. And We have prepared for the wrongdoers a painful punishment.﴾

This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence ﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾ [al-Furqan: 35], on the basis that the purpose is to describe his people by their denial and to report their destruction.

The phrase "the people of Noah" (qawma Nūḥ) is in the accusative by a verb omitted that is explained by "We drowned them" (aghraqnāhum), by way of the construction known as ishtighāl (the verb being occupied with a pronoun referring back to the noun). The interposition of the word "lammā" (when) does no harm, because it functions like a time adverb (ẓarf), and its answer (jawāb) is omitted, indicated by the explainer of the omitted verb. In this arrangement there is an emphasis on the people of Noah, since their condition is the place of lesson, so their mention is put first and then reinforced by their pronoun.

It is also permissible that "the people of Noah" be a coordination with the object pronoun in the phrase "fa-dammarnāhum" (so We destroyed them), meaning: and We destroyed the people of Noah. In that case the clause "when they denied the messengers, We drowned them" serves to explain the clause "We destroyed them."

"Āya" (sign) means a proof, that is, We made them a proof of the fate of those who deny their messengers. Making them a sign is that the report of their drowning spread widely as a sign.

The people of Noah are described as having denied the messengers, although they denied only one messenger, because in their denial they relied on the claim that God would not send a human being. They said: ﴿This is only a human being like you who wants to make himself superior over you. And if God had willed, He would have sent down angels. We have not heard of this among our first fathers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24]. Thus their denial entailed the denial of all the messengers in general. Also, they were the first to deny their messenger, so they became an example for those who denied after them.

The story of the people of Noah has already been covered in Surat al-A'raf and Surat Hud.

The sentence ﴿And We have prepared for the wrongdoers a painful punishment﴾ is coordinated with "We drowned them." The meaning is: We punished them in this world by drowning, and We have prepared for them a painful punishment in the Hereafter. The explicit noun "the wrongdoers" is used in place of the pronoun "for them," to convey that their punishment is a recompense for their wrongdoing through polytheism and denial of the Messenger.

**[Page 28]**

The four nouns are in the accusative by a verb that is omitted and implied by (*tabbarna*, "We destroyed"). Placing them first creates suspense for the reader to learn what will be said about them. It is also permissible for these nouns to be in the accusative by coordination with the object pronoun in His words: ﴿So We destroyed them with total destruction﴾ [al-Furqan: 36].

The nunation (*tanwin*) of "'Ad" and "Thamud," although the intended meaning is two nations, is as follows. The nunation of "'Ad" is a sound position, because it is a noun free of the feminine marker and not longer than three letters, so its rule is to be declined (*sarf*). As for the declension of "Thamud" in the reading of the majority, it is based on treating it as the name of a father. In my view, the more apparent reason is that its nunation is for pairing with "'Ad," as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿chains and shackles and a blazing fire﴾.

Hamzah, Hafs and Ya'qub read it without nunation, in accordance with what the apparent meaning of the name of the nation requires, namely its feminine sense as a nation. The mention of 'Ad has already occurred in Surat al-A'raf.

As for the companions of the *Rass*, the exegetes differed in identifying them, but they agreed that the *Rass* is a great well or a large pit. Since it is the name of a type of place on earth, the Arabs applied it to many places in the lands of Arabia.

Zuhayr said:

*They set out at dawn and reached the oasis at a time of pre-dawn,*
*so they and the valley of the Rass are like the hand to the mouth.*

They also named as *Rass* what they knew of the lands of Persia. The annexation of "companions" (*ashab*) to "*Rass*" is either because they were struck by a collapse in a *Rass*, or because they were camping by a *Rass*, or because they dug a *Rass*, just as the companions of the trench (*al-Ukhdud*), who dug it and set it on fire, were so named. The majority hold that it is from the lands of al-Yamamah, and it is called Falj.

The scholars differed about who is meant by "the companions of the *Rass*" in this verse. It was said: they are a people from the remnants of Thamud. Al-Suhayli said: they are a people who were in 'Adan, to whom Handhalah ibn Safwan was sent as a messenger. There was the 'Anqa', which is the largest of birds (it was called 'Anqa' because of the length of its neck), and it dwelt on a mountain called Fatih. It would swoop down on their children and snatch them away if hunting became difficult for it. Handhalah prayed against it, and God destroyed it with thunderbolts. They worshipped idols and killed their prophet, so God destroyed them. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: they were swallowed up by the earth along with their dwellings.

It was also said: they are the people of Shu'ayb. It was said: they were a people who were with the people of Shu'ayb. Muqatil and al-Suddi said: the *Rass* is a well in Antioch, and the companions of the *Rass* are the people of Antioch, to whom Habib the carpenter was sent. They killed him and threw him into a well. This is the one mentioned in Surat Ya Sin: ﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man running. He said, "O my people, follow the messengers"﴾ [Ya Sin: 20], and the verses that follow.

It was also said: the *Rass* is a valley in Adharbayjan, in Arran, which flows out of Qaliqala and empties into the lake of Jurjan. I do not think it is what is meant in this verse. Perhaps it is due to similarity of names. It is said that there were a thousand cities around it, which were destroyed by the earth's collapse. Other things were said that are even more remote.

**[Page 29]**

"The generations" (*al-qurun*) means the nations, since *qarn* is applied to a nation. This was already discussed at His words: ﴿Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ [al-An'am: 6], at the beginning of Surat al-An'am. In a hadith: "The best of generations is my generation, then those who follow them," and so on.

The pointing in His words "between that" refers to the nations already mentioned. The meaning of "between that" is that other nations came between those peoples, beginning from the people of Noah.

In this verse there is an indication of the great length and the multitude of these generations.

The nunation in "kullan" is compensatory nunation (*tanwin 'iwad*) for the omitted genitive complement. The estimate is: "and all of them, We struck examples for them." The first "kullan" is in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by "We struck for him," its estimate being: "We warned, or admonished, each one, and We struck for him examples." The second "kullan" is in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by "tabbarna." Both are of the type of *ishtighal* (a construction in which a noun is governed by a verb that is implicitly or explicitly tied to a pronoun referring to it, creating a choice of case).

*Tatbir* is the breaking into fragments of hard bodies such as glass and iron. *Tatbir* was used for destruction by way of metaphor: subsidiary (*taba'iyya*) in "tabbarna," and original (*asliyya*) in "tatbiran." It was discussed at His words: ﴿Indeed, these are destroyed in what they are doing﴾ [al-A'raf: 139], in Surat al-A'raf, and at His words: ﴿and that they might destroy what they had conquered with complete destruction﴾ [al-Isra': 7], in Surat al-Isra'. "*Tatbiran*" is in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*, a verbal noun that reinforces its verb) to emphasize the severity of this destruction.

The meaning of "striking examples" is stating them and making them clear. It was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to strike an example, whatever it may be﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The *mithl* (example) is the equal and the similar, that is, We made clear to them the likenesses and parallels in good and evil, so that they might present the state of their own souls by them. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, and it became clear to you how We dealt with them, and We struck for you examples﴾ [Ibrahim: 45].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 40:**

﴿Indeed, they have passed by the town that was rained upon with the rain of evil. Did they not used to see it? Rather, they did not expect a resurrection.﴾

Since the narration of the news of the people of Nuh, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of al-Rass (the Well), and the generations between them was intended to make Quraysh take heed from their fates, the arrangement of the speech here shifts to their neglect of taking heed from these, and from what is more evident to their eyes, namely the traces of the punishment that descended upon the town of the people of Lut.

The report is linked with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) to convey the sense of wonder at their failure to take heed, as mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿They have certainly been arrogant about themselves﴾ (25:21). Quraysh used to pass by the dwellings of the people of Lut on their journeys for trade to al-Sham, so their dwellings were on the road they traveled. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning and at night. Will you not reason?﴾ (37:137). Their trade route went from Makkah past al-Madinah, and they would enter the land of Palestine, passing alongside the Lake of Lut, on whose shore are the remains of the city of (Sodom), most of which the water has submerged. Its mention was given earlier, at His saying: ﴿And indeed, they were on a clear highway﴾ (15:79), in Surat al-Hijr.

*al-ityan* means coming. Its construction with (ʿala) is by way of tadmin (implicit meaning, i.e., the verb is given the sense of another verb), with the sense of "pass by," because the purpose of mentioning the coming to the town is to remind of the fate of its people. Their coming to it was thus like passing by its people. So the verb "coming" was given the meaning of "passing," since it resembles passing by. Passing by is related to inhabitants, whereas coming is related to a place; it is said "We came to Khurasan," but not "We passed by Khurasan." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning and at night. Will you not reason?﴾ (37:137).

He described the town as ﴿that was rained upon with the rain of evil﴾ because it was well known among the Arabs through the content of the connection with the People of the Book. This town is the one called (Sodom), with a fatha on the sin and a light dal. The people of Lut had five towns, the greatest of which was (Sodom). Its mention was given earlier, at His saying: ﴿And Lut, when he said to his people﴾ (7:80), in Surat al-A'raf.

(*matar al-saw*) is a punishment that descended upon them from the sky, consisting of stones of sulfur and ash. Calling it "rain" is by way of figurative resemblance, since the reality of rain is water from the sky.

*al-sawʾ* with a fatha on the sin means harm and punishment, while with a damma on the sin it means that which causes distress. The fatha is the original form of the verbal noun of *sāʾahu*. As for *al-suʾ* with a damma, it is an ism al-masdar (a noun functioning as a verbal noun), so the verbal noun came to be used for that which causes harm, and the ism al-masdar for the opposite of goodness.

Following from the confirmation of their coming upon the town together with their failure to benefit from it, there is a rhetorical (suri) question about the absence of their seeing it at the time they came upon it. Since they did not take heed from it, they were like one who asks about them: "Did they see it?" So the question serves to awaken the minds to investigate their condition. It is either used for denial and threat, or used to awaken them to know the cause of their failure to take admonition.

His saying: ﴿Rather, they did not expect a resurrection﴾ may be such that (*bal*) is a transitional idrab (a change of subject, marking a shift), "

صفحة ٣٠

" a transition from describing their denial of the Prophet ﷺ and their failure to take admonition from what befell the nations who denied, to mentioning their denial of the resurrection. In that case the speech ends at His saying: ﴿Did they not used to see it?﴾, and this is what follows the first reading of the question.

He expressed their denial of the resurrection by their not expecting it, because one who denies the resurrection does not hope from it for benefit nor fear from it for harm. So He expressed denial of the resurrection by one of the two aspects of denial, as an allusion that they are not like the believers who hope for the mercy of Allah.

*al-nushur* is the verbal noun of *nashara al-mayyit*, meaning he brought the dead to life, so that he came back to life (*nashara*, i.e., he lived). It is among the words that have been used in Arabic speech in the sense of imagination, since they do not believe in it. It is related that al-Muhalhil, in his fighting against Bani Bakr ibn Wa'il, who had killed his brother Kulayb, said:

*O Bakr, bring Kulayb back to me alive! O Bakr, where, where is the flight?*

If the attribution of the verse to him is sound, his purpose by this was to make them incapable, so that he could find a way to fight them.

The meaning is: they did not believe in the resurrection, so they had no readiness to take admonition, because taking admonition arises from vigilance and self-accounting in seeking salvation. These polytheists, having been raised in neglect of preparation for what follows death, had their understanding confined to this hastening world, so they cared only for the means and instruments of the immediate. Even with their keenness in discerning natures and marks, their watching the movement of the stars, the changes of rain and wind, and the scent of the dust of the dwellings of the living, they were in all of this turning their gaze away from contemplating divine matters and the life of the souls and the like. The root of all this misguidance followed for them from denying the resurrection. Therefore it is made here the cause of the absence of their taking admonition from the fate of a nation that denied its messenger and disobeyed its Lord. In this sense came His saying: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for those who discern﴾ (15:75), meaning: not for those who do not discern.

﴿When they see you, they take you only in mockery: "Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?"﴾ ﴿"He almost led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in them."﴾ [al-Furqan: 41-42].

What was previously narrated of the forms of their harm to the Messenger, peace be upon him, was in speech about him in his absence. So there was joined to it in this verse a specific harm, namely the harm of when they see him. This is a kind of harm that the sight of the Messenger stirs in them. He does not dress like the great and the affluent, does not trail his cloak, does not ride fine mounts, does not walk proudly, does not look with arrogance, keeps company with the righteous, turns away from the polytheists, is gentle with the weak, and keeps ties with the poor. Those people hold good character in contempt, because folly dominated their opinions. Therefore their situation with him was never free of mockery of him when they saw him, on the ground that his condition is not that of one whom God would choose for His message instead of them, nor is he fit to lead them and govern them. This statement came from Abu Jahl and the people of his assembly.

"Idhā" (when) is a temporal adverb that carries the meaning of a conditional, so its complement is made its answer. Thus the clause (﴿they take you only in mockery﴾) is the answer to "idhā". "Huzu'" (mockery), with two dammas, is the verbal noun of "hazi'a bihi" (he mocked him). It occurred earlier in His words: ﴿They said: "Do you take us in mockery?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67], in Surat al-Baqarah. The description is for emphasis in their mockery of him, to the point that he is as if the very essence of mockery, because they had wholly devoted themselves to it. The attribution of "yattakhidhūnaka" (they take you) to the plural pronoun indicates that their groups mock him when they see him while they are in their gatherings and assemblies. The form of restriction (ḥaṣr) serves to censure them, because their taking him was confined to mocking him; they persist in it and never mix with it any recollection of his words or his call. So the exception is from the general class of negated states: that is, they take you in no state except the state of mockery.

The clause ﴿"Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?"﴾ explains the clause ﴿they take you only in mockery﴾, because mockery is of the category of speech, so its explanation was given by what is among their words and by their trading of talk among themselves.

The interrogation is a denial that God would have sent him as a messenger.

The demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara) is used for belittlement, as you know from the beginning of the explanation of this verse.

The meaning is: a denial that the one pointed to should be a messenger, because in pointing to him there is enough to conclude, in their claim, that he is not the messenger of God. A near parallel to this clause occurred in His words: ﴿When those who disbelieve see you, they take you only in mockery: "Is this the one who mentions your gods?"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 36], in Surat al-Anbiya', except that the interrogation there is one of wonder, so consult it.

As for their words: ﴿"He almost led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in them."﴾ [al-Furqan: 42], the intent of it is their boasting of their firmness in their religion, and that they had nearly followed the Messenger's call through what he presented to them of persuasion and insistence. The effect of his words on their hearing was about to bring them to abandon the worship of idols, had they not delayed. In that delay they came to their senses from the veil of his words and the enchantment of his argument, and they looked clearly at his appearance, and it became evident to them that he does not deserve to be sent from God. Thus in their speech they combined the discrediting of his proof with the praise of their own steadfastness in a position that would unsettle those not firmly rooted in disbelief. This speech is tainted by corrupt structure and composed in the manner of the common crowd, for they speak as they wish and make the listeners seem foolish. Among the enchantments of their sophistry is their attributing the near-misleading to the Messenger rather than to themselves, out of disdain for admitting that they had come close to going astray from their gods, although his coming close to misleading them entails their coming close to error.

"In" (إنْ) is a lightened form of the emphatic "inna", and most commonly in speech it is left inactive, that is, it does not govern the accusative of the subject nor the nominative of the predicate. The clause that follows it must necessarily begin with a verb of the sisters of "kāna" or of the sisters of "ẓanna". This is one of the rare usages. If we hold that its subject is a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr sha'n) and that the clause after it is a predicate of that pronoun, as they held regarding the open-hamza "anna" when it is lightened, this would not be far-fetched. In the words of the author of al-Kashshaf there is evidence for this, in his explanation of His words: ﴿Though before this they were in clear error﴾ [Al 'Imran: 164], in Surat Al 'Imran. The clause after it is independent, and the "lām" in His words "layudillunā" (he would indeed mislead us) is the one that distinguishes the lightened "in" from the negating "in".

"Al-ṣabr" (steadfastness) is continuing in what is hard for the self to do. Its verb is governed by the preposition "ʿalā" because of what it implies of firmly holding to the thing that one persists in.

"Lawlā" is a particle of prohibition due to existence, that is, the non-occurrence of its answer because of the existence of its condition. It requires an answer for its condition, and the answer here is omitted, since what precedes "lawlā" indicates it, namely ﴿"he almost led us astray"﴾. The benefit of arranging the speech in this pattern, rather than beginning with the conditional particle followed by its answer, is to give attention to the report first, stating that it is established, and then to bring the condition after it as a restriction on the unrestricted report. The grammatical discipline regards the preceding as the indicator of the answer and the answer as omitted, because the grammarian's view is to establish the basic structure of the sentence. But the rhetoricians regard this as giving emphasis and restricting a report after its unrestricted statement. Therefore the author of al-Kashshaf said: "lawlā" in such a statement functions as a restriction of the absolute judgment in meaning, not in grammatical construction. This is the nature of conditions that come after a statement intended for its own sake, like His words: ﴿Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], up to His words: ﴿if you have gone forth in struggle in My way﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1]. His words "in kuntum" (if you are) are a restriction on the meaning of the prohibition against allying with the enemies of God. The condition is postponed so that it becomes clear that it restricts the act which is the indicator of the answer. Al-Kashshaf says: "(if you have gone forth) is linked to 'do not take', meaning: do not befriend them if you are My allies." End of quotation. And the grammarians' statement about such a case, that it is a condition whose answer is omitted because of what precedes it, is also correct. Likewise what has been placed before the condition, while its proper place is to be the answer to the condition, by way of placing it first to give attention to the answer, as in His words: ﴿Say: "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 93].

This is the answer to their saying (﴿If he had not persuaded us to stand firm in our devotion to our gods, he would almost have led us astray from them﴾), which implies that they were upon guidance in their religion. The answer cut off their argument and deferred the matter to the time when they would see the punishment descending upon them, and this contained a threat of punishment. The more apparent view is that what is meant is the punishment of the sword that descended upon them on the day of Badr, and among those who witnessed it was Abu Jahl, the lord of the people of the valley and the leader of the talk in that assembly.

Since the answer turned away from debate, the style of mockery (tahakkum) was employed in it, by making what the future would reveal to be the knowledge of which of the two parties was more astray, in the manner of going along with the wrongdoer and letting him run loose until he comes to recognize his error. Abu Jahl himself said on the day of Badr, while he was grievously wounded and in the throes of death, when Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said to him, "Are you Abu Jahl?", "Is there any greater man than one whom his own people have killed?"

And the interrogative (man) caused the verb (ya'lamuna, "they will know") to be suspended from acting (ta'liq).

This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*), addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning what came into his soul of grief over their repeated turning away from his call, since he was eager for their guidance and insistent in calling them. So He informed him that people like them are not expected to be guided, because they made their desire their god. The address is therefore to the Messenger (ﷺ).

The verb *ittakhadha* (took) takes two objects. It is one of the verbs of making (*af'al al-tasyir*), which are attached to the verbs of opinion in their grammatical operation, but it is closer in pattern to *kasa* (clothed) and *a'ta* (gave) than to *zanna* (thought). *Ittakhadha* means to make something into a state other than what it was, or into another form. The principle is that its first object is the one that undergoes the change into the state of the second object. Accordingly, the second object should not be placed before the first, unless there is no ambiguity in the sentence that would leave unclear which of the two objects underwent the change into what the other denotes, or unless the meaning resulting from the fronting equals the meaning resulting from the normal order in what the speaker intends.

So the Almighty's words, ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god?﴾, if read in the normal order, mean: he makes his god the thing whose worship his desire loves, that is, what he wishes to be a god for him, merely for the sake of appetite, not because his god deserves divinity. The meaning is: one who takes as a lord that which he loves. Those who worshipped idols did so because their desire lay in worshipping them, and they had no proof that these deserved worship. Thus the application of "his god" in this sense is literal. This suits His words before it: ﴿He almost led us astray from our gods﴾ (Al-Furqan: 42). This meaning is transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Ibn 'Arafa adopted it in his tafsir and asserted that it is the correct view to the exclusion of others, but his certainty in this is not well-founded, and some of his students debated him on it.

If, however, the second object is taken as fronted, the meaning becomes: one who takes his desire as a model for himself in his deeds, who does no deed except when it accords with his appetite; so his desire is, in effect, his god. On this reading, "his god" means something like "his god" in the sense of obedience, by way of eloquent simile (*tashbih baligh*).

This meaning is more comprehensive in censure, since it includes their worship of idols and also other reprehensible and vile deeds. Ibn 'Abbas inclined to it, and the author of the Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) and Ibn 'Atiyya also held this view. Both meanings should be considered possible interpretations of the verse.

Know that the two clauses together, ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god? Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾, form a single, continuous statement, the second connected to the first as an object is connected to its governing verb. The verb *ra'ayta* (have you seen) is thereby determined to be a heart-verb meaning "knowledge." The interrogative in the first clause, *a-ra'ayta*, is a rhetorical question of denial, as is the second in *a-fa-anta takunu 'alayhi wakilan* (would you then be a guardian over him). The two clauses together form a statement in the manner of summary followed by detail. The meaning is: Do you see yourself as a guardian over one who has taken his desire as his god? The *fa'* in *a-fa-anta* is the *fa'* of response to the relative pronoun, treating it as if it were a conditional. The second interrogative hamza is an emphasis on the first interrogative, like His words: ﴿When we are bones and dust, shall we indeed be resurrected?﴾ (Al-Isra: 98), according to the reading that repeats the interrogative hamza. The clause ﴿would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ serves as a substitute for the second object of *ra'ayta*, and the verb is suspended from acting on it because of the interrogative, as in His words: ﴿Then is one against whom the word of punishment has been fulfilled, can you save those in the Fire?﴾ (Az-Zumar: 19). Accordingly, one should not stop at "his desire," but continue the sentence. This is the arrangement followed by the Kashshaf.

If each of the two clauses is taken as independent of the other in the structure of the speech, the interrogative in the first clause is used to express wonder at the state of those who took their desire as their god, a wonder mingled with denial. The *fa'* in the second clause then serves to draw a consequence from that wonder and denial. The interrogative in the second clause, ﴿would you then be a guardian over him?﴾, is one of denial, meaning that you cannot pull him away from his misguidance, as indicated by His words before it: ﴿who is further astray from the way﴾ (Al-Furqan: 42).

The relative *man* (whoever) refers to the plural group spoken of in His words: ﴿They will know, when they see the punishment﴾ (Al-Furqan: 42). The pronouns within the relative clause follow the form of *man*, so they are singular. The meaning is: those who took their desire as their god, or those who took gods for the sake of their desire.

*Ilah* (god) is a generic noun that applies to several gods, if the meaning intended is: they took gods for the sake of their desires. The fronting of the subject before the verbal predicate in His words, ﴿you would be a guardian over him﴾, serves to emphasize, indicating a denial of what the Messenger (ﷺ) burdened himself with of eagerness and grief in seeking that they abandon desire. This is like His words: ﴿Would you then compel people until they become believers?﴾ (Yunus: 99). The meaning is: you would be a guardian over him in his state of faith, such that you would not cease repeating your call to faith until you compel him to it.

[p. 37]

﴿Or do you suppose that most of them hear or understand? They are only like livestock; rather, they are further astray in the way.﴾

This is a transition from despairing of their guidance, because their desires have overpowered their intellects, to a warning against supposing that they perceive the proofs and arguments. It is a second justification for turning away from disputing with them, which was signaled by His the Exalted's words: ﴿And they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in the way.﴾ [al-Furqan: 42]. So "am" (أم) is disjunctive (munqati'a), marking a transitional shift (al-idrab al-intiqali) from one denial to another. It indicates an interrogation which it conjoins to the interrogation preceding it. The implied sense is: "Or do you suppose that most of them hear or understand?"

The denial that "most of them hear" means the denial of the effect of hearing, which is grasping the truth, because whatever the Messenger ﷺ conveys is not doubted except by one who is like someone who has not heard it. This is like His the Exalted's words: ﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ [al-Naml: 80].

The conjunction of "or understand" (أو يعقلون) with "hear" (يسمعون) is to deny that they understand the non-verbal proofs, which are the proofs of the created world. He the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth. But signs and warnings do not avail a people who do not believe.﴾ [Yunus: 101].

The denial of understanding the auditory and rational proofs is attributed to most of them rather than all of them, because this is the condition of their common folk and their followers. Among them, however, are a group of intelligent people who understand and reason from the created world, but the love of leadership has overcome them, and they disdained to become followers of the Prophet ﷺ and equals of the believers from among the weak of Quraysh and their slaves, such as 'Ammar and Bilal.

The clause ﴿They are only like livestock﴾ is a resumptive clause of explanation (isti'naf bayani), because what preceded, the denial that they hear, arouses in the minds of the listeners a question about the denial of their understanding of what they hear, despite the soundness of their faculty of hearing. So comparing them to livestock clarifies how the sounds of the call reach their ears while they gain no benefit from them, since they are not prepared to give them attention. Thus the purpose of the comparison is closeness and plausibility, like the saying of Abu al-Tayyib:

"Even if you surpass mankind, though you are of them,
Musk is but a part of the blood of the gazelle."

The plural pronouns refer to "most of them" in view of the meaning of its wording, just as the pronoun of "hear" (يسمعون) referred to it.

[p. 38]

In describing their state, the discourse moves to something more severe than the state of livestock: they are "further astray in the way" than livestock. Going astray in the way means failing to be guided to the intended goal, because livestock understand some of what they hear, such as the shouts of herders and drivers and the like, whereas these people understand nothing of the voice of their guide and tender, who is the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace. This is like His the Exalted's words: ﴿Yet their hearts became hard like stones, or even harder. For indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74], and the verse continues.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verses 45–46 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shade? And had He willed, He would have made it stationary. Then We made the sun over it an indicator.﴾ ﴿Then We draw it in toward Us, a gradual drawing.﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) which moves from establishing the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) and establishing that the Qur'an is from Allah, whom He sent down upon His Messenger, and the attributes of the Messengers, and what has intervened of warning. From this perspective it is connected to His saying: (﴿And those who disbelieved say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]) and so on.

It also moves to the argument for the invalidity of their polytheism and the affirmation of the Oneness of Allah, and from this aspect it is connected to His saying at the beginning of the surah (﴿And they have taken, besides Him, deities which create nothing﴾ [al-Furqan: 3]) and so on.

The directing of the address to the Prophet (ﷺ) requires that the speech is connected to its counterpart in His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿Say, "It has sent it down, the One who knows the secret within the heavens and the earth"﴾ [al-Furqan: 6]), and what is conjoined to it: (﴿Say, "Is that better?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 15]), (﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾ [al-Furqan: 20]), (﴿And sufficient is your Lord as a guide and helper﴾ [al-Furqan: 31]); all of them are addresses to the Prophet (ﷺ). The extension of the shade and its drawing in have been made an illustration of the wisdom of gradualness in the divine creations, and of their deviation from sudden leaping in bringing into being, so that this illustration stands in the position of the major premise of an analogy, to demonstrate that the gradual sending down of the Qur'an in installments follows the wisdom of gradual progression, because it is more feasible in achieving the intended aim. This is what His earlier saying indicates: (﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]). So in His saying: (﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shade﴾) and so on, there is an addition to the reasoning beyond what is in His saying: (﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]).

This entails an allusion to the illustration of the descent of the Qur'an by the rising of the sun in the places that had been shaded, since He, Exalted, said: (﴿Then We made the sun over it an indicator﴾). The state of people in misguidance before the descent of the Qur'an is likened to the state of the extension of the darkness of the shade, and what had been shaded became exposed to the sun, and the removal of that shade was gradual until the shadow ceases to exist.

Thus the composition of the verse, with what it includes of illustration, conveys the illustration of the manner of the Qur'an's descent in installments by the manner of the extension of the shade progressively, and "had He willed, He would have made it stationary."

And its composition, when taken according to the literal sense of its structure, conveys the lesson of the extension and drawing in of the shade in establishing the subtleties of the power of Allah, Exalted. These two meanings are of the kind of using a word in its literal and figurative senses, which we mentioned in the ninth introduction. And the composition of the speech with the meaning of what it contains of explicit metaphor is the likening of guidance to the light of the sun. With this subtlety, His saying: (﴿Then We draw it in toward Us, a gradual drawing﴾) is conjoined to His saying: (﴿And made the day a resurrection﴾ [al-Furqan: 47]).

The interrogative is for confirmation (taqrir), so it is suitable for all levels of listeners: from the heedless, who is asked about his heedlessness so that he acknowledges it, as an incitement to reflection; from the denier, who is rebuked for his neglect of reflection; and from the one granted success, who is urged to increase in reflection.

The seeing is visual, and the verb has been made to imply the meaning of looking (nazar), so it is transitive to the object seen by the preposition (ila). The extension (madd) is the spreading out of a thing that is contracted and folded, as one says: "He extended the rope" and "He extended his hand." The extension is also applied to increase in a thing, which is a common metaphor, and here it means the increase in the measure of the shade.

Then, if the intended object of the act of seeing is a state of the essence's conditions that can be seen, it is permissible to transitivize the verb to the state, as in His saying: (﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ [al-Fil: 1]), (﴿Have you not seen how Allah created seven heavens in layers?﴾ [Nuh: 15]). It is also valid to transitivize it to the name of the essence qualified by the intended state through a circumstantial clause, an adverbial phrase, or a relative clause, such as: (﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 17]), (﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258]), (﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, "Send us a king"?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246]).

The difference between the two transitivities is that in the first, the concern is with the state, not its possessor. Thus the purpose of the verse in Surat al-Fil is the favour upon the people of Makkah by what befell those who violated its sanctity of annihilation, and the purpose of the verse in Surat al-Ghashiyah is the lesson in the manner of His creating the camels for the wondrous benefits it includes. Likewise the last two verses. Since the context here is the context of establishing the Oneness and the true divinity of Allah, Exalted, the attachment of the verb of seeing to the name of the essence was preferred at the outset, and then the coming of the state afterward, like the coming of the substitute of inclusion after mention of what it substitutes.

As for His saying in Surat Nuh: (﴿Have you not seen how Allah created﴾ [Nuh: 15]) without saying "Have you not seen your Lord, how He created," it is because his people were obstinate in disbelief, and he had argued with them about Allah more than once, so he knew that if he began with calling them to reflect on the Oneness, they would put their fingers in their ears and not listen to him, so he forestalled them by calling them to reflect on the manner of creation.

In any case, (kayfa) here is stripped of interrogation and is a noun indicating the manner, so it is in the position of a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) for (rabbika), and the estimate is: "Have you not considered your Lord, toward the form of His extending the shade?" The removal of (kayfa) from interrogation has already been mentioned at His saying: (﴿He it is who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 6]) in Surat Ali 'Imran, for the day is never without the presence of shade.

In the existence of the shade there are subtleties of the states of the solar system, for the shade is a determined measure of darkness that arises from the interposition of a body between the rays of the sun and the place upon which the ray falls, so a measure of shade is impressed upon the place, determined by the manner of the intervening body, according to the direction of that intervening body from its subtle or massive side. The extension of that darkness, shaped by the manner of that body, varies according to the variation of the distance of the direction of the rays from their position and from the intervening body, and differs according to the evenness or curvature of the place. That variation in the measures of the shadow of one thing is what is expressed by "extension" in this verse, because whenever the measure of the darkness shaping itself to the manner of the intervening object increases, the extension of the shade increases. All of these are many proofs of the subtleties of divine creation and great power.

This meaning has been conveyed completely by the verb (madda).

This extension increases according to the facing of the rays toward the intervening object: whenever the rays are directed at the body from a lower side, the shade is wider, and when they are directed toward it from above, its shade contracts gradually until the rays become perpendicular to the top of the body, falling upon it, and its shade vanishes entirely or nearly vanishes. This is the meaning of His saying: (﴿And had He willed, He would have made it stationary﴾), i.e., not increasing; because since the extension of the shade resembles the appearance of motion, the name of stillness was applied to the absence of extension, by its remaining at one fixed measure that neither decreases nor increases. That is: had Allah willed, He would have made the earth fixed in one direction toward the rays of the sun, so the measure of the shadows of the bodies upon the earth would not vary, and their shadows would remain in one state, and great benefits would be lost.

The contrast of His saying: (﴿extends the shade﴾) with His saying: (﴿made it stationary﴾) indicates an implied state in the speech, namely the state of the shade's covering the entire surface of the earth, i.e., the original state of darkness that preceded the direction of the sun's rays toward the surface of the earth, as indicated by the saying of the Torah: ("And the earth was without form, and darkness was upon the face of the deep." Then it said: "Let there be light"; and there was light...). And God separated the light from the darkness (one chapter of the Book of Exodus). So the Qur'an's argument from the shade is more fruitful than argument from darkness, because darkness is a privation, and one hardly perceives its beauty, unlike the shade, which combines darkness and light, so both of its indications are clear.

The clause (﴿And had He willed, He would have made it stationary﴾) is an intervening clause (mu'taridah) serving to remind that the shade contains a favour.

His saying: (﴿Then We made the sun over it an indicator﴾) is conjoined to the clause (extends the shade), and (then) indicates that the meaning of what is conjoined by it is distant in rank from the meaning of what it is conjoined to, as is the case with (thumma) when it conjoins a clause. Distance in rank means that it is more remote in consideration, i.e., more elevated in influence or in existence, since the existence of the sun is the cause of the existence of the shade for the bodies upon the earth, and the cause is higher in rank than the effect. That is, Allah extended the shade by making the sun an indicator of the measures of its extension. The commentators have not clarified the meaning of this clause with satisfying clarity.

The shift from the third person to the first person in His saying (﴿Then We made﴾) is because the first-person pronoun is more suited to conferring favour than the third-person pronoun, and it implies that this making is a blessing, namely the blessing of the light by which the states of visible things are distinguished. Accordingly, His saying (﴿Then We made the sun over it an indicator﴾) is an ascent in bestowing favour.

The indicator (dalil) is the guide to the way and the one who leads to it. So the extension of the shade, by the variation of its measures, is made like the extension of the road and its markers, like the milestones of the road, and the sun, inasmuch as it is the cause of the appearance of the measures of the shade, is made like a guide to stages, by way of eloquent metaphor. Just as the guide informs the traveller where he should alight on the road, so the sun, by causing the measures of the extension of the shade, informs the one reasoning by the shade of the times of his activities, so that he may commence them.

The transitivity of (dalil) with the preposition (ʿala) indicates that the sun's indication of the shade here is an indication of alerting to something that may be hidden, like the saying of the poet: (إلّا عَلَيَّ دَلِيلٌ). This includes both states, extension and drawing in.

The clause (﴿Then We draw it in toward Us﴾) etc. is conjoined to the clause (extends the shade), or to the clause (We made the sun over it an indicator), because the drawing in of the shade is one of the effects of making the sun an indicator over the shade.

The second (thumma) is, like the first, indicating distance in rank, because the content of the clause (﴿We draw it in toward Us, a gradual drawing﴾) is more significant in consideration than the content of (﴿We made the sun over it an indicator﴾); for in the drawing in of the shade there is an indication from the sun which is the reverse of its indication of the shade's extension, so it is more wondrous, since it is an action contrary to the first action, and the emanation of two opposites from a single cause is more wondrous than the emanation of only one of them, the one mentioned earlier.

Drawing in (qabd) is the opposite of extension (madd), so it is used in the sense of decrease, i.e., We decreased its extension; and the drawing in here is a metaphor for decrease. Its transitivity with (ilaynā) is an imaginative figure (takhyil): the shade is likened to a rope or a garment which its owner folds up after having spread it out, by way of metaphor (makniyyah), and the preposition (ila) with its genitive is an imaginative figure.

The placement of the description of the drawing as "gradual" (yasir) here is that it is intended that this drawing occurs slowly, without leaping, for in deliberateness there is facilitation of its drawing in; because divided work is generally easier on souls than gathered work. So ease is mentioned and what is intended is its customary implied meaning, which is gradualness with slowness, by way of metaphor (kinayah), so that it may be suitable for another meaning which we shall address at the end of our discourse.

The transitivity of drawing in with (ilaynā) is because it is the opposite of extension, which was attributed to Allah in His saying: (madda al-zill). And it has been known from the meaning of (qabadnāhu) that this drawing in occurs after the extension, so it is subsequent to it.

In the extension and withdrawal of the shade there is the blessing of knowing the times of the day for the prayers and for people's affairs, and the blessing of alternation in the benefit that communities and regions derive from the rays of the sun and the benefits of the shade (al-fay'), such that the group that was under the rays is cooled by the arrival of shade, and the group that was in the shade benefits from its withdrawal.

This is the place of the lesson (ʿibrah) and the favour (minnah), which the minds of people grasp according to the differences in their capacities. Behind that lies a great scientific lesson, clarified by the rules of the solar system, the Earth's movement around the Sun, and the appearance of darkness and light. Shade is nothing but an effect of darkness, for darkness is the origin of the states of existing things. Then light emerged through the Sun, and from the alternation of darkness and light arose the system of night and day, and from that the system of the seasons and the lines of longitude and latitude of the terrestrial globe, by which the zones of heat and cold became known.

Beyond that is an allusion to the origin of created things: how existence came upon them after they were non-existent, how their being extends during the stage of their growth, and then how they return to non-existence gradually in the stage of their decline until they come to nothingness. This is what is indicated by ﴿Then We withdraw it to Us, a easy withdrawal﴾. Thus there results from the reminder of the states of the shade in this verse, together with the favour and the indication of the system of divine power, an approximation to the state of human creation and the conditions of youth and the advance of age,

[page 44]

and that after this they are heading to their Lord on the Day of Resurrection, a destination with no doubt or distance, as they claim. Since the withdrawal of the shade became an example of the people's return to God through resurrection, the withdrawal was described as "easy," alluding to His saying: ﴿That is a gathering easy for Us﴾ [Qaf: 44].

In this illustration there is also an indication that life in this world is like a shade that extends and contracts, and it is nothing but a shade.

These two meanings in the verse are among the scientific miracles of the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verses 45–46 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shade? And had He willed, He would have made it stationary. Then We made the sun over it an indicator.﴾ ﴿Then We draw it in toward Us, a gradual drawing.﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) which moves from establishing the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) and establishing that the Qur'an is from Allah, whom He sent down upon His Messenger, and the attributes of the Messengers, and what has intervened of warning. From this perspective it is connected to His saying: (﴿And those who disbelieved say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]) and so on.

It also moves to the argument for the invalidity of their polytheism and the affirmation of the Oneness of Allah, and from this aspect it is connected to His saying at the beginning of the surah (﴿And they have taken, besides Him, deities which create nothing﴾ [al-Furqan: 3]) and so on.

The directing of the address to the Prophet (ﷺ) requires that the speech is connected to its counterpart in His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿Say, "It has sent it down, the One who knows the secret within the heavens and the earth"﴾ [al-Furqan: 6]), and what is conjoined to it: (﴿Say, "Is that better?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 15]), (﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾ [al-Furqan: 20]), (﴿And sufficient is your Lord as a guide and helper﴾ [al-Furqan: 31]); all of them are addresses to the Prophet (ﷺ). The extension of the shade and its drawing in have been made an illustration of the wisdom of gradualness in the divine creations, and of their deviation from sudden leaping in bringing into being, so that this illustration stands in the position of the major premise of an analogy, to demonstrate that the gradual sending down of the Qur'an in installments follows the wisdom of gradual progression, because it is more feasible in achieving the intended aim. This is what His earlier saying indicates: (﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]). So in His saying: (﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shade﴾) and so on, there is an addition to the reasoning beyond what is in His saying: (﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]).

This entails an allusion to the illustration of the descent of the Qur'an by the rising of the sun in the places that had been shaded, since He, Exalted, said: (﴿Then We made the sun over it an indicator﴾). The state of people in misguidance before the descent of the Qur'an is likened to the state of the extension of the darkness of the shade, and what had been shaded became exposed to the sun, and the removal of that shade was gradual until the shadow ceases to exist.

Thus the composition of the verse, with what it includes of illustration, conveys the illustration of the manner of the Qur'an's descent in installments by the manner of the extension of the shade progressively, and "had He willed, He would have made it stationary."

And its composition, when taken according to the literal sense of its structure, conveys the lesson of the extension and drawing in of the shade in establishing the subtleties of the power of Allah, Exalted. These two meanings are of the kind of using a word in its literal and figurative senses, which we mentioned in the ninth introduction. And the composition of the speech with the meaning of what it contains of explicit metaphor is the likening of guidance to the light of the sun. With this subtlety, His saying: (﴿Then We draw it in toward Us, a gradual drawing﴾) is conjoined to His saying: (﴿And made the day a resurrection﴾ [al-Furqan: 47]).

The interrogative is for confirmation (taqrir), so it is suitable for all levels of listeners: from the heedless, who is asked about his heedlessness so that he acknowledges it, as an incitement to reflection; from the denier, who is rebuked for his neglect of reflection; and from the one granted success, who is urged to increase in reflection.

The seeing is visual, and the verb has been made to imply the meaning of looking (nazar), so it is transitive to the object seen by the preposition (ila). The extension (madd) is the spreading out of a thing that is contracted and folded, as one says: "He extended the rope" and "He extended his hand." The extension is also applied to increase in a thing, which is a common metaphor, and here it means the increase in the measure of the shade.

Then, if the intended object of the act of seeing is a state of the essence's conditions that can be seen, it is permissible to transitivize the verb to the state, as in His saying: (﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ [al-Fil: 1]), (﴿Have you not seen how Allah created seven heavens in layers?﴾ [Nuh: 15]). It is also valid to transitivize it to the name of the essence qualified by the intended state through a circumstantial clause, an adverbial phrase, or a relative clause, such as: (﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 17]), (﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258]), (﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, "Send us a king"?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246]).

The difference between the two transitivities is that in the first, the concern is with the state, not its possessor. Thus the purpose of the verse in Surat al-Fil is the favour upon the people of Makkah by what befell those who violated its sanctity of annihilation, and the purpose of the verse in Surat al-Ghashiyah is the lesson in the manner of His creating the camels for the wondrous benefits it includes. Likewise the last two verses. Since the context here is the context of establishing the Oneness and the true divinity of Allah, Exalted, the attachment of the verb of seeing to the name of the essence was preferred at the outset, and then the coming of the state afterward, like the coming of the substitute of inclusion after mention of what it substitutes.

As for His saying in Surat Nuh: (﴿Have you not seen how Allah created﴾ [Nuh: 15]) without saying "Have you not seen your Lord, how He created," it is because his people were obstinate in disbelief, and he had argued with them about Allah more than once, so he knew that if he began with calling them to reflect on the Oneness, they would put their fingers in their ears and not listen to him, so he forestalled them by calling them to reflect on the manner of creation.

In any case, (kayfa) here is stripped of interrogation and is a noun indicating the manner, so it is in the position of a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) for (rabbika), and the estimate is: "Have you not considered your Lord, toward the form of His extending the shade?" The removal of (kayfa) from interrogation has already been mentioned at His saying: (﴿He it is who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 6]) in Surat Ali 'Imran, for the day is never without the presence of shade.

In the existence of the shade there are subtleties of the states of the solar system, for the shade is a determined measure of darkness that arises from the interposition of a body between the rays of the sun and the place upon which the ray falls, so a measure of shade is impressed upon the place, determined by the manner of the intervening body, according to the direction of that intervening body from its subtle or massive side. The extension of that darkness, shaped by the manner of that body, varies according to the variation of the distance of the direction of the rays from their position and from the intervening body, and differs according to the evenness or curvature of the place. That variation in the measures of the shadow of one thing is what is expressed by "extension" in this verse, because whenever the measure of the darkness shaping itself to the manner of the intervening object increases, the extension of the shade increases. All of these are many proofs of the subtleties of divine creation and great power.

This meaning has been conveyed completely by the verb (madda).

This extension increases according to the facing of the rays toward the intervening object: whenever the rays are directed at the body from a lower side, the shade is wider, and when they are directed toward it from above, its shade contracts gradually until the rays become perpendicular to the top of the body, falling upon it, and its shade vanishes entirely or nearly vanishes. This is the meaning of His saying: (﴿And had He willed, He would have made it stationary﴾), i.e., not increasing; because since the extension of the shade resembles the appearance of motion, the name of stillness was applied to the absence of extension, by its remaining at one fixed measure that neither decreases nor increases. That is: had Allah willed, He would have made the earth fixed in one direction toward the rays of the sun, so the measure of the shadows of the bodies upon the earth would not vary, and their shadows would remain in one state, and great benefits would be lost.

The contrast of His saying: (﴿extends the shade﴾) with His saying: (﴿made it stationary﴾) indicates an implied state in the speech, namely the state of the shade's covering the entire surface of the earth, i.e., the original state of darkness that preceded the direction of the sun's rays toward the surface of the earth, as indicated by the saying of the Torah: ("And the earth was without form, and darkness was upon the face of the deep." Then it said: "Let there be light"; and there was light...). And God separated the light from the darkness (one chapter of the Book of Exodus). So the Qur'an's argument from the shade is more fruitful than argument from darkness, because darkness is a privation, and one hardly perceives its beauty, unlike the shade, which combines darkness and light, so both of its indications are clear.

The clause (﴿And had He willed, He would have made it stationary﴾) is an intervening clause (mu'taridah) serving to remind that the shade contains a favour.

His saying: (﴿Then We made the sun over it an indicator﴾) is conjoined to the clause (extends the shade), and (then) indicates that the meaning of what is conjoined by it is distant in rank from the meaning of what it is conjoined to, as is the case with (thumma) when it conjoins a clause. Distance in rank means that it is more remote in consideration, i.e., more elevated in influence or in existence, since the existence of the sun is the cause of the existence of the shade for the bodies upon the earth, and the cause is higher in rank than the effect. That is, Allah extended the shade by making the sun an indicator of the measures of its extension. The commentators have not clarified the meaning of this clause with satisfying clarity.

The shift from the third person to the first person in His saying (﴿Then We made﴾) is because the first-person pronoun is more suited to conferring favour than the third-person pronoun, and it implies that this making is a blessing, namely the blessing of the light by which the states of visible things are distinguished. Accordingly, His saying (﴿Then We made the sun over it an indicator﴾) is an ascent in bestowing favour.

The indicator (dalil) is the guide to the way and the one who leads to it. So the extension of the shade, by the variation of its measures, is made like the extension of the road and its markers, like the milestones of the road, and the sun, inasmuch as it is the cause of the appearance of the measures of the shade, is made like a guide to stages, by way of eloquent metaphor. Just as the guide informs the traveller where he should alight on the road, so the sun, by causing the measures of the extension of the shade, informs the one reasoning by the shade of the times of his activities, so that he may commence them.

The transitivity of (dalil) with the preposition (ʿala) indicates that the sun's indication of the shade here is an indication of alerting to something that may be hidden, like the saying of the poet: (إلّا عَلَيَّ دَلِيلٌ). This includes both states, extension and drawing in.

The clause (﴿Then We draw it in toward Us﴾) etc. is conjoined to the clause (extends the shade), or to the clause (We made the sun over it an indicator), because the drawing in of the shade is one of the effects of making the sun an indicator over the shade.

The second (thumma) is, like the first, indicating distance in rank, because the content of the clause (﴿We draw it in toward Us, a gradual drawing﴾) is more significant in consideration than the content of (﴿We made the sun over it an indicator﴾); for in the drawing in of the shade there is an indication from the sun which is the reverse of its indication of the shade's extension, so it is more wondrous, since it is an action contrary to the first action, and the emanation of two opposites from a single cause is more wondrous than the emanation of only one of them, the one mentioned earlier.

Drawing in (qabd) is the opposite of extension (madd), so it is used in the sense of decrease, i.e., We decreased its extension; and the drawing in here is a metaphor for decrease. Its transitivity with (ilaynā) is an imaginative figure (takhyil): the shade is likened to a rope or a garment which its owner folds up after having spread it out, by way of metaphor (makniyyah), and the preposition (ila) with its genitive is an imaginative figure.

The placement of the description of the drawing as "gradual" (yasir) here is that it is intended that this drawing occurs slowly, without leaping, for in deliberateness there is facilitation of its drawing in; because divided work is generally easier on souls than gathered work. So ease is mentioned and what is intended is its customary implied meaning, which is gradualness with slowness, by way of metaphor (kinayah), so that it may be suitable for another meaning which we shall address at the end of our discourse.

The transitivity of drawing in with (ilaynā) is because it is the opposite of extension, which was attributed to Allah in His saying: (madda al-zill). And it has been known from the meaning of (qabadnāhu) that this drawing in occurs after the extension, so it is subsequent to it.

In the extension and withdrawal of the shade there is the blessing of knowing the times of the day for the prayers and for people's affairs, and the blessing of alternation in the benefit that communities and regions derive from the rays of the sun and the benefits of the shade (al-fay'), such that the group that was under the rays is cooled by the arrival of shade, and the group that was in the shade benefits from its withdrawal.

Thus there results from the reminder of the states of the shade in this verse, together with the favour and the indication of the system of divine power, an approximation to the state of human creation and the conditions of youth and the advance of age,

and that after this they are heading to their Lord on the Day of Resurrection, a destination with no doubt or distance, as they claim. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 47:

﴿It is He who made the night a garment for you, and sleep a rest, and made the day a resurrection.﴾

The transition from the argument based on the conditions of the shade and the forenoon to the consideration of the conditions of the night and the day is evident, for the night resembles the shade in that it is darkness that follows the light of the sun.

The point on which the argument turns is the restrictive meaning (qasr) of exclusivity (qasr ifrad) derived from the definition of the two parts of the sentence, namely that no other shares with Him in making the night and the day. As for the fact that this making is by the creation of God, they acknowledge it; but when they assigned to Him partners in general terms, their partnership was refuted by restricting the disposal of the times to God Most High, for when their disposal over some of the existents is nullified, the reality of divinity (uluhiyya) is removed from them, since divinity does not admit of division.

The phrase "for you" (lakum) is connected to "made" (ja'ala), meaning: among the things for which the night was created is that it be a garment for you. This does not imply that the night was created for this alone, since the night is the return of darkness to one side of the earthly sphere, screened from the rays of the sun by its rotations, and from it arise numerous benefits, among them what is in His words after this: ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day succeeding each other for whoever wishes to remember﴾ [al-Furqan: 62], etc.

The style of speech has shifted from the first person to the third person by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

"A garment" (libas) is the second term of a comparison in the manner of the eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh), meaning: a covering for you that conceals some of you from others. In this covering are many favours, for the fulfilling of needs that must be kept hidden.

The consideration of the night's covering is placed before the consideration of sleep in order to preserve the resemblance of the night to the shade, as already mentioned, unlike His words in surah al-Naba' (78:8): ﴿And We created you in pairs, and made your sleep a rest, and made the night a garment﴾, for the blessing of sleep is more important than the blessing of covering, and because the connection between the blessing of the creation of pairs and sleep is stronger.

The verse combines argument and favour: it is a proof of the greatness of the power of the Creator, and it is also a reminder of His blessings. For in the alternation of night and day there are numerous signs for what the occurrence of darkness indicates of the precision of the system of the earth's rotation around the sun and of the precision of the system of the creation of the sun, and for what the existence of day depends upon of the variation in the earth's rotation and of the benefits of the sun's light. Then there is, within this, the system of sleep suited to darkness, when people's nerves relax, so that through sleep their vigour is renewed, and the use of the darkness of night for concealment; and from the system of day comes the renewal of vigour and the rising of people to work, and their weariness of ease, together with the light suited to this, by which those who work see what they intend.

Subat (rest/sleep) has several meanings in the language, arising from the extension of the root s-b-t, which means "to cut." The meaning most fitting to the context of favour is rest, although both meanings involve consideration of the subtle craftsmanship of God Most High. al-Zamakhshari interpreted subat as sleep, by way of the eloquent metaphor, looking in this to its contrast with His words ﴿and made the day a resurrection﴾.

The repetition of the verb "made" (ja'ala) in His words ﴿and made the day a resurrection﴾, without its repetition in His words ﴿and sleep a rest﴾, indicates that it is a notice that this is a making different from the making of the night as a garment. That is because He reported about it with the word "resurrection" (nushur), and nushur means the raising of the dead, and this is an incorporation (idmaj) of a reminder of the resurrection and an allusion to the argument against those who deemed it impossible, by bringing it near through the stirring (hubub) during the day. In this sense is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he awoke: "Praise be to God who gave us life after He had caused us to die, and to Him is the resurrection."

Nushur: life after death. It was mentioned shortly before, at His words (Exalted is He): ﴿Nay, they did not expect a resurrection﴾ [al-Furqan: 40]. Here it may bear two meanings: it may be intended as emergence and dispersal, in which case it is the opposite of the garment in His words ﴿It is He who made the night a garment for you﴾, and the reporting of it about the day is then literal, and the favour lies in the fact that people disperse during the day for their needs and their earning. Or it may be intended as the raising of bodies after their death, in which case the reporting is by way of the eloquent metaphor.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verses 48–50 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is He who sends the winds as heralds of His mercy, and We send down from the sky pure water﴾ ﴿that We may give life thereby to a dead land and give it to drink, of what We have created, cattle and many humans﴾ ﴿And We have certainly varied it among them that they may remember, but most of the people refuse except ingratitude﴾

This is an argument for God's sole creation (al-infirad bil-khalq) and a reminder of the favour (imtinan) of the formation of the winds, the clouds and the rain. The transition here, from what was in the preceding argument concerning the state of resurrection and the favour of it, moves to what is in the winds of resurrection, by describing them as "nushur" according to the reading of the majority (al-Jumhur), or because they are so in reality according to the reading of 'Asim. The purpose of the argument is restricting the sending of the winds and what is conjoined with it to God the Exalted, refuting the claim of the associates (al-shuraka') in divinity, by negating partnership in the disposal of these beings. The polytheists do not deny this, as was previously shown by a similar statement in His words: (﴿It is He who made the night for you as a garment﴾ [al-Furqan: 47]) etc.

The verb "arsala" (to send), which is literally used for dispatching something and directing it, is applied to the formation of the winds, because the movement of the winds resembles travel. The use of "irsal" for letting loose horses in a race is also widespread.

This is an argument from the subtle creation of God in the formation of the winds. The common people take lessons from what falls within their observation of it, while the elite understand the manner in which the winds arise, blow and vary, and that arises from the meeting of the heat of one part of the atmosphere with the coldness of another part. Then, the winds, by blowing hot at one time and cold at another, form the clouds and announce the rain; therefore they are described as "nushur" (heralds) before the rain.

The majority read "arsala al-riyah" in the plural form. Ibn Kathir read "al-rih" in the singular form, in the sense of the genus. The two readings are equivalent in meaning, but the plural "riyah" predominates for winds of goodness, and the singular "rih" for winds of punishment. This was stated by Ibn 'Atiyya. It was mentioned earlier in His words: (wa tasrif al-riyah) in Surat al-Baqarah.

The majority read "nushuran" with a nun at its beginning and two dammas, as the plural of "nashur," like "rasul" and "rusul." Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma then a sukun, for lightening the vowel. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the shin, as a description by the verbal noun. All of them derive from "al-nashr," which is spreading, as a folded garment is spread out; because the winds spread the clouds. 'Asim read it with a single ba' and a sukun on the shin, as the plural of "bashur," from "al-tabshir" (giving good news), because they announce the rain. His saying (﴿It is He who sends the winds as heralds before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]) was mentioned earlier in Surat al-A'raf.

The shift from the third person (ghayba) to the first person (mutakallim) in the words "wa anzalna," "li-nuhyiya," "wa nusqiyahu," and "la-qad sarrafnahu" is for the motive that was mentioned earlier in His words: (﴿Then We made the sun over it a guide, then We drew it to Us in gradual retraction﴾ [al-Furqan: 45]).

What is meant by "rahmatihi" (His mercy) is the rain, because it is mercy for people and animals through what it causes to grow of trees and pasture.

The clause (﴿and We send down from the sky pure water﴾) is conjoined to the clause "arsala al-riyah" etc., so it falls within the scope of the restriction, meaning: He is the One who sent down from the sky pure water. The pronoun in "anzalna" is a shift from the third person to the first person, because the first person is more fitting to the context of favour. The meaning of sending down water from the sky was mentioned earlier at His words: (﴿or like a rainstorm from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19]) in Surat al-Baqarah.

"Tahur" with a fatha on the ta' is one of the forms of intensification in describing by the verbal noun, as one says "rajul sabur" (a very patient man). Rainwater reaches the utmost degree of purity, since nothing mixes with it that would make it turbid or foul; and in chemistry it is the purest of waters, being free of all microbes, so it is truly the pure. The meaning is that the water descending from the sky is at the utmost limit of purity among the kinds of waters. Describing water as "tahur" implies that it purifies other things, since the deviation from the pattern "fa'il" to the pattern "fa'ul" is for adding meaning to the description. Its implication in this verse that it purifies other things is an implied implication (iqtida' iltizami)

in order that it be complete in the description of purity both intrinsic and transitive. So mention of this description is an insertion (idmaj) of a favour within the course of the intended favours, like His words: (﴿and He sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you by it﴾ [al-Anfal: 11]), which describes intrinsic purity and its purifying. Thus this description is an insertion. Were it not so, the more fitting for the context of favour would have been describing the water as clear or the like.

"Al-baldah" means the land. Describing it with life and death are two metaphors for irrigation and dryness, because the watering of the land produces plants, which resemble the living, and the dryness of the land causes the plants to wither, which resembles the dead.

Rainwater has the property of giving life to every land, because, being free of microbes and of some of the mineral and earthy parts that spring and river and valley waters contain, it is suitable for every land and every plant, despite the differences in the natures of lands and places of growth.

"Al-baldah" is "al-balad." "Balad" is masculine and feminine, like many names of kinds of places, as they say "dar" and "darah." "Baldah" was described with "maytan," which is a masculine description, by interpreting "baldah" in the sense of "makan" (place) for the sake of lightness. In al-Kashshaf it is said, in meaning: since it indicates intensification in being characterized by death and was not following the patterns of intensification, it was treated as a rigid noun (i.e., it was not changed). Better than this is that what is meant by it is the noun "mayyit" (dead), and describing the land with it is a description in the sense of eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh).

In His words: (﴿that We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾) there is an allusion to bringing the possibility of resurrection near.

"Wa nusqiyahu" with a damma on the nun is the present tense of "asqa," like the one with a fatha on the nun; it is said that they are two dialects. One says "asqa" and "saqa." God the Exalted said: (﴿They said: We do not water﴾ [al-Qasas: 23]) with a fatha on the nun. It is said: "saqa" means to give drink, and "asqa" means to prepare water for drinking. This saying is more solid, because distinctions between the meanings of words are among the beauties of the language; so the meaning is: We prepared it for the drinking of cattle and people, so whoever needed to drink drank from it, whether he drank or did not drink.

"An'aman" is the second object of "nusqiyahu." The phrase "mimma khalaqna" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "an'aman wa anasiyy." "Min" is partitive, and "ma" is a relative pronoun, meaning: some of what We have created; the relative pronoun is for alluding to the cause of the predicate, meaning: We give them drink because they are creatures. The benefit of this circumstantial clause is pointing to God's mercy towards them, because they are His creation. In it is an allusion that other kinds of creatures are also watered by rainwater, but mention is limited to cattle and humans because they are the locus of the favour: cattle, by which the nomads' livelihood is sound through their milk, wool, hair and meat, drink from rainwater in pools and ponds.

This is an argument for God's sole creation (al-infirad bil-khalq) and a reminder of the favour (imtinan) of the formation of the winds, the clouds and the rain. The transition here, from what was in the preceding argument concerning the state of resurrection and the favour of it, moves to what is in the winds of resurrection, by describing them as "nushur" according to the reading of the majority (al-Jumhur), or because they are so in reality according to the reading of 'Asim. The purpose of the argument is restricting the sending of the winds and what is conjoined with it to God the Exalted, refuting the claim of the associates (al-shuraka') in divinity, by negating partnership in the disposal of these beings. The polytheists do not deny this, as was previously shown by a similar statement in His words: (﴿It is He who made the night for you as a garment﴾ [al-Furqan: 47]) etc.
