This is an argument from the subtle creation of God in the formation of the winds. The common people take lessons from what falls within their observation of it, while the elite understand the manner in which the winds arise, blow and vary, and that arises from the meeting of the heat of one part of the atmosphere with the coldness of another part. Then, the winds, by blowing hot at one time and cold at another, form the clouds and announce the rain; therefore they are described as "nushur" (heralds) before the rain.

The majority read "arsala al-riyah" in the plural form. Ibn Kathir read "al-rih" in the singular form, in the sense of the genus. The two readings are equivalent in meaning, but the plural "riyah" predominates for winds of goodness, and the singular "rih" for winds of punishment. This was stated by Ibn 'Atiyya. It was mentioned earlier in His words: (wa tasrif al-riyah) in Surat al-Baqarah.

All of them derive from "al-nashr," which is spreading, as a folded garment is spread out; because the winds spread the clouds. 'Asim read it with a single ba' and a sukun on the shin, as the plural of "bashur," from "al-tabshir" (giving good news), because they announce the rain. His saying (﴿It is He who sends the winds as heralds before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]) was mentioned earlier in Surat al-A'raf.

He described "anasiyy," which is a plural, with "kathir," which is singular, because "fa'il" may be meant as plural, like "rafiq," and likewise "qalil." God the Exalted said: (﴿And remember when you were few﴾ [al-A'raf: 86]).

The mention of cattle before humans is required by the arrangement of speech in the manner of rulings, in its being followed by His words: (﴿And We have certainly varied it among them that they may remember﴾); had "anasiyy" been mentioned first, the arrangement would have fallen apart. The mention of "al-nas" (people) was not placed first in His words: (﴿as a provision for you and your cattle﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 33]) in Surat al-Nazi'at, because there was no motive for placing it first, so it came in the original order.

The pronoun in "sarrafnahu" refers to "ma'an tahuran." "Tasrif" means change. What is meant here is the change of the states of the water, that is, its quantities and places.

The sentence is emphasized with the oath particle lam and "qad," to establish the reason, because the variation of rain is established and does not need emphasis. What was not known to them is that among the wisdom of its variation among people is that they should remember God's favour upon them both when it descends upon them and when it is withheld from them, because many people do not appreciate the value of a blessing except when it is lost; so they would know that God is the One Lord, the chooser in creating causes and effects, whereas they had not contemplated the wisdom of the Creator and attributed effects to imaginary or apparent influences.

Since remembrance includes thanking the Benefactor for the rain's arrival, and the deprived's noticing the cause of their deprivation, so that perhaps they would seek forgiveness, the verb "li-yadhdhakkaru" was used in the causal clause so that it would be the reason for both states of variation among them.

His words: (﴿but most of the people refuse except ingratitude﴾) is a construction that has, by its material and form, become like a proverb in reporting the determination of the one reported about upon what follows the particle of exception. That requires the existence of a deterrent from the excepted thing, meaning: they resolved upon ingratitude and do not turn back from it. This is because the exception is from the generality of unspecified things, all of which are made to be among what the refusal is attached to, as if the refusers were presented with matters (from people or from their thoughts), and they reconsidered and accepted from them only ingratitude, even if there was no presentation or refusal there. From this is His saying in Surat Bara'ah: (﴿and God refuses except that He perfect His light﴾ [al-Tawbah: 32]). Do you not see that this was used here in the context of the polytheists' opposition to monotheism, and in Surat Bara'ah in the context of the People of the Book's opposition to Islam. The severity of both groups in their disbelief is well known and manifest, and it was not used in His words in Surat al-Saff: (﴿They want to extinguish God's light with their mouths, but God perfects His light﴾ [al-Saff: 8]).

"Al-kufur" is a verbal noun meaning disbelief. Its counterpart was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Isra', meaning: they refused except to associate partners with God and not to remember.

The majority read "li-yadhdhakkaru" with shaddah on the dhal and shaddah on the kaf, with the ta' assimilated into it, and its origin is "li-yatadhakkaru." Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a sukun on the dhal and a light kaf with a damma, meaning: "li-yadhkuru" (that they may recall) what they are heedless of.

From the verse it is taken that the water sent down from the sky does not vary in its quantity, but the quantities of its distribution to the places of rainfall vary. Ibn 'Abbas said: "No year is less in rain than another, but God divides it among His servants as He wills," and he recited this verse. Al-Qurtubi mentioned from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: ("There is no year with more rain than another, but when a people commit sins God turns it to others; and when they all disobey, God turns it to the deserts and the seas"). Thus it results from this that the amount of rain which God has bestowed upon this land does not vary in quantity, but its distribution varies. This is a truth established by scholars of atmospheric phenomena in the present century, so it is one of the scientific miracles of the Qur'an, falling under the third aspect of the tenth introduction to this commentary.

Some scholars permitted that the pronoun in (ṣarrafnāhu) refers to something not mentioned explicitly in the context, meant to be the Qur'an. They said: because it is the main subject of this surah, which opens with mention of it, and it recurs in His words: ﴿Indeed, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned﴾ [al-Furqan: 30]. The origin of this interpretation is related from ʿAṭāʾ. It also fits His words after it: ﴿And strive against them with it, a great striving﴾ [al-Furqan: 52].

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the speech mentioned, meaning: "And We have indeed varied this speech and repeated it through the tongues of the Messengers, so that they might be reminded."

[p. 51]

This clause is an interjection (*jumlat i'tirad*) between the mention of the proofs of God's sole creation and the mention of His favour upon creation. The connection of this clause, and its placement as a consequence of the verse before it, is obscure. Ibn 'Atiyya said, regarding His words (﴿Had We willed, We would have sent a warner to every town﴾): "It is an abrupt transition (*iqtidab*) indicated by what was mentioned. Its implied sense is: 'Rather, We singled you out for warning and entrusted you with it, so do not obey the disbelievers.'" End of quote.

If by his words "*iqtidab*" he meant the technical sense of *iqtidab* among the scholars of literary eloquence (*adab*) and rhetoric (*bayan*), namely the failure to observe a connection between the speech left and the speech moved to, then this is a departure from the obligation to seek a connection between this verse and the verse before it. The absence of connection is not unprecedented, for the author of *Talkhis al-Miftah* said: "It may be moved from what the speech was introduced with, that is, to what does not suit it, that is, does not fit the subject left, and this is called *iqtidab*, and it is the practice of the Arabs and those who follow them among the *mukhadramun* (those who lived into both the pre-Islamic and Islamic periods)," and so on.

But if Ibn 'Atiyya meant by *iqtidab* the sense of *qat'* (cutting off, i.e., omission from the speech), that is, the concise omission, as his words "what was mentioned indicates it, its implied sense is..." suggest, then he did not turn to the connection of this verse with the one before it.

In *al-Kashshaf* (by al-Zamakhshari): "Had We willed, We would have lightened for you the burdens of warning the many towns, and We would have sent to every town a prophet to warn it. But We confined the matter to you and exalted you above the other messengers, that is, in the universality of the call. So you are to meet this with patience." End of quote.

al-Tibi said: "The axis of the surah is that he (ﷺ) was sent to mankind in its entirety, and for this reason it opens with what establishes the universality of the message of Muhammad (ﷺ) to all people, with His words: (﴿That he may be a warner to the worlds﴾) [al-Furqan: 1]."

There is nothing in the words of *al-Kashshaf* and al-Tibi except an explanation of the verse's connection to the major themes of the surah, without explaining its connection to the verse before it.

What I choose is that this verse is connected to His words: (﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"﴾) [al-Furqan: 32], and so on. After He had shown the refutation of their criticism, saying (﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾) [al-Furqan: 32], He moved to comparing the Qur'an with the Book given to Musa (peace be upon him), and how God uprooted those who denied him. Then He digressed by mentioning peoples who denied their messengers. Then He moved to the mockery of the polytheists toward the Prophet (ﷺ), and alluded to the Prophet's distress at his people's turning away from his call, with His words: (﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god? Would you then be responsible for him?﴾) [al-Furqan: 43].

[p. 52]

The continuity of the speech through the striking of the parable of the extension and withdrawal of the shade, and through the states of night and day, and through the sending of the winds, is a sign of the mercy of His rain by which dead lands are revived, until it reaches His words: (﴿Had We willed, We would have sent a warner to every town﴾). What supports what we have mentioned is that the consequence contains a pronoun referring to the Qur'an in His words: (﴿and strive against them with it﴾).

What further strengthens this verse's connection to His words (﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"﴾) [al-Furqan: 32] is that sending a warner to every town involves something greater than sending the Qur'an in parts. For if God had sent a warner to every town, the disbelievers would have said: "Why was not one messenger sent to all people together?" Their criticisms do not stop at any limit, as He said: (﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, "Why were its verses not explained in detail? Is it non-Arabic and Arab?"﴾) [Fussilat: 44], in the surah Ha Mim al-Sajdah.

The consequence (*tafri'*) of (﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾) upon the clause (﴿Had We willed, We would have sent a warner to every town﴾) is because the clause implies that he was sent to the polytheists of Makkah, while they were asking him to cease his call to them and to cease disparaging their idols.

The prohibition is used to express warning and admonition, and the verb (*tuti'*, "obey") in the context of a prohibition conveys the generality of warning against even the slightest obedience.

Obedience (*ta'ah*) is a person's acting upon what is demanded of him. That is: do not weaken in the call out of regard for their desire that you should soften toward them.

After He warned him against weakness in the call, He commanded him to be earnest and to exert himself in it. He expressed this by *jihad*, which is the comprehensive term for the utmost effort. The form *mufa'alah* in it (*jahid*, from *jahada*, with the pattern of mutual striving) is to convey the matching of their effort with his effort, so that he does not weaken or grow feeble. For this reason it is described as a *great jihad*, that is, one comprising every striving.

The pronoun in (*bihi*, "with it") refers to something not mentioned explicitly. It may refer to the Qur'an, since it is understood from the context of warning. Or it may refer to what is understood from (*la tuti'*, "do not obey"), which is steadfastness in his call by disobeying them, for the prohibition of a thing is a command to its opposite, as the verse of Abu Hayyah al-Numayri shows:

*They said to her in secret: "We ransom you! Let him not go away unharmed; and if you do not kill him, then afflict him."*

He answered his words "let him not go away unharmed" with his words "and if you do not kill him, then afflict him," as if he had said: "We ransom you, so kill him."

The meaning is: confront them with your patience. The greatness of the *jihad* lies in its repetition, in resolve within it, and in the severity of the hardship one meets in it. This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to his companions upon returning from one of his military campaigns: "We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad." They said: "What is the greater jihad?" He said: "The striving of the servant against his desire." Narrated by al-Bayhaqi with a weak chain (*isnad*).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 53:**

﴿It is He who has released the two seas, one sweet and palatable, the other salty and bitter, and placed between them a barrier and a forbidding partition.﴾

A return to the argument (istidlal, reasoning from evidence) for God's sole creation. This verse combines argument, illustration, affirmation and promise. Its explicit content is an argument for a great sign of divine power, namely the meeting of rivers and seas, as will come. Implicitly, it is an illustration of the state of the call of Islam in Mecca on that day, and of the mixing of believers with polytheists, by way of the passing of the two seas: one sweet and palatable, the other salty and bitter. The illustration likens faith to the sweet, palatable water and polytheism to the salty, bitter water. And just as God placed between the two seas a barrier (barzakh) that protects the sweet water from being polluted by the bitter, so He set a separation between the Muslims and the polytheists, so that the polytheists cannot slip their disbelief in among the Muslims. In this there is an affirmation for the Muslims that God holds back from them the harm of the polytheists, in accordance with His saying: ﴿They will not harm you except with a little hurt﴾ [Al-Imran: 111]. There is also in this an indirect allusion (ta'rid kinā'ī) that God supports this religion so that polytheism does not pollute it.

Because of its illustration, affirmation and promise, its placement after the sentence ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it a great striving﴾ [al-Furqan: 52] is most fitting. It is conjoined to the sentence ﴿It is He who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-Furqan: 48]. The reason it follows the preceding verse is that both are arguments from the signs of power in the creation of the various waters. The implication of the restrictive construction (qasr) here is similar to what preceded in the two previous verses.

Al-maraj means mixing. It is used here metaphorically for close adjacency, and the indicator is His saying: ﴿and placed between them a barrier and a forbidding partition﴾. Al-bahr is water in abundance, that is, great and vast. Al-'adhb is sweet. Al-furat is extremely sweet. Al-milh, with a kasra on the mim, is described with a meaning of the salty (al-malih), and in eloquent usage one says only milh; malih is rare. What is meant here is the meeting point of the waters of the two rivers, the Euphrates and the Tigris, with the water of the Gulf of Persia (Khalij al-'Ajam).

Al-barzakh is the intervening barrier between two things. The meaning of the barzakh here is the likening of what is in the composition of the salt water, which repels the infiltration of sweet water into it, so that neither mixes with the other and each remains preserving its taste at the place of outflow.

(*Hijran*) is a verbal noun in the accusative as an object, because it is conjoined to the object of (*ja'ala*, "He placed"). It is not used here in the sense of seeking refuge, as in His saying just before: ﴿and they say, "A forbidding partition"﴾ [al-Furqan: 22]. (*Mahjuran*) is a qualifier of (*hijran*), derived from its root, to indicate the firmness of the meaning from which it is derived, as they say: "night that is extremely dark" (*layl alyal*). This has been mentioned earlier in this surah. In al-Kashshaf there is a strained interpretation in making (*hijran mahjuran*) here mean seeking refuge, like what is in His saying: ﴿and they say, "A forbidding partition"﴾ [al-Furqan: 22]. There is no need for that, because what they mentioned about the use of ﴿hijran mahjuran﴾ [al-Furqan: 22] in the sense of seeking refuge does not require that it is used only in that way.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 54:

﴿And He it is who created from water a human being, and made him [a relative by] lineage and marriage. And your Lord is ever Competent.﴾.

The occasion of this argument's placement after what precedes it is that it is an argument from the subtle signs of power in the creation of waters and in making them a cause of life of differing forms and conditions. Among the greatest of these is the subtlety of the water from which the most noble of the species on earth was created, namely the sperm-drop of man, in that it is the cause of the generation of offspring for humankind, for it is at first water, and then from it there is formed the great human being. Thus the tanwin in His saying (basharan) is for magnification.

The restriction (qasr) derived from the definiteness of the two components is a restriction of specification (qasr ifrad), to nullify the claim that the idols share in divinity with God.

Al-Bashar: the human being. It has already been mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: (﴿So she presented herself before him as a man in all respects﴾ [Maryam: 17]) in Surah Maryam. The pronoun in the accusative in (fa-ja'alahu) refers to the human being, meaning: so He made the human being whom He created from water into [a relative by] lineage and marriage; that is, God divided human beings into two categories: lineage (nasab) and marriage (sihr). So the waw is for division, with the meaning of (aw) ("or"), and waw is better than aw in division.

(Nasaban wa sihran) are two verbal nouns by which two kinds of kinship were named, on the presumption of: "one of lineage and marriage," and this usage became common in speech.

Lineage (nasab) necessarily involves fatherhood, sonship and brotherhood for those, and sonship for that brotherhood.

As for marriage (sihr), it is the name for the relationship between a man and the kin of his spouse and her relatives, a bond, and it is also called musaharah (affinal relationship), because it arises from two sides. It is a conventional bond that is established by its relation to that to which it is attached: the marriage-kin (sihr) of a man is the kin of his wife, and the marriage-kin of a woman is the kin of her husband. For this reason it is said: "So-and-so became related by marriage (sahara) to so-and-so" if he married from his kin, even a distant kinship such as tribal kinship. Human beings, whether married or unmarried, are not free of this.

The term sihr is also applied to one who has with another the relationship of affinity, by the use of the verbal noun in the place of a descriptive. Most often, in that case, it is restricted to the near relatives of a man's spouse; as for the near relatives of a woman's spouse, they are her khatan or hamm. No one is free of a bond of marriage-kinship, even if distant. He has indicated, with His saying (﴿And your Lord is ever Competent﴾), the subtle order of natural and social creation contained in this wondrous creation, meaning: of great power, since from this water He brought into being a great creature possessing intellect and reflection, distinguished by the connection of bonds of lineage and bonds of marriage. This became the foundation of the system of human society, for the formation of tribes and peoples and their cooperation, which brought about this civilization advancing with the ages and regions. He, exalted is He, said: (﴿O mankind, indeed We created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]).

In the construction (﴿And your Lord is ever Competent﴾) there is a subtle indication that His power is firm and necessary to Him, and that He is characterized by it from eternity, by what the verb (kana) requires; and what is in the form (qadir) of intensity indicates the strength of power, which requires the completeness of will and knowledge.

The waw here is for the circumstantial clause (*hal*), and it is used to express wonder at their persistence in *shirk* (associating partners with God). It follows the mention of what God has granted people by way of His kindness in the workings of creation: He made the night and the day for them, created water for them so that He brings forth crops by it, and gives drink by it to people and livestock. Alongside this is the evidence of His power that accompanies it. The mention of their worship of what does not benefit people returns to relating some of the circumstances of the polytheists of Makkah.

The negation of harm after the negation of benefit serves to draw attention to the removal of any doubt that idol-worshippers might have about their *shirk*, because what motivates worship is either hope for benefit or fear of the harm of the one worshipped, and both of these are negated of the idols by direct observation.

The use of the present-tense verb indicates the continual renewal of their worship of idols and the failure of the clear signs that refute them to be of any use to them.

The clause ﴿وكانَ الكافِرُ عَلى رَبِّهِ ظَهِيرًا﴾ is a *tadhyil* (an appended concluding statement) to what precedes it. The *lam* in "al-kafir" (the disbeliever) is for *istighraq* (comprehensive inclusion), meaning: every disbeliever is a helper against his Lord.

[p. 57]

He made the predicate concerning the disbeliever the predicate of *kana* (was), to indicate that his being characterised by this predicate is a fixed and habitual matter for every disbeliever.

*Al-zahir* means *al-mudahir*, that is, the helper. It was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿ولَوْ كانَ بَعْضُهم لِبَعْضٍ ظَهِيرًا﴾ [al-Isra: 88] ("even if some of them were to others a helper") in Surat al-Isra. It is of the pattern *fa'il* in the sense of *mufa'il*, meaning *mudhahir*, like *hakim* in the sense of *muhkim* (one who makes firm), and *'awin* in the sense of *mu'awin* (helper). The verse of 'Umar ibn Ma'di Karib:

"From Raihana, the one who calls, the one who hears"
meaning: the one who makes hear.

In the *Kashshaf* he said: "The coming of *fa'il* in the sense of *mufa'il* is not rare." It is derived from *zaharahu 'alayhi*, when one helps the one who opposes another to overcome him. Its origin is *al-zahr* (the back), which is a noun denoting a solid thing, namely the back of a human or of an animal. This is because the one who helps someone to overcome another is as if he carries the victor upon the vanquished, just as a load is carried on the back of the bearer. The polytheist, in his associating of partners with God despite the clear evidence that the idols are not worthy of divinity, is thus treated as if he supports the idols against his true Lord. Mentioning the "Lord" carries an implicit reproach that the disbeliever is ungrateful towards his Master.

From Abu 'Ubayda: *zahir* means *mazhur* (one who is overcome), that is, the disbelief of the disbeliever is trivial to God. He means that *fa'il* here carries the sense of *maf'ul*, that is, one who is overcome against him. According to this view, *'ala* (against) is connected to the verb *kana* (was), meaning: he was trivial before God.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 56–57:

﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner.﴾ ﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it, except that whoever wills may take a way to his Lord.﴾

When the discourse, through its varied transitions, arrived at expressing wonder at their persistence in worshipping what neither harms them nor benefits them, it was followed by something that indicates their persistence in denying Muhammad ﷺ in his claim to prophethood, by attributing what he conveyed to them to falsehood, to the "fables of the ancients," and to sorcery. So all their claims were refuted by describing the Prophet as one sent from God, and by restricting him to the two attributes of bringing good tidings and warning. This statement, given in refutation of them, combines the nullification of their denial of his prophethood with the consolation of the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, by affirming that he does not lead anyone astray, but is only a bringer of good tidings and a warner. It also contains an allusion that he should not grieve over their denial of him.

Then He commanded him to address them, saying that he does not seek from their call that they should strengthen him by following him,

so that they may think that if they turn away from him they have achieved their aim of harming him. Rather, his only duty is to convey with good tidings and warning for their own benefit; he does not desire from them any recompense for his work.

And "ajr" (wage, reward) means the compensation for work, even if it is by another work intended as a recompense.

The exception (istithna') is an emphasis of the negation that he would ask them for a wage, because it is an exception from general conditions, the implied elements of which are omitted for the purpose of generalization. The exception is the criterion of generality, so it is common in the speech of the Arabs to make the emphasis of a verb take the form of an exception, which is called "emphasis of praise by what resembles blame," or, more precisely, "emphasis of a thing by what resembles its opposite." It has two levels. One is pure emphasis, which is where the excepted item is entirely disconnected from what it excepts, such as the saying of al-Nabigha:

"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords, by them, are notched from the clashing of the battalions."

For the notches of their swords are in no way of the same kind as a fault in them. The other level is emphasis in general, where the excepted item is not of the same kind as what it excepts, but is close to it by resemblance, and is not given the name of the thing it resembles by what the exception includes, as in His saying: (﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it, except the affection due to kinship﴾ [al-Shura: 23]). Do you not see that He negated that he asks them for any wage absolutely, in His saying: (﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it, and I am not of those who affect [what is not theirs]﴾ [Sad: 86])? So His saying, Exalted is He, (﴿except whoever wills to take a way to his Lord﴾) belongs to the second level, because the statement is with an omitted modifier that corresponds to "wage," the intended meaning being: except the work of whoever wills to take a way to his Lord, and that is following the religion of Islam. Since this was a response to the call of the Messenger ﷺ, it resembled a wage for that call, and thus it was the counterpart of His saying (﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it, except the affection due to kinship﴾ [al-Shura: 23]). Some call this kind of exception the "disconnected exception" (al-istithna' al-munqati'), and they interpret it as an exception of correction (istidrak).

"Al-sabil" means the road. The taking of a way has already been mentioned just before, in His saying: (﴿Would that I had taken a way with the Messenger﴾ [al-Furqan: 27]). The way is attributed here to God, because it is a means to answering Him in what He has called them to, and this is like His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿So whoever wills may take to his Lord a return﴾ [al-Naba': 39]).

The mention of the description "Lord" (Rabb) rather than the proper name (Allah) indicates that He deserves to be the destination of the journey, because the servant is bound to return to his Lord, otherwise he would be a runaway slave.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 58:

﴿And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die, and glorify Him with His praise; and sufficient is He as Knower of the sins of His servants.﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿Say, "I do not ask you for any wage for it"﴾. That is: say this to them, and rely upon Allah in your call to the religion, for it is He who will reward you for that and reward them.

Al-tawakkul (reliance) is dependence and the entrusting of affairs to the one relied upon, who is the Wakil, i.e., the one who takes charge of the affairs of others. It has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿So when you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾ [Al-Imran: 159] in Al-Imran.

﴿Al-Hayy alladhi la yamutu﴾ (the Ever-Living who does not die) is Allah, exalted is He. He turned away from the name Allah to these two attributes because of what this implies as a reason for the command to rely upon Him; for He is the Everlasting, so this conveys the meaning of restricting reliance to relying upon Him. The definite article in al-Hayy is for perfection, meaning one whose life is perfect, since His life is necessary, lasting and continuous, whereas the life of others is exposed to ceasing through death and exposed to the corruption of its effect through heedlessness, such as sleep and the like, for that is of the same kind as death. Thus reliance upon other than Him is exposed to corruption and to collapse. In mentioning the two attributes there is an allusion against the polytheists, since they pinned their hopes on idols, which are dead and not living.

The verse also indicates that the perfect person trusts only in Allah, because reliance upon living beings, who are exposed to death, although it may benefit at times, does not endure.

As for His command to glorify Him, it is exalting Allah above what does not befit Him, and the first of that is association in divinity. That is: if the matter of the polytheists' turning away from the call of Islam concerns you, then take care of yourself, and so glorify Allah.

The ba' in ﴿bi-hamdihi﴾ (with His praise) is for accompaniment, meaning: glorify Him with a glorification accompanied by praise of Him with what is due to Him. Thus in this matter there is combined the removal (takhliyah) and the adornment (tahliyah), with removal given precedence, because the nature of reform is to begin with the removal of deficiency.

The command to the Prophet ﷺ includes the community (ummah) so long as there is no evidence of particularity.

The clause ﴿and sufficient is He as Knower of the sins of His servants﴾ is a parenthetical insertion at the end of the speech, and it conveys the sense of a concluding summation (tadhyil), because of what it contains of indication of the comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge of the sins of creation, and among that are the circumstances of

[page 60]

the polytheists, who are the purpose of the speech. In "sins of His servants" there are two generalities: the generality of all their sins, since the plural noun in the genitive conveys the generality of the singular noun in the genitive, and the generality of people, since "servants" is attached to the pronoun of the Divine Name, meaning all His servants. Together with that, the form khabir (Knower) carries intensity of knowledge, which implies generality, so it was like a third generality. Al-kifayah (sufficiency) is adequacy, and the verb kafa conveys that He needs none other than Himself; it is used in the sense of a command to be content with entrusting the matter to Him.

The ba' is for emphasizing the attribution of the verb to its agent. The insertion of the emphatic ba' after the verb kafa upon its agent or its object has become common, and it has already been mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Sufficient is your own self against you this Day as a reckoner﴾ [Al-Isra: 14] in Surat al-Isra.  Khabiran is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in bihi, meaning: sufficient is He with respect to being Knower.

Knowledge of the sins is a metonymy (kinayah) for its necessary consequence, which is that He will recompense them for their sins, and shirk is the all-encompassing sin. There is also in the speech an allusion to consoling the Messenger ﷺ over what he encounters of their harm.

This relative clause was placed as a second description of (the Living One who does not die), because it entails breadth of knowledge, breadth of power, and great glory. Its bearer is therefore worthy of being relied upon, and the matter of recompense is to be entrusted to Him. This is a transition back to the argument from God's exercise of creative power.

The discussion of the creation of the heavens and the earth in six days has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah, and the discussion of the istiwa' (establishment upon the Throne) has passed in Surat al-A'raf.

(al-Rahman) is the khabar (predicate) of a deleted mubtada' (subject), meaning: "He is al-Rahman." This is the common deletion of the musnad ilayhi (the subject) in usage, when predicates or descriptions have preceded concerning its bearer, and then one intends to report about him something that expresses a description comprehensive of what came before, or more important to the purpose than what preceded. The description al-Rahman is more important to the purpose for which the speech is directed, namely the command to rely upon Him, since it is a description that entails that He manages the affairs of whoever relies upon Him with powerful assistance.

Page 61

The statement ﴿So ask about Him one who is well-informed﴾ follows as a consequence of the description (al-Rahman). It indicates that in His mercy there is such greatness and comprehensiveness that expression falls short of it. So instead of further description, He refers the matter to one who knows the workings of His mercy, who has tested it and who receives its reports from those who knew it and tested it.

The indefinite form of (khabiran) indicates generality, so that it is not taken to mean a specific expert. This is because when an indefinite noun is the object of a verb, it implies generality, as evidenced by the saying: "Whichever expert you ask will inform you."

This operates in the manner of a proverb, and perhaps it is one of the novel formulations of the Qur'an, in contrast to the Arabs' saying: "You have fallen upon the expert" (ʿalā al-khabīr saqaṭta), which is said by one who knows a thing when he is asked about it. Although the two proverbs are equal in the number of letters pronounced, the Qur'anic proverb is more eloquent, since it is free from the heaviness of the convergence of the qaf, ta' and ta' in (saqaṭta). It is also more noble, since it is free from the meaning of falling, and it is more expressive in meaning because it encompasses every expert, unlike their saying "You have fallen upon the expert," which is said of a specific individual.

Close in meaning to (﴿So ask about Him one who is well-informed﴾) is the verse of al-Nabighah:

"Why did you not ask the Banu Dhubyan about my lineage, when the smoke envelops the grey-haired and the decrepit?"

Up to his saying:

"Their man of honour will inform you about me, and their scholar; and one who knows is not like one who is ignorant."

The bāʾ in (bihi) is in the sense of ʿan ("about"), meaning: "ask about Him," like the saying of ʿAlqamah:

"If you ask me about women, then I am one who knows the ailments of women, a physician."

It is also permissible for the bāʾ to be connected to (khabiran), and the fronting of the prepositional phrase is both for the sake of rhyme before the closing word (al-fasilah) and for emphasis. Thus it has two reasons.

[Page 62]

Since the description of God as "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman) appeared alongside other attributes, the commentary digressed to the disbelief of the polytheists in this attribute. You have already learned, in the discussion of the basmalah (the formula "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate") at the beginning of this commentary, that describing God as "al-Rahman" is a usage introduced by the Qur'an and was not familiar to the Arabs. As for the verse of the poet of al-Yamamah praising Musaylimah:

[Page 62]

*You rose to glory, O son of the most noble fathers,*
*and you are the rain of the people; may you never cease to be "Rahman."*

That occurred after the emergence of Islam, during the period of apostasy (al-ridda). For this reason, when they heard it in the Qur'an, they rejected it deliberately, as a way of finding fault with the Prophet (ﷺ). This was not due to ignorance of the meaning of this attribute, nor because it did not follow the patterns of their language, nor because they thought that if God is described by it, it means a single Lord and that multiplicity lies only in the names. Rather, they used to say: "Look at this Sabian (ṣābi'), who forbids us from calling upon two gods, yet he calls upon God and calls upon the Rahman." In this regard the words of God were revealed: (﴿Say: Call upon God or call upon the Most Merciful; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-Isra' 17:110]). This was discussed at the end of Surah al-Isra'. This verse refers to that verse of Surah al-Isra'.

The statement here is used figuratively (kinayah) to express wonder at their obstinacy and their slander, and the purpose is not to inform about them of this, since it is a matter already known about them.

The prostration they were commanded to perform was the prostration of acknowledging Him as the One God, and it is the emblem of Islam. Prostration was not part of their worship; they used to circumambulate the idols. As for the prostration of the prayer (ṣalah), which is among the pillars of Islam, it is not intended here, since they were not among those commanded to pray, and there would be no benefit in obligating them to it before they had embraced Islam. This is supported by the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal when the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him to Yemen, and commanded him to call them to the testimony that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God. Then he said: "If they obey you in that, inform them that God has enjoined upon them five prayers in the day and the night," and so on. The question of obligating disbelievers to the branches of the Sharia has no fruitful outcome.

The conjunction waw in their saying (﴿And what is the Most Merciful?﴾) is for coordinating their speech with the speech that was addressed to them concerning the command to prostrate to the Most Merciful, in the manner of a conjunction entering between the speech of two speakers, as in His words: (﴿He said: Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people. He said: And from my descendants?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:124]). The "mā" in their saying (﴿And what is the Most Merciful?﴾) is interrogative.

The interrogation is used to express astonishment, meaning that they feign ignorance of this name. For this reason they asked about it using "mā" rather than "man" (who), in consideration that the question concerns the meaning of this name.

The interrogation in (﴿Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾) is a denial and refusal, meaning: we will not prostrate to something you command us to prostrate to, whether "mā" is an indefinite qualifying noun, or: we will not prostrate to the one you command us to prostrate to, if "mā" is a relative pronoun. The returning pronoun from the qualifier or the relative clause has been omitted together with what it is attached to, because of what preceded it. Their purpose in this is to refuse prostration to God, because the prostration they were commanded to perform is a prostration to God with the intention of God being singled out without any other. They would not respond to that, as God the Exalted said: (﴿They were called to prostration while they were sound [and able]﴾ [al-Qalam 68:43]), meaning: so they refuse. And He said: (﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow﴾ [al-Mursalat 77:48]). What indicates this is His saying: (﴿And it increases them in aversion﴾), for aversion from prostration preceded the hearing of the name al-Rahman.

Reading: The majority of readers read (taʾmuruna) with the second-person address (tā' of address). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the third-person (yā' of absence), on the basis that they were saying this among themselves and not addressing the Prophet (ﷺ) directly with it.

The hidden pronoun in (zādahum) refers to the statement derived from (﴿when it is said to them﴾). Nufur (aversion) is fleeing from a thing. It is applied here to its consequence, which is distance. The attribution of the increase of aversion to the statement is because it is the cause of that increase: they were already people of aversion from prostration to God, so when they were commanded to prostrate to the Most Merciful, they increased in distance from faith. This is like His saying in Surah Nuh: (﴿But my calling them has only increased them in flight﴾ [Nuh 71:6]).

This is a place of one of the prostrations of the Qur'an, by consensus. The wisdom of prostrating here is to demonstrate opposition to the polytheists, since they refused to prostrate to the Most Merciful. When their refusal to prostrate to the Most Merciful was reported in the context of wonder at their condition, this was reinforced by acting in contradiction to them. Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated here, opposing them in action, in order to intensify his opposition to them, after he had nullified their disbelief by His saying: (﴿And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die﴾ [al-Furqan 25:58]), the three verses. The Messenger (peace be upon him) established prostration at this place.

This is a passage from the commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 61:

﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky great stars (burūj) and placed within it a lamp and a moon giving light.﴾

This is an independent new statement (istiʾnāf ibtidāʾī), serving as a preface to His saying: (﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan: 63]) and the verses that follow, which are the product of the third of the three pillars (diʿāmah) on which the structure of this surah is built. Each of these pillars opens with (Blessed is He who...) etc., as has passed at the beginning of the surah. This was opened with the praise of Allah for blessing and goodness, because of what He made for creation of benefits. "Tabaraka" has been discussed at the beginning of the surah, and in His saying: (﴿Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]) in Surat al-A'raf.

The burūj (sing. burj): the stations through which the sun passes, as observed by astronomers. Its discussion has already been treated at His saying, exalted is He: (﴿And We have certainly placed in the sky great stars﴾ [al-Hijr: 16]) at the beginning of Surat al-Hijr.

The favor (imtinan) in them is because people fix their times by them.

The majority of readers recited (sirajan) in the singular form. The siraj (lamp) is the sun, as in His saying: (﴿and made the sun a lamp﴾ [Nuh: 16]) in Surat Nuh. The connection of this with what follows it, His saying: (﴿And it is He who made the night and the day succeeding one another﴾ [al-Furqan: 62]).

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited (surujan) with a damma on the sin and the ra, the plural of sirāj, so it includes, along with the sun, the stars; thus it is a favor by the beauty of their appearance to people, as in His saying: (﴿And We have certainly beautified the nearest heaven with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]). The favor by the excellent creations is found in the Qur'an, and He, exalted is He, said: (﴿And for you therein is beauty when you bring them in at evening and when you send them out to pasture﴾ [al-Nahl: 6]).

The discourse proceeds according to eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh), because the reality of the sirāj is a lamp shining with light. The intended meaning is that He made the sun removing darkness like a lamp, or He created the stars like a lamp in their glimmering and beauty of appearance.

The indication of the creation of the burūj, the sun and the moon of great power is a clear proof to the intelligent person; likewise His indication of precise craftsmanship and its order, such that it does not malfunction or vary, until people were enabled to observe their conditions and to tie their reckoning to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 62:

﴿And it is He who made the night and the day succeed each other, for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful.﴾

This argument is based on what the night and the day contain of difference in condition, between darkness and light, and cold and heat, of which one aspect may be more suitable to some people than to others. This differs from the argument in His saying: (﴿And it is He who made for you the night as a garment and sleep as rest, and made the day a resurrection.﴾ [al-Furqan: 47]), so this is a different indication, and the wisdoms in the created things are many.

The restriction here is a true restriction (qasr haqiqi), not a relative one (qasr idafi), and therefore it is not intended as a refutation of the polytheists, unlike the earlier forms of restriction from His saying: (﴿And it is He who made for you the night as a garment﴾ [al-Furqan: 47]) up to His saying: (﴿And your Lord is ever Powerful﴾ [al-Furqan: 54]).

Al-khilfah, with a kasra on the kha' and a sukun on the lam, is a noun for that which succeeds another in some of what suits it. This noun was formed on the pattern fi'lah, because it originally means "one who has a succession" (dhu khilfah), i.e., one possessing a state in which he succeeds another, and then its usage became widespread so that it became a noun. Zuhayr said:

"Among them the wild cattle and the gazelles walk in succession, and their young ones rise from every resting place."

That is: one herd walks and another herd succeeds it, and so they alternate in this manner. The meaning is: He made the night a succession and the day a succession, i.e., each of them is a succession to the other, in what one does in them of reflection upon the proofs of the creed, worship, and remembrance.

The lam in (﴿for whoever wishes to remember﴾) is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), and it is connected to (ja'ala, made). This indicates that this making is beneficial for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful.

Al-tadhakkur (remembrance) is a form of tafa'ul from al-dhikr, i.e., making an effort to remember. Al-dhikr in the Qur'an comes with the meaning of reflecting upon the proofs of the religion, and it also comes with the meaning of recalling what has been missed or forgotten, and what combines both meanings is recalling what has been hidden from thought.

Al-shukur, with a damma on the shin, is a verbal noun synonymous with al-shukr, and al-shukr is recognizing the goodness of the benefactor. What is meant here is worship, because it is gratitude to God, exalted is He.

The verse thus conveys the meaning: that the reflective person may consider their alternation, and know that their transition from one state to another requires a deliberate, wise Originator, and thereby infer the oneness of the Creator and know that He is of immense power, and so be certain that none other than Him deserves divinity; and that the grateful person may give thanks for the great blessings in the alternation of night and day, among which is what is mentioned in His saying: (﴿And it is He who made for you the night as a garment and sleep as rest, and made the day a resurrection.﴾ [al-Furqan: 47]), so that the thankful increase according to their different conditions and circumstances. It also conveys the meaning: that the forgetful person may make up what he missed at night because of overpowering sleep or fatigue, by doing it during the day, or what occupations of work in the day prevented him from, by doing it at night when free, so that this does not diminish for him the reward of his deeds. It is related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab prolonged the Duha prayer one day, and it was said to him: "You have done something you did not used to do?" He said: "Something of my daily portion (wird) remained for me, so I wished to make it up," and he recited His saying: (﴿And it is He who made the night and the day succeed each other﴾), the verse. And for whoever wishes to draw near to God in gratitude to Him through prayer or fasting, so that the night is more favourable for some of that and the day for some other, this is a great benefit in a wondrous brevity.

The plural of those who remember is expressed with His saying (an yadhdhakkara, "to remember"), indicating renewal through the present tense (al-mudari'). For the side of those who are grateful, he restricted himself to the verbal noun in His saying (aw arada shukuran, "or wishes to be grateful"), because gratitude occurs in a single instance. And because of the difference between the two constructions, the verb (arada, "wishes") was repeated, since coordinating (shukuran) with (an yadhdhakkara) would not fit.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read (an yadhdhakkara) with a shadda on the dhal, fathah, and its original form is yatadhakkaru; the ta' was assimilated into the dhal because they are close in articulation. Hamzah and Khalaf read (an yadhkura) with a sukun on the dhal and a damma on the kaf, and it has the same meaning as the doubled form, except that the doubled form is stronger in effect; and both effects are attained in the night and the day.

[Page 67]

This is the conjunction of one sentence to another. The conjoined sentence is "the servants of the Most Merciful" and so on. Its subject is "the servants of the Most Merciful," and its predicate is "those who walk upon the earth in humility" and so on. It has also been said that the predicate is "those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber for their patience" [al-Furqan: 75]. The sentence conjoined to is "And it is He who made the night and the day to succeed one another" [al-Furqan: 62] and so on. Thus, on the occasion of mentioning those who wished to be mindful, the discourse moves on to the qualities of the believers, the followers of the Prophet ﷺ, so that the surah completes its aims of extolling the Qur'an, the one who brought it, and those who followed him, as we indicated when we summarized its most important aims at the beginning of its tafsir (exegesis). This is among the most brilliant transitions (takhallus), since it comes unexpectedly to the listener, who thinks it is an incidental digression like what preceded it, until it surprises him with what announces the conclusion, which is "Say: My Lord would not care for you" [al-Furqan: 77] and the verse that follows.

The term "the servants of the Most Merciful" primarily refers to the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ. The eight qualities described in this verse are therefore a description of their attributes, which were specific to them.

Since these qualities were ascribed to them in a context of praise and promise of the reward of Paradise, it is known that whoever possesses these qualities is promised a similar reward. God has honored them by making their title "His servants," and He chose for them, in the attribution to His name, the name "the Most Merciful," because their mention comes after the mention of the group who were told, "Prostrate yourselves to the Most Merciful," and they said, "And what is the Most Merciful?" Thus, if "the servants of the Most Merciful" is taken to refer to the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, then the predicate is "those who walk upon the earth in humility" and the subsequent conjoined phrases, and His later statement "those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber for their patience" [al-Furqan: 75] is a new sentence (isti'naf) explaining that they are worthy of what follows the demonstrative noun.

If "the servants of the Most Merciful" refers to all believers who possess the content of these relative clauses, then those relative pronouns and their clauses are descriptions of "the servants of the Most Merciful," and the predicate is the demonstrative noun in His statement "those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber" [al-Furqan: 75] and so on.

In the elaboration on their good qualities, there is an allusion that those who refused to prostrate to the Most Merciful and whose aversion increased are the opposite of these praiseworthy traits. This is an allusion indicated by the attribution of "servants" to "the Most Merciful."

Know that these relative clauses which were applied to "the servants of the Most Merciful" come in four categories. One category concerns adorning oneself with religious perfections, and these are the ones that begin with His statement, "those who walk upon the earth in humility," up to His statement "peace" (salaman).

Another category concerns abandoning the errors of the people of polytheism, and it is from His statement "and those who do not call upon another god with God" [al-Furqan: 68].

Another category concerns steadfastness upon the laws of Islam, and it is His statement "and those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing" [al-Furqan: 64], and His statement "and those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant" [al-Furqan: 67] and the verse, and His statement "and who do not kill the soul" [al-Furqan: 68] up to His statement "and who do not witness falsehood" [al-Furqan: 72] and so on.

And another category concerns seeking increase in the goodness of one's condition in this life, and it is His statement "and those who say, 'Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses'" [al-Furqan: 74] up to His statement "an imam for the righteous" [al-Furqan: 74].

The apparent meaning of His statement "who walk upon the earth in humility" is that it praises a manner of walking with the feet, and this is what most of the exegetes (mufassirun) have adopted.

Al-Zajjaj permitted that His statement "walk" (yamshun) be an expression for their conduct in dealing with people, so that this is expressed by movement upon the earth. Ibn 'Atiyyah followed him, and what he mentioned is derived from what was narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, as will come. According to the first interpretation, restricting the walking to being "upon the earth" serves so that the description of it as "humble" implies that they walk this way by choice, and not when walking on steep ascents or over rocks.

Al-Hawn means gentleness and kindness. Here it occurs as an attribute of a verbal noun of walking that has been omitted, its implied form being "walking" (mashyan), so it is in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq).

Humble walking is that in which there is no stamping of the feet or flapping of sandals. It is contrary to the walk of the arrogant tyrants who are self-admiring and proud of their own strength. This humility arises from humbleness before God, the adoption of the manners of a noble soul, and the removal of the insolence of the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance). Thus this manner of walking was among the characteristics of those who believed, in contrast to the walk of the people of the Jahiliyyah. It is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he saw a youth strutting in his walk and said to him, "Strutting is a manner of walking that is disliked except in the way of God." God the Exalted has praised peoples with His saying: "And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility" [al-Furqan: 63], so aim for moderation in your walk. God the Exalted also related from Luqman to his son: "And do not walk upon the earth exultantly" [Luqman: 18].

Adopting this character is a manifestation of adopting the trait of mercy, which is fitting for the servants of the Most Merciful, because mercy is the opposite of harshness, so humility accords with its nature, and in it there is safety from jostling those who pass by.

It is narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam that he said: "I used to ask about the interpretation of His statement, 'Those who walk upon the earth in humility,' and I found no cure in that. Then I saw in a dream someone who came to me and said: 'They are those who do not wish to cause corruption upon the earth.'" This is an opinion of Zayd ibn Aslam which was inspired to him, and it makes the meaning of "walk upon the earth" a metaphor for working upon the earth, like His saying: "And when he turns away, he strives upon the earth to cause corruption therein" [al-Baqarah: 205]. And it makes "humility" a metaphor for doing good, since he was gentle (hawwana) toward people, just as good is called ma'ruf.

Their description with humility in their bearing, which is walking upon the earth humbly, is paired with another attribute that suits humility and the dislike of arrogance, namely, abandoning those who act ignorantly toward them in address with harm and abuse. These ignorant ones, on that day, were the polytheists, since they used to confront the Muslims with harm and abuse. So God taught them to leave the foolish alone. Thus "ignorance" here is the opposite of forbearance (hilm), and this is the most well-known usage of it among the Arabs before Islam, as is known in much poetry and prose.

"Peace" (salaman) is in the accusative as an absolute object. He mentioned the description "the ignorant" instead of others that are more blameworthy, such as "the disbelievers," because this description implies that the address issuing from them is address of ignorance and harshness.

"Peace" (al-salam) may be a verbal noun in the sense of safety, meaning: there is no good between us and no evil, so we are safe from you. It may also be that the word of greeting (al-tahiyyah) is intended by it, so that it is used in its implication, which is disengagement, because the basic use of the word "peace" in greeting indicates security, that is, the absence of agitation. And security is the first thing with which a person greets one whom he wishes to honor. So the verse has the sense of His statement: "And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it and say, 'To us are our deeds and to you are your deeds. Peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant'" [al-Qasas: 55].

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "I was shown in some histories that Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi, who was among those inclined toward 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said one day in the presence of al-Ma'mun, with a group present: 'I used to see 'Ali ibn Abi Talib in sleep, and I would say to him, "Who are you?" He would say, "'Ali ibn Abi Talib." I would come with him to a bridge, and he would go ahead of me in crossing it. I would say, "You claim this matter through a woman, and we are more worthy of it than you."'" He said: "I did not see in his reply any eloquence as is mentioned about him." Al-Ma'mun said: "And how did he answer you?" He said: "He would say to me: 'Salaman.'" The narrator said: "It seems that Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi did not remember the verse, or it escaped him at that moment, so al-Ma'mun drew the attention of those present to the verse and said: 'By God, O uncle, it is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and he answered you with the most eloquent of answers.' Ibrahim was humiliated and felt ashamed."

Because of the correspondence between the two forms, this clause was conjoined to the first relative clause. The relative pronoun was not repeated as it was repeated in the descriptions after it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 64:

﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord prostrating and standing.﴾ It is a conjunction of another attribute with their two preceding attributes, in the manner of the poet's saying:

To the lordly king, the generous son of the noble one, and the lion of the battalion in the crush of the throng.

The repetition of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is to emphasize that they are recognized by this relative clause. Apparently, these relative pronouns and all their clauses are descriptions or attributes of the servants of the Most Merciful. It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that when he recited (﴿Those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan: 63]) he said: "This is the description of their day." Then when he recited (﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord prostrating and standing﴾) he said: "This is the description of their night."

Al-qiyam (standing) is the plural of qa'im, like al-sihab (companions). Prostration (al-sujud) and standing (al-qiyam) are the two pillars (ruknan) of prayer (al-salah, the ritual prayer). So the meaning is: they spend the night praying. There is therefore an elaboration (itnab) in expressing prayer through its two pillars, to draw attention to both of them. The placing of "prostrating" (sujjadan) before "standing" (qiyaman) is for the sake of the rhyme (al-fasilah), along with an indication of the importance given to prostration, which the Prophet ﷺ explained by saying: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating." The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were much given to tahajjud (night prayer), as Allah praised them for it by saying: (﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾ [al-Sajdah: 16]).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verses 65–66:

﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell; indeed, its punishment is ever-adhering destruction."﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a place of settlement and residence.﴾

Their supplication in this manner is a sign of the intensity of their fear of sins, so they strive to attain the good pleasure of their Lord in order to be saved from the punishment. Thus, what is meant by averting the punishment is their being saved from it by facilitating righteous deeds, abundantly providing them, and avoiding evil deeds.

Page 71

The clause (﴿indeed, its punishment is ever-adhering destruction﴾) may be a quotation from the words of those who say it, or it may be from the words of God Most High, placed as a parenthetical clause between the two relative pronouns. In either case, it is a justification for their request that its punishment be averted from them.

Al-gharam: constant, insistent destruction; its use has become predominantly applied to continuous evil.

The clause (﴿indeed, it is evil as a place of settlement and residence﴾) may be a quotation of the words of those who say it, in which case it is a second justification, reinforcing their first justification. It may be from God Most High, not from what precedes it, in which case it is a confirmation of the justification of those who say it. Or it may be from God Most High together with what precedes it, in which case it is a repetition of the parenthetical clause.

Al-mustaqarr: the place of settling. Al-istiqrar: the strength of staying. Al-muqam: the name of the place of dwelling, i.e., it is evil as a place for those who settle in it without dwelling, such as the sinners among the people of religions, and for those who dwell in it from among those who denied the messengers sent to them.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 25, verse 67:**

﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever justly balanced between that.﴾

His saying "﴿when they spend﴾" indicates that spending is one of their characteristics, as if he had said: "Those who spend, and when they spend, etc." By spending here is meant voluntary spending, not obligatory spending, which is a person's spending on his household and companions, because extravagance is not blamed in obligatory spending, and forbidden spending is not praised at all, let alone stinginess in it being blamed. Moreover, in his saying "when they spend" there is an implication that they chose to spend and that it was not obligatory upon them.

Extravagance (al-israf) is exceeding the limit that spending requires according to the condition of the spender and the condition of the one spent upon. The meaning of extravagance was mentioned earlier in His saying, may He be exalted: (﴿And do not consume their property extravagantly﴾ [An-Nisa 4:6]) in Surah An-Nisa, and in His saying: (﴿And do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not like those who are excessive﴾ [Al-An'am 6:141]) in Surah Al-An'am.

Stinginess (al-iqtar) is its opposite. The people of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) used to be extravagant in spending on pleasures, they would overpay for wine, and they would complete the bets in the game of chance (maysir). Their statements on this are numerous in their poetry,

Page 72

and they are found in the Mu'allaqa of Tarafa, in the Mu'allaqa of Labid, and in the Mimiyya of al-Nabigha. They boasted of squandering wealth so that the nobles would speak of them for that. The poet said, praising:

*A giver and a squanderer: when you come to him, he beams and quivers like a sharpened sword.*

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read (﴿wa lam yuqtiru﴾) with a damma on the initial yaʾ and a kasra on the taʾ, from iqtar, which is synonymous with taqtir. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the yaʾ and a kasra on the taʾ, from iqtar, which is synonymous with taqtir. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the yaʾ and a kasra on the taʾ, from qatara, of the pattern ḍaraba, and this is a dialect. 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a fatha on the yaʾ and a damma on the taʾ, from the verb qatara of the pattern naṣara.

Iqtar and qatr mean scrimping and falling short of what wealth allows and what the condition of the one spent upon requires. The people of the Jahiliyyah used to be stingy toward the needy and the weak, because they did not hear the praise of the nobles for that. This was mentioned earlier at His saying: (﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, is a bequest for parents and relatives﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:180]).

The reference in His saying "between that" is to what was mentioned earlier, by way of interpreting it as "the thing mentioned," i.e., extravagance and stinginess.

Qawam, with a fatha on the qaf, means justice and moderation between two extremes.

The meaning is that they place expenditures in their proper and suitable places as God has commanded them, so their spending endures. Islam has encouraged the kind of action that its doer sustains, and so that the order of the community runs smoothly with sufficiency, without exposing it to paralysis. Extravagance, by its nature, exhausts wealth, so spending does not endure; and stinginess, by its nature, withholds wealth, so those who deserve it are deprived.

His saying "between that" is the predicate of (kana) [the verb "was"], and "qawaman" is a emphatic circumstantial accusative for the meaning of "between that." It contains an implication of praising what lies between those two, as being the correct course in which there is no crookedness. It is also permissible that "qawaman" be the predicate of (kana) and "between that" be an adverbial phrase of place governed by it. The verse has been arranged with regard to the prevailing conditions of people's spending. Al-Qurtubi said: "Qawam differs for each individual according to his dependents and his condition, and for this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) allowed Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) to give away all of his wealth in charity, but prevented others from doing so."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 68–69:

Page 73
﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah any other god, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right, nor commit adultery. And whoever does that will meet with penalty.﴾ ﴿The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein in humiliation.﴾

This is another category of the attributes of the servants of the Most Merciful, namely the category of abstaining from the corruptions that were constant among their people, the polytheists. The servants of the Most Merciful kept themselves free from them because of their faith. Mentioned here is their abstention from shirk, from killing the soul, and from fornication, and these three vices were predominant among the polytheists.

The description of the soul with ﴿which Allah has forbidden﴾ serves to explain the sanctity of the soul, which was established from the time of Adam, as Allah related in the dialogue of the son of Adam with the words: ﴿"Surely I will kill you"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 27], and the verses that follow. Thus the prohibition of killing a soul was established from the earliest times of humanity, and no one among the descendants of Adam was ignorant of it. This is the meaning of describing the soul by the relative clause in His saying: ﴿which Allah has forbidden﴾. Killing of souls was widespread among the Arabs through enmities and raids, and through the burying alive of their daughters among many tribes, and through killing out of excessive jealousy, as Imru' al-Qays said:

I passed through guards toward her, and a group eager against me, who would conceal my killing, if they could.

And 'Antarah said:

I fell in love with her, while I kill her people, claiming, by the life of your father, that it is no mere claim.

As for His saying ﴿except by right﴾, what is meant by it at that time is the killing of the slayer of one of them. This was a preparation for the legitimacy of jihad after a period from the revelation of this surah. At that time the Muslims did not have authority to enforce retaliation (qisas) and the prescribed penalties (hudud). The discussion of fornication has passed in Surat Subhan.

The abstention from these three crimes has been combined in one relative clause and the relative pronoun was not repeated as it was repeated in mentioning the qualities of their virtues, to indicate that, since they gave up shirk and did not invoke any other god with Allah, they had surely given up the gravest vices closest to shirk, which are killing the soul and fornication. Thus this was made like one single characteristic and placed in one relative clause.

Page 74
It may be that the repetition of (لا) substitutes for repeating the relative pronoun and suffices to indicate that each of these vices necessitates the doubling of the punishment. This is supported by what is in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which sin is greatest?' He said: 'That you set up a rival to Allah, when He created you.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'That you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife.' Then Allah the Exalted revealed its confirmation: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah any other god﴾ up to ﴿penalty﴾." In the narration of Ibn 'Atiyyah: "Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse."

You have known that these three verses up to His saying ﴿Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 70] were said to have been revealed in Medina.

The indication by ﴿that﴾ refers to the grave sins mentioned, interpreting it as "the mentioned," as was previously stated in its like just above. What is apparent from the indication is that it refers to the totality, meaning: whoever does all three of them; and it is known that the recompense of one who does some of them and leaves others, other than shirk, is less than the recompense of one who does all of them, and that some of them also have degrees. The meaning is not that whoever does each one of what is mentioned will meet with penalty, because meeting penalty is explained here by the doubling of the punishment and abiding therein. Strong evidences from the Book and the Sunnah have established that sins other than disbelief do not necessitate eternal abiding, which requires interpreting the apparent meaning of the verse.

It is also permissible that the doubling of the punishment is used in the sense of its intensity, meaning: he will be punished with a severe punishment, and it is not for the repetition of a punishment that is estimated.

Athām, with a fatha on the hamzah, is the recompense of sin, on the pattern of wabāl and nakāl, and it is more severe than ithm, meaning he will be requited for that with evil, because they are sins.

The clause ﴿the punishment will be doubled for him﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for ﴿he will meet with penalty﴾, and substitution of a verb by a verb is substitution of a clause. If in the clause there is a verb that admits inflection, the grammatical position of the place appears in that verb, since it is the pillar of the clause. The recompense is made the doubling of the punishment and abiding.

As for the doubling of the punishment, it means that he is punished for each offence mentioned with a punishment appropriate to it, and one is not content with the greatest punishment for the greatest crime, which is shirk, as a warning that shirk does not save its holder from the consequence of what he commits of crimes and corruptions. This is because the call of Islam to people came with abstaining from shirk and from all corruptions. This is the meaning of the statement of those scholars who said that disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the Sharia, meaning address of accountability for what they were forbidden to commit; it does not mean that they are required to act, since their good deeds are not accepted without faith. For this reason some of the scholars of usul sought to restrict the dispute to address of obligation (khitab al-taklif) and not to address of destruction and offences, and to address of legal status (khitab al-wad') entirely.

As for abiding in the punishment, it is required by shirk.

His saying: (مُهانًا, humiliated) is a circumstantial state (hal), intended to depict their condition in the Hereafter as wretched, meaning: he is punished and humiliated with a humiliation additional to the humiliation of punishment, by being abused and degraded.

Al-Jumhur read (يُضاعَفْ, yudaʻaf) with an alif after the ḍād and with the verb in the jussive. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read (يُضَعَّفْ, yuḍaʻʻaf) with a shaddah on the ʻayn and in the jussive. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr ibn 'Asim read (يُضاعَفُ, yudāʻafu) with an alif after the ḍād and with the verb in the nominative, on the basis that it is a resumptive explanatory statement (isti'naf bayani).
