The clause ﴿the punishment will be doubled for him﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for ﴿he will meet with penalty﴾, and substitution of a verb by a verb is substitution of a clause. If in the clause there is a verb that admits inflection, the grammatical position of the place appears in that verb, since it is the pillar of the clause. The recompense is made the doubling of the punishment and abiding.

As for the doubling of the punishment, it means that he is punished for each offence mentioned with a punishment appropriate to it, and one is not content with the greatest punishment for the greatest crime, which is shirk, as a warning that shirk does not save its holder from the consequence of what he commits of crimes and corruptions. This is because the call of Islam to people came with abstaining from shirk and from all corruptions. This is the meaning of the statement of those scholars who said that disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the Sharia, meaning address of accountability for what they were forbidden to commit; it does not mean that they are required to act, since their good deeds are not accepted without faith. For this reason some of the scholars of usul sought to restrict the dispute to address of obligation (khitab al-taklif) and not to address of destruction and offences, and to address of legal status (khitab al-wad') entirely.

As for abiding in the punishment, it is required by shirk.

His saying: (مُهانًا, humiliated) is a circumstantial state (hal), intended to depict their condition in the Hereafter as wretched, meaning: he is punished and humiliated with a humiliation additional to the humiliation of punishment, by being abused and degraded.

Al-Jumhur read (يُضاعَفْ, yudaʻaf) with an alif after the ḍād and with the verb in the jussive. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read (يُضَعَّفْ, yuḍaʻʻaf) with a shaddah on the ʻayn and in the jussive. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr ibn 'Asim read (يُضاعَفُ, yudāʻafu) with an alif after the ḍād and with the verb in the nominative, on the basis that it is a resumptive explanatory statement (isti'naf bayani).

The exception from the generality conveyed by the conditional *man* ("whoever") in His saying ﴿And whoever does that﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]. The sense is: *except for one who repents, for he will not have his punishment doubled and will not abide in it forever.* This is a reassurance to a group of believers who had taken on the traits of the people of polytheism and then repented of them through their repentance from polytheism. Otherwise, in their calling upon another god alongside Allah, there is no additional praise after the description of them as "the servants of the Most Merciful."

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: some people among the polytheists had killed many and committed much fornication, so they came to Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: "What you say and call to is good. If only you would tell us that there is an expiation for what we have done!" Then there was revealed ﴿And those who do not call upon another god with Allah﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], up to the end of the verse. The meaning is that he will be pardoned from the punishment for the sins from which he repented, and it does not occur to the mind that he will be punished with a punishment that is not doubled and not everlasting, because that is not among the usages of the Arabic language. Rather, the original principle, when a restricted thing is lifted, is that what is intended is lifting the whole thing, not lifting its restrictions, unless there is an indicator.

Repentance (tawbah) is abandoning sin, regret for what was neglected, and resolve not to return to sin. Since mention of polytheism preceded, repentance here is adopting faith (*iman*). Faith after disbelief necessitates the absence of accountability for what the polytheist committed during his polytheism, as in the hadith: "Islam erases what came before it." For this reason, *wa-amana* ("and believed") is conjoined to *man taba* ("whoever repents") to honor faith, and so that His saying ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾ may be built upon it. The righteous deeds are the legislated obligations of Islam, as an encouragement to good deeds and an indication that they are not counted except together with faith, as He said in Surat al-Balad: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17], and He said in the opposite case: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one takes to be water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾ [al-Nur: 39].

The killing of a soul that occurred during the period of polytheism is erased by the faith of the killer, because of the excellence of faith; and Islam erases what came before it without disagreement. The disagreement among the early generations (*al-salaf*) regarding the validity of the repentance of a killer concerns only a believer who kills another believer deliberately. Since this is among what this verse includes, because its context is praise of the believer, the verse indicates that repentance erases the sins of every one of the enumerated sins, among them the killing of a soul without right, which is known from the general texts of the Book and the Sunnah. This was explained in detail in Surat al-Nisa' at His saying ﴿And whoever kills a believer deliberately﴾ [al-Nisa': 93], up to the end of the verse.

The exception is followed by the consequence: that those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. This is a statement given to explain the excellence of the mentioned repentance, which is faith after polytheism, because *man taba* is an exception from *man yaf'al dhalika*. So it is determined that the evil deeds attributed to them are the well-known evil deeds, i.e., those previously mentioned, which they committed during their time of polytheism.

Replacement (*tabdil*) is making one thing a substitute for another. It was discussed at His saying ﴿Then We replaced the evil with good﴾ [al-A'raf: 95] in Surat al-A'raf. That is: Allah will give them many good deeds in exchange for those evil deeds they committed before repentance. This replacement has come in general terms, and it is a replacement that has an effect in the Hereafter, by compensating them, for the requital of their evil deeds, with the reward of good deeds that are the opposites of those evil deeds. This is due to the excellence of faith in relation to polytheism, and the excellence of repentance in relation to the sins committed by Muslims.

By this the position of the demonstrative in His saying ﴿fa-ulaika﴾ ("then those") becomes clear, which conveys alerting to the fact that they are deserving of what is reported about them after the demonstrative, because of the attributes mentioned before the demonstrative. That is: "Then those" are the repentant, believing, righteous-deed-doing ones in faith, for whom Allah will replace the punishment for their evil deeds that they committed—polytheism, killing, and fornication—with reward. The verse does not address the amount of the reward, which is left to the bounty of Allah. For this reason it is followed by His saying ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾, which implies that He is of great forgiveness.

[p. 76]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 71:

﴿And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then indeed he turns back to Allah with a [proper] return.﴾

When a statement is made about a thing, or a description of it, or a state of it, using a term synonymous with what preceded it, with the same meaning and no addition, it becomes necessary that the second statement be used to convey something among the implications of the meaning of the statement, which the context makes clear, as in the verse of Abu al-Tamahan al-Qaini:

"And indeed I am of the people who are [themselves] the people"

And the verse of Abu al-Najm:

"I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is [truly] my poetry"

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): ("Whoever sees me in a dream has indeed seen me.")

So His statement here, ﴿And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then indeed he turns back to Allah with a [proper] return.﴾, is a statement about the penitent that he is a penitent, since al-matab is a mimi verbal noun meaning repentance (tawbah). It is therefore necessary that it be interpreted to convey a meaningful sense. It is permissible that the intended meaning is His words "to Allah," so that it is a metaphor (kinayah) for the greatness of His reward.

It is also permissible that the intended meaning is what the imperfect verb indicates of continuity and renewal, i.e., that he will continue in his repentance and not turn back on his heels; this is then a promise from Allah, Exalted, that He will make him firm in the firm word, if he has repented and supported his repentance with righteous deeds.

It is also permissible that the intended meaning is the emphasis carried by the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq), i.e., whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then indeed his repentance is the complete, sincere repentance purely for Allah, in the manner of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: ("Actions are only by intentions, and every person will only have what he intended. So whoever's migration was to Allah and His Messenger, his migration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's migration was for a worldly gain he might obtain or a woman he might marry, his migration is to what he migrated for.") So it is like His statement, Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, repent to Allah with sincere repentance﴾ [At-Tahrim: 8]. The exegetes mentioned other, distant possibilities.

The emphasis with "inna" (indeed) under all these interpretations is to affirm the content of the statement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 72:

﴿And those who do not bear witness to falsehood, and when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity.﴾

He follows the three attributes of the believers, which are the pillars of faith (qiwam al-iman), with other attributes of theirs that belong to the perfection of faith, to cultivating its virtues, and to keeping away from the conditions of the people of polytheism (shirk). These are three attributes, the first of which is expressed by His saying here: ﴿And those who do not bear witness to falsehood﴾ up to the end of the verse.

The verb shahida is used in the sense of "to be present" (hadara), which is its primary usage, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. It is also used in the sense of "to report something one has witnessed and known," as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a witness from among her family testified﴾ [Yusuf: 26].

Al-zur is falsehood, whether in speech or in action, and it has become predominantly applied to lying. It was discussed at the beginning of the surah. So it is possible that the meaning of the verse is that they do not attend the gatherings of falsehood that the polytheists used to attend, namely gatherings of amusement, singing, backbiting and the like, and likewise the festivals and games of the polytheists. In this case, al-zur is the direct object of (yashhadun). This is a praise of the believers for their separation from and avoidance of the polytheists. As for attending the places of idol worship, that has already been included in His saying: ﴿And those who do not call upon another god along with Allah﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]. In the same sense as this verse is His saying in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And when you see those who engage in [mocking] Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in another topic. And if Satan should cause you to forget, then do not sit after the reminder with the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-An'am: 68].

It is also possible that the verb (yashhadun) means "to report what they know," and al-zur is then in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning: they do not bear witness to falsehood; or it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) explaining the type of testimony, meaning: they do not bear a testimony which is falsehood rather than truth.

His saying ﴿and when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ fits both clauses.

Al-laghw is meaningless and foolish speech that has no good in it. It was discussed in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk﴾ [Maryam: 62] in Surat Maryam. The meaning of passing by it is passing by its speakers while they are engaged in their idle talk. The passing is attributed to the idle talk itself to indicate that those engaged in it are involved in it at the time of passing.

The meaning of ﴿they pass by with dignity﴾ is that they pass by while in a state of dignity, that is, not involved in participating in the idle talk. For foolish people, when they pass by those engaged in idle talk, they become familiar with them, stop with them, and join them in their idle talk; when they do that, they are not in a state of dignity.

Karamah (dignity) is purity and good qualities, and its opposite is baseness and vileness. The original meaning of karamah is the preciousness of a thing within its kind. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿We caused to grow therein of every noble pair﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 7]. One of the poets of Himyar said in al-Hamasah:

"Their rider does not avoid the encounter until he breaks through the ranks by his karam (courage)."

That is: his bravery. And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And He has prepared for them a noble reward﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44].

When people of honor pass by those engaged in idle talk, they keep themselves free from joining them and pass beyond their assembly, so they are in a state of dignity. This is a praise of the believers for rising above what they used to be upon in the age of ignorance (jahiliyyah), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion﴾ [al-An'am: 70], and His saying: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say, "To us are our deeds and to you are your deeds. Peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant"﴾ [al-Qasas: 55].

The repetition of the verb (marru) is to build the state (hal) upon it, and that is among the eloquent usages, like the saying of al-Ahwas:

"So when he moves, he moves away from one in fury, whose outbursts are feared by his peers."

And from it is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, these are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray just as we went astray﴾ [al-Qasas: 63], as mentioned by Ibn Jinni in Sharh Mushkil Abyat al-Hamasah. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 73:

﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall down before them deaf and blind﴾.

The purpose is to distinguish the believers by their opposition to a state that is among the states of the polytheists, namely their condition of hearing the call of the Messenger (ﷺ) and what it contains of Qur'anic signs, and being asked to reflect on the evidences of God's oneness. Therefore the relative clause was brought in order to obtain praise for them, together with an implicit disparagement of the condition of the polytheists. For the polytheists, when they were reminded of the signs of God, would fall down deaf and blind, like one who does not want to see something and so puts his face to the ground. Thus "falling down" (al-khurur) is used metaphorically to express intense aversion and distance, such that their state upon hearing the Qur'an is like that of one who falls to the ground, so as not to see what he dislikes, to the point that he retains nothing of standing upright or rising. That is a state which is the utmost in negating the possibility of acceptance.

Among this usage is the metaphor of "sitting" (al-qu'ud) for holding back from fighting. In the opposite sense, turning towards, receiving, and standing are used metaphorically for giving attention to a matter and caring for it.

It is also permissible that the falling down be actual, either from all of them or from some of them, in the literal sense; for they would be sitting in their gatherings and assemblies, and when the Messenger (ﷺ) invited them to Islam, they would lower their heads and bring them close to the ground, because that for one who is seated stands in the place of flight, or of covering the face. Compare the words of a Bedouin satirizing a people of Tayy, which al-Mubarrad cited:

When it is said, "Which of them is to so-and-so?" the shoulders and heads become alike.

Close to this meaning is His saying, exalted is He, in Surah Nuh: (﴿And they covered themselves with their garments, and persisted, and grew arrogant with great arrogance﴾ [Nuh: 7]). The literal falling down has already occurred in His saying: (﴿They fall down upon their chins prostrating﴾ [al-Isra': 107]) in Surah al-Isra', and His saying: (﴿The roof fell down upon them from above them﴾ [al-Nahl: 26]), and His saying: (﴿And Musa fell down unconscious﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]) in Surah al-A'raf.

Page 81

"Deaf and blind" (﴿ṣumman wa-'umyanan﴾) are two circumstantial accusatives (hal) from the pronoun in (yakhirru), intended as a simile with the particle of comparison omitted, i.e.: they fall down like the deaf and the blind, in not benefiting from what is heard of the signs and what is seen of them, by which they are reminded. Accordingly the negation here is directed at the verb and at its qualifier, and this usage is very common in speech. This is the more likely view.

It is also permissible that the negation be directed at the qualifier, as is the more common usage, and this is the preference of the author of al-Kashshaf. The meaning then is: they did not fall down upon them in a state like deafness and blindness, but they fall down upon them hearing and seeing; so falling down is used metaphorically for eagerness to act with the whole heart, as one says "he bent over such-and-such" meaning he exerted his effort in it. The disparagement is then of the polytheists in that they make themselves deaf and blind to the signs, yet at the same time fall down to receive them, feigning eagerness for that. This view is weak, because it would only fit if those alluded to were hypocrites. How could it be so, since the surah is Meccan? As for the polytheists, they turned away openly from receiving the call, as God said: (﴿And those who disbelieve said: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise over it, that perhaps you may prevail"﴾ [Fussilat: 26]) and He said: (﴿And they say: "Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a veil"﴾ [Fussilat: 5]).

[Page 82 of the commentary]

Ibn 'Ashur on Surah 25 (al-Furqan), verse 74:

﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and our offspring comfort to our eyes, and make us leaders for the God-conscious."﴾

This is the third attribute of the believers: they are concerned with the spread of Islam and the multiplication of its followers, so they ask God to grant them spouses and offspring who will be a comfort to their eyes. As for the spouses, they obey them by following Islam and its laws, since some of the spouses of Muslims were opposed to their husbands in religion. As for the offspring, when they grow up, they grow up as believers. All of this is brought together in the phrase "comfort to our eyes," for it encompasses completeness in religion and the soundness of one's circumstances in life, since the eyes of believers are comforted only by believing spouses and believing children. God forbade the Muslims from keeping disbelieving women in marriage, saying: (﴿And do not hold on to marriage ties with disbelieving women﴾ [Al-Mumtahanah: 10]), and He said: (﴿And the one who said to his parents, "Uff to you both! Do you threaten me that I will be brought forth?"﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 17]), and so on. For this reason, their supplication has been made one of the causes of their reward with Paradise, even though there is in it a share for their own selves in the comfort of their eyes, since the share of the self does not conflict with the share of religion in their deeds.

This is like the statement of 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah when he was leaving for the Battle of Mu'tah, and the Muslims prayed for him and for those with him that God would return them safe. He said:

*But I ask the Merciful for forgiveness,*
*and for a striking blow with a wide wound that spews out foam,*

*or a thrust by the hands of a man from Harran, a deadly one,*
*with a spear that pierces the entrails and the liver,*

*so that when they pass by my grave they will say:*
*"May God guide you, O warrior, for you have been guided."*

In his saying "so that they will say," there is a share for his self in good remembrance, even though in it is a supplication for him to be guided, and this too is a religious share. His saying "for you have been guided" is pure good remembrance. In the *al-Jami'* of *al-'Utbiyyah*, from the *Ahadith* of Ibn Wahb, Malik said: "I saw a man asking Rabi'ah, saying: 'I truly love to be seen going to the mosque.'" It seems that Malik disliked his statement and did not approve of anyone loving to be seen in any of the acts of goodness. Ibn Rushd said in his commentary: "This is contrary to Malik's view in the *Rasm al-'Uqul* from the *Sama'* of Ashhab, in the Book of Prayer, that there is no harm in that provided its initial intention is for God, i.e., the primary aim of the act is for God." Ibn Rushd also said in another place in his commentary: God the Exalted said: (﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39]), and He said: (﴿And grant me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 84]). Al-Shatibi said in *al-Muwafaqat*: Malik counted that among the category of *waswasah* (the whisperings of Satan), meaning that Satan remains with a person: when the sight of people praising him for goodness pleases him, Satan says to him, "You are indeed a show-off." That is not the case; rather, it is a matter that occurs in the heart and cannot be controlled.

In *al-Mi'yar*, from the book *Siraj al-Muridin* of Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, he said: "I asked our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Shirazi, the Sufi, about the saying of God the Exalted: (﴿except those who repent, make amends, and make clear﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 160]). What is 'made clear'? He said: 'They display their deeds to people through righteousness and acts of obedience.'"

Al-Shatibi said: This point is a place of disagreement if the aforementioned intention follows the intention of worship. Al-Ghazali committed himself, in this and similar matters, to holding that they are outside of *ikhlas* (sincerity), but on condition that the act becomes lighter for him because of these purposes. As for Ibn al-'Arabi, he took a view contrary to that, and it seems that the field of consideration turns toward the separability of the two intentions. Moreover, the view that the separation is valid in cases where separation is valid is more correct, due to what has come in the evidences concerning that, and so on to its end.

[Page 83]

The *min* in His saying (﴿from our spouses﴾) is for the beginning (of the source), meaning: grant us comfort to our eyes that arises from our spouses and our offspring.

The majority of readers recited (*wa-dhurriyyatina*, "and our offspring") as the plural of *dhurriyyah*. The plural refers to the groups of those who make this supplication, since one of the supplicants might have only one child. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Ya'qub, and Khalaf recited (*dhurriyyatina*) without an alif after the *ya'* (i.e., in the singular form). The meaning of plurality is derived from the attachment to the pronoun of (those who say), meaning: the offspring of each one of them.

"The eyes" refers to the eyes of those who supplicate, i.e., the comfort of our eyes. Since the supplication was issued by all of them, this requires that they desire the comfort of the eyes of all of them.

Just as they asked for success and good for their spouses and their offspring, they asked for themselves, after God had guided them to faith, that He make them an exemplar (*qudwah*) whom the God-conscious would follow. This requires that they ask for themselves to attain the great ranks of God-consciousness, for an exemplar must reach the utmost limit of the work in which those who are concerned seek perfection. It also requires that they ask to be callers to entry into Islam and that people be guided to it through them.

The root meaning of *imam* is the model and mould upon which something is made in its shape, and made from its like. Al-Nabighah said:

*His father before him, and his father's father,*
*built the glory of life upon an imam.*

The term *imam* was applied to an exemplar by way of comparison to the model and mould, and this usage became dominant, so *imam* came to mean exemplar. This has already been discussed in His saying (﴿Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 124]) in Surah al-Baqarah. The predicate "imaman" is given in the singular while the subject is in the plural pronoun form (of "we"), because what is intended is that each one of them be an imam who is followed; so the statement is distributive. Or it is meant that *imam* carries its literal meaning and the speech proceeds by way of an eloquent metaphor. It has also been said that *imam* is a plural, like *hijan* and *siyam*, and its singular is *imm*.

[Page 84]

﴿Those will be rewarded with the high chamber for what they endured patiently, and they will be met therein with greetings and peace.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein forever; how excellent it is as a place of settlement and dwelling.﴾

The introduction with the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) is to alert the listener that what follows is what they deserved because of what was mentioned before the demonstrative. Together these make eleven qualities: humility, forbearance, night prayer, fear (of Allah), avoiding extravagance, avoiding stinginess, keeping oneself free from shirk, avoiding fornication, avoiding killing a soul, repentance, avoiding lying, pardoning the one who wrongs them, accepting the call to the truth, and expressing their need for Allah through supplication. The demonstrative refers back to the statement ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 63], as was mentioned earlier, according to the more probable of the two opinions.

The ghurfa (chamber) is an elevated house reached by stairs, and it is a more honoured dwelling than a ground-floor house. The definite article in "al-ghurfa" is the generic definite (ta'rif al-jins), which applies equally to the singular and the plural, like His saying ﴿And We sent down with them the Book﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. So the meaning is: they will be rewarded with chambers (ghuraf), that is, from Paradise. He, may He be exalted, said ﴿And they will be secure in the chambers﴾ [Saba': 37]. The ba' (in bima sabaru) indicates causation (sababiyya), and "ma" in His saying "bima sabaru" is a verbal ma (ma masdariyya), meaning: because of their patience. This patience is their patience in bearing the harm they suffered from the polytheists, their patience in restraining their desires for the sake of upholding the laws of Islam, and their patience in the hardship of acts of worship.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa yulaqqawna" with a dammah on the ya', a fathah on the lam, and a shaddah on the qaf with a fathah, the imperfect of laqqahu, meaning when one makes him meet (laqiyan). Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Khalaf read "wa yalqawna" with a fathah on the ya', a sukun on the lam, and a lightened qaf with a fathah, the imperfect of laqiya. Al-luqiyy and al-liqa' mean encountering something and coming upon it. This was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿And fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqara: 223] in Surat al-Baqara, and in His saying ﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve in battle array﴾ [al-Anfal: 15] in Surat al-Anfal. Earlier His saying was also mentioned: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68].

The word luqiyy has been used metaphorically (isti'ara) for hearing greetings and peace, meaning that they hear this in Paradise without encountering any harm, and without any harm reaching them. Rather, they come upon greetings of honour and praise, like the greetings of great people and kings, which poets and reciters recite.

[Page 85]

It is also permissible that the use of luqiyy for hearing the words of greeting and peace is intended to hint that they hear the greeting from the angels who meet them with it. This is then a metonymy by ellipsis (majaz bil-hadhf). He, may He be exalted, said ﴿And the angels will receive them, saying: This is your day which you were promised﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103] in Surat al-Anbiya'.

His saying ﴿how excellent it is as a place of settlement and dwelling﴾ is the opposite of what was said about the polytheists: ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a place of settlement and dwelling﴾ [al-Furqan: 66]. Greeting (tahiyya) was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting﴾ [al-Nisa': 86] in Surat al-Nisa', in His saying ﴿And their greeting therein will be peace﴾ [Yunus: 10] in Surat Yunus, and in His saying ﴿A greeting from Allah, blessed and good﴾ [al-Nur: 61] at the end of Surat al-Nur.

[Page 84]

﴿Those will be rewarded with the high chamber for what they endured patiently, and they will be met therein with greetings and peace.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein forever; how excellent it is as a place of settlement and dwelling.﴾

The introduction with the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) is to alert the listener that what follows is what they deserved because of what was mentioned before the demonstrative. Together these make eleven qualities: humility, forbearance, night prayer, fear (of Allah), avoiding extravagance, avoiding stinginess, keeping oneself free from shirk, avoiding fornication, avoiding killing a soul, repentance, avoiding lying, pardoning the one who wrongs them, accepting the call to the truth, and expressing their need for Allah through supplication. The demonstrative refers back to the statement ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 63], as was mentioned earlier, according to the more probable of the two opinions.

The ghurfa (chamber) is an elevated house reached by stairs, and it is a more honoured dwelling than a ground-floor house. The definite article in "al-ghurfa" is the generic definite (ta'rif al-jins), which applies equally to the singular and the plural, like His saying ﴿And We sent down with them the Book﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. So the meaning is: they will be rewarded with chambers (ghuraf), that is, from Paradise. He, may He be exalted, said ﴿And they will be secure in the chambers﴾ [Saba': 37]. The ba' (in bima sabaru) indicates causation (sababiyya), and "ma" in His saying "bima sabaru" is a verbal ma (ma masdariyya), meaning: because of their patience. This patience is their patience in bearing the harm they suffered from the polytheists, their patience in restraining their desires for the sake of upholding the laws of Islam, and their patience in the hardship of acts of worship.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa yulaqqawna" with a dammah on the ya', a fathah on the lam, and a shaddah on the qaf with a fathah, the imperfect of laqqahu, meaning when one makes him meet (laqiyan). Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Khalaf read "wa yalqawna" with a fathah on the ya', a sukun on the lam, and a lightened qaf with a fathah, the imperfect of laqiya. Al-luqiyy and al-liqa' mean encountering something and coming upon it. This was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿And fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqara: 223] in Surat al-Baqara, and in His saying ﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve in battle array﴾ [al-Anfal: 15] in Surat al-Anfal. Earlier His saying was also mentioned: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68].

The word luqiyy has been used metaphorically (isti'ara) for hearing greetings and peace, meaning that they hear this in Paradise without encountering any harm, and without any harm reaching them. Rather, they come upon greetings of honour and praise, like the greetings of great people and kings, which poets and reciters recite.

[Page 85]

It is also permissible that the use of luqiyy for hearing the words of greeting and peace is intended to hint that they hear the greeting from the angels who meet them with it. This is then a metonymy by ellipsis (majaz bil-hadhf). He, may He be exalted, said ﴿And the angels will receive them, saying: This is your day which you were promised﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103] in Surat al-Anbiya'.

His saying ﴿how excellent it is as a place of settlement and dwelling﴾ is the opposite of what was said about the polytheists: ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a place of settlement and dwelling﴾ [al-Furqan: 66]. Greeting (tahiyya) was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting﴾ [al-Nisa': 86] in Surat al-Nisa', in His saying ﴿And their greeting therein will be peace﴾ [Yunus: 10] in Surat Yunus, and in His saying ﴿A greeting from Allah, blessed and good﴾ [al-Nur: 61] at the end of Surat al-Nur.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 25, verse 77:

﴿Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your calling [upon Him]. But you have denied, so the punishment will be inevitable.﴾

When the surah had fully covered the aims of affirming the Messenger and the Qur'an, and what it contains of the Oneness of God, the arrogance of the stubborn deniers and their excuses, and the states of the believers, and when the decisive proofs had been established against those who turn away, it was concluded with God's command to His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to address the polytheists with a comprehensive statement by which their delusion and self-admiration would be removed. They had reckoned that they had quenched their rage against the Messenger by turning away from his call and by their persistent wrangling with him. So He made clear to them their insignificance before God, the Exalted, and that He had sent His Messenger to them and addressed them with His Book only out of mercy towards them, to set their condition right and to cut off their excuse. Since they denied, the punishment will befall them.

The "mā" in His words "mā ya'ba'u" is a negation particle. The construction "mā ya'ba'u bihi" indicates belittling, while its opposite, "'abā'a bihi," conveys esteem.

The meaning of "mā ya'ba'u" is: he does not mind and does not concern himself. It is the present tense of 'abā'a, on the pattern of malā'a (to fill), derived from the root al-'ib' (with a kasra on the 'ayn), which is the load (al-ḥiml, with a kasra on the ḥā' and a sukūn on the mīm), that is, the heavy thing that is loaded onto a camel. For this reason al-'ib' is also applied to a saddlebag (al-'idl, with a kasra and sukūn). Many other usages then branched out from this. The original sense of "mā ya'ba'u" is therefore "what does not bear a burden," as an image drawn from the state of one who is wearied by something; thus the intended meaning became "does not concern himself and does not care," which is a metonymy for little regard.

The "bā'" in it indicates causation, that is, "because of you." It involves the omission of a modifier, which the context indicates. So the implied meaning here is: "he does not care for your address."

Al-du'ā' means calling to something. Here it is grammatically a noun with its object as the genitive complement, and the subject is indicated by "my Lord." That is, "were it not for His calling you," meaning "were it not that He calls you." The object of the calling is omitted because it is evident from His words "but you have denied," namely, the one who calls, who is Muhammad (ﷺ). Thus it is determined that the calling is the invitation to Islam. The meaning is that God gains nothing from it and is not strengthened by you. This is like His statement, the Exalted: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me. I do not want provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me.﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56].

The pronoun of address in His words "du'ā'ukum" (your calling) is directed at the polytheists, as evidenced by the consequence stated after it, "but you have denied," which is a threat to them. That is: you have denied the caller, who is the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. This interpretation is what the meaning requires, and it is supported by the statements of Mujahid, al-Kalbi and al-Farra'. Some exegetes interpreted the calling as worship and made the address directed at the Muslims, and this interpretation entailed artificial constructions. Adhering to the correct meaning has made it unnecessary to address them. Whoever wishes may consider them carefully, so that he will know that there is no reason for them.

The consequence "but you have denied" follows His words "were it not for your calling." The implied meaning is: He has called you to Islam, but you denied the One who called you through His tongue.

The pronoun in "yakūnu" (it will be) refers back to the denial derived from "you have denied." That is: their denial will be lizām for you, meaning inseparable from you, with no escape from it. This is a threat of the consequences of denial, phrased in an awe-inspiring manner through its vagueness, just as you say to a criminal: "You have done such-and-such, so you will bear what you did." This threat includes what will befall them in this world, such as killing, captivity and defeat, and what will befall them in the Hereafter, namely punishment.

Al-lizām is a verbal noun of lāzama (to cling to), and it is formed on the pattern of mufā'ala to convey adherence, that is, not separating. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been lizām﴾ [Ta-Ha: 129] in Surah Ta-Ha. The hidden pronoun in "kāna" (it would have been) refers to the punishment of the Hereafter in His words: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting﴾ [Ta-Ha: 127]. Thus, reporting it as lizām is from the category of reporting by the verbal noun for emphasis. In it two kinds of emphasis are combined: emphasis in its form, which conveys the strength of its adherence, and emphasis in reporting it, which conveys the certainty of the attribute's establishment.

From Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b: al-lizām is the punishment of the Day of Badr. Their meaning by this is that it is a particular instance among the particulars of the lizām promised to them. Perhaps this became widespread until lizām became almost a proper name, by dominance, for the Day of Badr. In the Sahih, from Ibn Mas'ud: "Five have passed: the smoke, the moon, the Romans, the assault, and the lizām." He means that lizām is other than the punishment of the Hereafter.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
Surah al-Shu'ara'

It was known among the early generations as Surah al-Shu'ara' (The Poets), because it is unique among the surahs of the Qur'an in mentioning the word "al-shu'ara'." Likewise, this is how it is named in the books of Sunnah. It is also called Surat Ta-Sin-Mim.

In Ibn al-'Arabi's Ahkam, it is also called al-Jami'ah (The Comprehensive). Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti in al-Itqan attributed this to the tafsir of Malik, as transmitted from him. The reason for describing it by this description has not become clear. Perhaps it is the first surah that gathered the mention of the messengers who brought known laws, together with the Muhammadan message.

It is Meccan. It has been said that all of it is Meccan, and this is what is transmitted from Ibn al-Zubayr, and a narration from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn 'Atiyyah attributed it to the majority. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And the poets, the misguided follow them﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 224] to the end of the surah, was revealed at Medina, concerning the poets of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): Hassan ibn Thabit, Ibn Rawahah, and Ka'b ibn Malik. They are the ones referred to in His statement: ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 227], and so on. Perhaps this verse is what led these people to say that those verses are Medinan. From al-Dani: he said, "The verse ﴿And the poets, the misguided follow them﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 224] was revealed concerning two poets who satirized each other in the pre-Islamic period."

I say: There were poets in Mecca who satirized the Prophet (ﷺ), among them al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, al-'Awra' bint Harb, the wife of Abu Lahab, and others like them, and they are the ones intended by the verses: ﴿And the poets, the misguided follow them﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 224]. The poets of Medina had embraced Islam before the Hijrah, and there were Muslim poets in Mecca among those who emigrated to Abyssinia, as will come later.

From Muqatil: His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 197] was revealed at Medina. What led him to this is that the association with the scholars of the Children of Israel took place after the Hijrah. But it is not hidden that the proof does not depend on the occurrence of association with the scholars of the Children of Israel. The Qur'an has mentioned this same proof in verses revealed at Mecca. Among them is His statement: ﴿Say: Sufficient is God as witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43], in Surat al-Ra'd, which is Meccan; and His statement: ﴿Those whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾ [al-Qasas: 52], in Surat al-Qasas, which is Meccan; and His statement: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you the Book, and those whom We gave the Book believe in it﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 47], in Surat al-'Ankabut, which is Meccan. The condition of the scholars of the Children of Israel was well known in Mecca, and the people of Mecca had connections with the Jews of Medina and consultation between them concerning the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), as was mentioned earlier at His statement: ﴿And they ask you about the soul﴾ [al-Isra': 85] in Surat al-Isra'. Therefore, what we are certain of is that the entire surah is Meccan.

It is the forty-seventh surah in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Surat al-Waqi'ah and before Surat al-Naml. In the commentary on His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And warn your closest kinsmen﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 214], there will come what indicates that this verse was revealed before the revelation of Surat Abi Lahab, and we will address the possibility of reconciling the statements.

The people of Medina, the people of Mecca, and the people of Basra counted its verses as two hundred and twenty-six, while the people of Syria and the people of Kufa counted them as two hundred and twenty-seven.

* * *

The aims that the surah includes:

The first of them is the affirmation of the Qur'an, and an allusion to their inability to produce its equal, and consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding what he encounters from his people's turning away from the Oneness that the Qur'an called them to.

Within this is a warning to them against exposing themselves to the anger of God, the Exalted, and the presentation of examples to them of what befell the nations that denied their messengers and turned away from the signs of God.

I reckon that it was revealed following the request of the polytheists that the Messenger bring them miracles. So it opens with consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), affirmation for him, and steadying of his heart, by showing that what he encounters from his people is the custom of the messengers before him with their peoples, such as Moses, Abraham, Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb. Therefore every argument brought against the polytheists who denied was concluded with one single appendix, namely His statement: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 158] and ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 9]. This is a recording against them that the signs of Oneness and the truthfulness of the messengers are numerous and sufficient for whoever seeks the truth, but most of the polytheists do not believe; and that God is Mighty, able to bring punishment upon them, and that He is Merciful to His messengers, so He supports them against their enemies.

Al-Kashshaf says: Each story among the stories mentioned in this surah is like a separate revelation. In it there is the same lesson as in others, so each of them has the right to end with what its companion ended with. And because repetition establishes the meanings in souls, and the more it is repeated the more firmly it settles in the heart, the more deeply it is grasped and the further from forgetting. And because these stories have struck ears that were deafened to listening to the truth, they were reinforced with exhortation and reminder and were repeated with reiteration and recurrence, perhaps that will open an ear or unlock a mind. End of quote.

Then the affirmation of the Qur'an, the testimony of the People of the Book to it, the response to their accusations against the Qur'an and their description of it as 'idin (fragments), and that it is exalted above being poetry or the words of devils, the command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to warn his closest kin, that the Messenger has no duty except conveyance, and what lies between these in the way of proofs.
